knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minkowski addition and scalar multiplication of sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\) be subsets of a real vector space \(E\), let \(a\in E\), and let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic set addition and scalar multiplication; convexity preservation is included, but closedness preservation is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski sum and scalar image are \[C+D:=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\},\qquad \alpha C:=\{\alpha c:c\in C\}.\] More generally, \[\alpha C+\beta D:=\{\alpha c+\beta d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}.\] Translation is the special case \(C+a=C+\{a\}\), and reflection is \(-C=(-1)C\). Minkowski addition is associative and commutative, with \(C+\{0\}=C\). If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, then \(\alpha C+\beta D\) is convex for all real \(\alpha,\beta\). For a convex \(C\) and nonnegative \(\alpha,\beta\), \[\alpha C+\beta C=(\alpha+\beta)C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski sum C+D contains every sum c+d with c in C and d in D. Scalar multiplication applies the scalar to every point of a set, and weighted set sums combine these operations. Translation, reflection, and dilation are special cases. Minkowski addition is associative and commutative, and weighted sums of convex sets are convex. For one convex set and nonnegative weights, alpha C plus beta C equals (alpha+beta)C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C,D\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \alpha C+\beta D\text{ convex}\), and for convex \(C\) with \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\), \(\alpha C+\beta C=(\alpha+\beta)C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C+D\) is the image of \(C\times D\) under the linear addition map \((c,d)\mapsto c+d\).
\(x\in C+D\iff C\cap(x-D)\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: \(C+\{a\}=C+a\) is translation by \(a\).
\(0C=\{0\}\) when \(C\neq\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite Minkowski sums of convex sets are convex.
For convex \(C\), \(\theta C+(1-\theta)C=C\) whenever \(0\leq\theta\leq1\).
boundary_notes: Minkowski subtraction is not generally an inverse to Minkowski addition.
The sum of two closed convex sets need not be closed unless additional hypotheses hold.

notation.meaning: reflection of C through the origin

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of a Fiberwise Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity under addition of fibers sharing the same first coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m+p}\) be convex, and define
\[
C=\left\{(y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^p:\exists z_1,z_2\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ (y,z_1)\in C_1,\ (y,z_2)\in C_2,\ z_1+z_2=z\right\}.
\]
Then \(C\) is convex in \(\mathbb{R}^{m+p}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two convex sets in coordinates (y,z), retaining a common y-coordinate and adding the corresponding z-coordinates produces another convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Summand Closedness Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a compact set to a closed set preserves closedness in finite dimensions, and a sum of compact sets is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(C\) is closed and \(D\) is compact, then \(C+D\) is closed. If both sets are compact, then \(C+D\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C+D\text{ is closed};\qquad C,D\text{ compact}\Longrightarrow C+D\text{ compact}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional topological guarantee; two merely closed summands need not have a closed sum.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Laws of Minkowski Addition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition is commutative and associative, has the zero singleton as identity and the empty set as an absorbing element, and addition of a singleton is translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(A,B,C\) of a real vector space, \(A+B=B+A\), \((A+B)+C=A+(B+C)\), \(A+\{0\}=A\), and \(A+\varnothing=\varnothing\). For every \(a\), \(A+\{a\}=\{x+a:x\in A\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(A,B,C\) are subsets of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure set-addition laws, including empty-set and singleton behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski sum consists of all pairwise sums of one point from each set. The Minkowski sum of two convex sets is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(C,D\subseteq X\). The Minkowski sum of \(C\) and \(D\) is \[C+D:=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}.\] If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, then \(C+D\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(C,D\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Their Minkowski sum is \(C+D=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}\). If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, then \(C+D\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary Minkowski addition of subsets of a common real vector space.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of C and D

knowledge_statements.title: Composition and Invertibility of Set Scaling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set scaling composes multiplicatively; nonzero scaling is invertible, negative-one scaling reflects, and zero scaling distinguishes nonempty sets from the empty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every subset \(C\) of a real vector space and scalars \(\lambda,\mu\), \(\lambda(\mu C)=(\lambda\mu)C\), \(1C=C\), and \((-1)C=-C\). If \(\lambda\ne0\), scaling by \(\lambda\) is bijective with inverse scaling by \(1/\lambda\). If \(\lambda=0\), then \(0C=\{0\}\) for \(C\ne\varnothing\), whereas \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the exceptional zero and empty-set regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Invariance Under Nonzero Scaling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonzero scalar multiplication preserves standard topological properties and commutes with closure and relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda\ne0\), then \(x\mapsto\lambda x\) is a homeomorphism. Hence \(C\) is closed, open, bounded, or compact if and only if \(\lambda C\) has the corresponding property. Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}(\lambda C)=\lambda\operatorname{cl}C\), and for convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{ri}(\lambda C)=\lambda\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional topology; zero scaling is excluded because it collapses nonempty sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Multiples of Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar multiple of a set contains all scalar multiples of its points. Scalar multiplication preserves convexity, with a nonempty set collapsing to the origin when the scalar is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\), and let \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). The scalar multiple of \(C\) by \(\lambda\) is \[\lambda C:=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}.\] If \(C\) is convex, then \(\lambda C\) is convex. In particular, if \(C\neq\varnothing\), then \(0C=\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space, \(C\subseteq X\), and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scalar multiple is \(\lambda C=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}\). If \(C\) is convex, then \(\lambda C\) is convex, including the regime \(\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar multiplication is the image of a set under the linear map \(x\mapsto\lambda x\).

notation.meaning: Scalar multiple of the set C

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Weights Do Not Suppress Empty Summands
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the literal selection-based definition, an empty component makes the weighted combination empty even when its weight is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i=\{\sum_i\lambda_ic_i:c_i\in C_i\text{ for every }i\}\), the combination is empty whenever any \(C_i\) is empty, even if its coefficient is zero. Deleting zero-weight indices is therefore valid only when their sets are nonempty, or under a different explicit zero-term convention.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge1\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(C_i\) are subsets of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the seed's literal point-selection definition and the convention \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Idempotence of Normalized Minkowski Averaging
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized weighted Minkowski average of copies of the same nonempty convex set equals that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space and let \(\lambda_i\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\). Then \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC=C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All component sets coincide; this is the set-valued form of closure under convex combinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Minkowski Combinations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted Minkowski combination consists of weighted sums formed by selecting one point from each set. It is convex when all the component sets are convex; normalized weights make each such sum a convex combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be convex subsets of a real vector space \(X\), and let \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0\). Their weighted Minkowski combination has the representation \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i c_i:c_i\in C_i\text{ for every }i\right\}.\] This set is convex. If additionally \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), each represented point is a convex combination of selected points \(c_i\in C_i\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space, \(m\geq1\), \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq X\) are convex, and \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted Minkowski combination \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i=\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i c_i:c_i\in C_i\}\) is convex. If \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), every represented point is a convex combination with its \(i\)-th point selected from \(C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative weighted sums of convex sets; normalization of the weights is required only for the convex-combination interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex hull of a set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic convex hull formed by finite convex combinations; closure is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex hull of \(S\) is the smallest convex subset of \(E\) containing \(S\): \[\operatorname{conv}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq E:S\subseteq C,\ C\text{ convex}\}.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i:m\geq1,\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Thus \(S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\), the set \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is convex, and for every convex \(C\) with \(S\subseteq C\), one has \(\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a nonempty set S is the intersection of all convex sets containing S. It is equivalently the set of all finite convex combinations of points of S. It contains S, is convex, and is contained in every convex set that contains S. The definition is algebraic and does not automatically take a topological closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is the unique smallest convex set containing \(S\), and it equals the set of all finite convex combinations from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) iff there exist finitely many \(s_i\in S\) and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i\).
\(S\) is convex iff \(S=\operatorname{conv}S\).
special_cases_latex: For two points, \(\operatorname{conv}\{x,y\}=\{\theta x+(1-\theta)y:0\leq\theta\leq1\}\).
For a finite set \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), its hull is \(\{\sum_i\lambda_i x_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull formation is monotone: \(S\subseteq T\Rightarrow\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}T\).
Convex-hull formation is idempotent: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{conv}S\).
boundary_notes: A convex hull need not be closed when the generating set is unbounded.
The closed convex hull is \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\), a distinct object.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Hull Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a nonempty set consists exactly of all convex combinations of finitely many points from that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty subset of a real vector space \(X\). Its convex hull is exactly the set of all finite convex combinations of points of \(S\): \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\bigcup_{m\geq1}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i:s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] For the empty set, adopt the convention \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(S\neq\varnothing\), \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\bigcup_{m\geq1}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i:s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Under the convention \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\), the representation also covers the empty-set case separately.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The representation uses arbitrary finite support; no finite-dimensional bound on the support size is asserted.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative coefficient in a finite convex combination

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability-Simplex Representation of a Finite Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(X=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_m]\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and define \(\Delta_m:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\lambda\geq0,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generator lists in Euclidean space; repetitions and redundant generators are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite convex hull is
\[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m\right\}=X\Delta_m.\]
Consequently,
\[x\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\iff\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\ X\lambda=x,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1,\ \lambda\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) is the linear image \(X\Delta_m\) of the probability simplex. Thus membership is equivalent to feasibility of \(X\lambda=x\), \(\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\), and \(\lambda\geq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\{X\lambda:\lambda\in\Delta_m\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), \(x=\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\) with \(0\leq\lambda\leq1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite convex hull is a bounded polyhedron, hence a polytope.
boundary_notes: The coefficient vector need not be unique when the generators are affinely dependent.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the generators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex representation of a finite convex hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(m\geq1\), and let \(M=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hulls of a prescribed finite list; redundant or repeated generators are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite hull representation of \(X\) is \[\operatorname{conv}X=\left\{M\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\right\}=M\Delta_m.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{conv}X\) exactly when the linear system \[M\lambda=x,\qquad \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1,\qquad \lambda\geq0\] has a solution. Any feasible \(\lambda\) is a barycentric or convex-coordinate representation of \(x\) relative to the listed generators. Its support \(\{i:\lambda_i>0\}\) records the active generators, but neither the coefficients nor their support need be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many points collected as the columns of M, their convex hull is the image of the standard simplex under the map lambda to M lambda. A point x belongs to the hull exactly when there is a nonnegative coefficient vector lambda summing to one and satisfying M lambda=x. Such a coefficient vector gives convex coordinates; redundant generators can make this representation nonunique.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}X=M\Delta_m\).
The finite hull is the affine image of the coefficient simplex under \(\lambda\mapsto M\lambda\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), the coefficient simplex yields the line segment between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).
If \(x_1,,x_m\) are affinely independent, every point of their affine hull has unique affine coordinates and every point of their convex hull has unique convex coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite convex-hull membership is a linear feasibility problem in the coefficient vector.
The hull of finitely many points is compact because it is the continuous image of the compact simplex \(\Delta_m\).
boundary_notes: Uniqueness fails when the generators are affinely dependent.
This representation does not say that all listed points are necessary; zero coefficients may remove generators.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the hull generators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull and Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), equipped with its usual topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean closure; the distinction between algebraic convex hull and closed convex hull is explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The algebraic convex hull is
\[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\}.\]
The closed convex hull is
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^n:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\]
These regimes are related by
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S,\]
with equality exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary convex hull of \(S\) consists of its finite convex combinations. The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed convex sets containing \(S\). In Euclidean space it equals the closure of the ordinary convex hull. Thus the two regimes coincide precisely when the convex hull is already closed; otherwise the closed hull adds limit points.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{cl}S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
The closed convex hull is the unique smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is compact in \(\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and hence \(\operatorname{conv}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\).
For a finite set \(S\), its convex hull is a compact polytope and is closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Both hull operations are monotone and idempotent.
Closing first does not change the closed convex hull, although it can change the ordinary convex hull.
boundary_notes: A closed but unbounded set can have a nonclosed convex hull, so closedness of \(S\) alone is insufficient.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the closure depends on the chosen topology; this record uses the Euclidean topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic and closed convex hulls
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and let \(\operatorname{cl}\) denote Euclidean closure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean topology; algebraic convexification is distinguished from closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algebraic convex hull is \(\operatorname{conv}S\), the set of finite convex combinations from \(S\). The closed convex hull is \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:S\subseteq C,\ C\text{ closed and convex}\}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S).\] Hence \[S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S.\] The two hulls coincide exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed. In particular, if \(S\) is compact, then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and therefore closed, so no additional closure is needed. A closed but unbounded generating set may nevertheless have a nonclosed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algebraic convex hull consists of finite convex combinations. The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed convex sets containing S, equivalently the Euclidean closure of the algebraic convex hull. They coincide precisely when the algebraic hull is closed. Compact generating sets have compact, hence closed, convex hulls, while closed unbounded sets can fail to have closed convex hulls.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
\(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{cl}S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{conv}S)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is finite, then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and equals its closed convex hull.
If \(S\) is compact, \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed-convex-hull formation is monotone and idempotent.
Limits of sequences of finite convex combinations belong to \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\), even when they do not belong to \(\operatorname{conv}S\).
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(S\) alone does not guarantee closedness of \(\operatorname{conv}S\).
In infinite-dimensional spaces, compactness and closure behavior require additional care and are outside this scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull Operator Laws
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex hull is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and its fixed points are exactly the convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(A,B\) of a real vector space \(X\), \[A\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(A),\qquad A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow\operatorname{conv}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(B),\qquad \operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{conv}(A))=\operatorname{conv}(A).\] Moreover, \(A\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}(A)=A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(A\mapsto\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is a closure operator whose fixed points are precisely the convex subsets of \(X\).

The convex hull of \(S\) is defined by \[\operatorname{conv}(S):=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is the unique smallest convex subset of \(X\) containing \(S\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convex-Hull Operator Laws
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex hull is an extensive, monotone, idempotent operator whose fixed points are the closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(S,T\) of a Hausdorff topological real vector space, \[S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S),\qquad S\subseteq T\implies\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(T),\] and \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\bigr)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S).\] Moreover, \(S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\) exactly when \(S\) is closed and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(S,T\) are subsets of a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\) is a closure operator with fixed points equal to the closed convex subsets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are the closure-operator properties of closed convex generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Net Representation of the Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed convex hull exactly when it is a limit of finite convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\). A point \(x\in X\) belongs to \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\) if and only if there exists a net \((x_\alpha)\) in \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) converging to \(x\). Equivalently, every \(x_\alpha\) is a finite convex combination of points of \(S\). If \(X\) is first countable, the net may be replaced by a sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequences suffice in first-countable spaces, including normed spaces; general topological vector spaces may require nets.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is the smallest closed convex set containing the original set, and it equals the closure of the ordinary convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological real vector space and let \(S\subseteq X\). The closed convex hull of \(S\) is defined by \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S):=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\] Since the closure of a convex set in a topological vector space is convex, \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S)).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed convex hull satisfies \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S)).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and closure refer to the given topology on the ambient vector space.

knowledge_statements.title: A Closed Planar Set with Nonclosed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed unbounded planar set can have a nonclosed convex hull: adjoining the origin to the epigraph of 1/x yields the open positive quadrant together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq x^{-1}\},\qquad S:=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(S\) is closed, while \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(u,v):u>0,\ v>0\}.\] Consequently \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed; for example, \((1,n^{-1})\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) converges to \((1,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is closed but \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup(0,\infty)^2\) is not closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space example shows that finite convex-combination generation need not produce a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2\) with its norm topology, let \((e_n)_{n\geq1}\) be its standard orthonormal basis, and set \(S:=\{e_n:n\geq1\}\). For \(N\geq1\), define \[x_N:=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N e_n.\] Then \(x_N\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) and \(\|x_N\|_2=N^{-1/2}\to0\), so \(0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))\). Every element of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is a finite nonnegative combination of the \(e_n\) whose coefficients sum to \(1\), so it is nonzero. Thus \[0\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{conv}(S)\neq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences, the convex hull of the standard unit vectors is not closed. Uniform averages of the first N unit vectors lie in the hull and converge to zero, but zero itself is not a finite convex combination of those vectors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex and Conic Carathéodory Witnesses
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. Define \(\operatorname{cone}S\) as the set of finite nonnegative combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional convex and conic representation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex Carathéodory witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) is a representation
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n+1,\quad x_i\in S,\quad \lambda_i\geq0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1.\]
For nonzero \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\), a conic Carathéodory witness is a representation
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i x_i,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n,\quad x_i\in S,\quad \mu_i>0,\]
where the selected vectors may be chosen linearly independent. Carathéodory's theorem asserts that every point in the respective hull possesses such a witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) has a convex representation using at most \(n+1\) points of \(S\). Every nonzero point of \(\operatorname{cone}S\) has a positive representation using at most \(n\) linearly independent vectors of \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\1\leq |T|\leq n+1}}\operatorname{conv}T.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull and nonzero conic-hull membership in finite dimensions admit exact certificates whose support is bounded by dimension.
boundary_notes: The conic statement treats \(x=0\) separately; the zero vector is represented by the empty sum or by zero coefficients.
These are exact representation results, not approximation bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Carathéodory witness number and its principal regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. For \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\), a convex witness is a finite tuple \((x_i,\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m\) with \(x_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex and conic support bounds; the record defines the family of witness regimes rather than supplying a proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Carathéodory number of \(S\) is \[c(S):=\min\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}:\text{every }x\in\operatorname{conv}S\text{ has a convex witness using at most }k\text{ points of }S\right\}.\] The classical ambient-dimensional regime asserts \(c(S)\leq n+1\). If \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\), the intrinsic affine-dimensional regime asserts \(c(S)\leq d+1\). For conic generation, a conic witness for \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\) is \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i x_i\) with \(\mu_i\geq0\); the corresponding finite-dimensional regime permits at most \(n\) linearly independent active generators for nonzero \(x\). These are the principal convex, intrinsic, and homogeneous members of the Carathéodory family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex witness represents a hull point using finitely many generators and nonnegative coefficients summing to one. The Carathéodory number is the smallest uniform bound on the number of generators needed for all hull points. In n-dimensional space the classical bound is n+1; if the generating set has affine dimension d, the intrinsic bound is d+1. The conic analogue drops normalization and bounds a nonzero conic representation by n linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family consists of the bounds \(c(S)\leq n+1\), \(c(S)\leq\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)+1\), and the conic bound of at most \(n\) linearly independent generators.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(c(S)\leq k\) iff every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) lies in the convex hull of some subset of \(S\) having at most \(k\) elements.
The intrinsic bound is the ambient theorem applied within the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}S\), whose dimension is \(d\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) lies on an affine line, then \(c(S)\leq2\).
If \(S\) is a singleton, then \(c(S)=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex-hull membership assertion in finite dimension has a uniformly sparse finite witness.
The supporting generators may depend on the represented point; the definition does not require one fixed generating subset for the whole hull.
boundary_notes: The coefficients and supporting points need not be unique.
For \(x=0\) in a conic hull, the empty or all-zero representation depends on convention; the stated conic independence form concerns nonzero \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Ambient-Dimension Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior point of a full-dimensional d-simplex needs all d+1 vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(d\geq0\), choose affinely independent \(v_0,\ldots,v_d\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_d\})\). No convex representation of \(x\) using these generators has fewer than \(d+1\) points. Hence the ambient Caratheodory bound \(d+1\) is best possible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness is uniform over all generating subsets of the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Caratheodory Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the convex hull of a subset of d-dimensional Euclidean space is a convex combination of at most d+1 points from that subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\). If \(x\in \operatorname{conv}(S)\), then there exist an integer \(m\le d+1\), points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge 0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist an integer \(m\le d+1\), points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge 0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the standard finite-dimensional Caratheodory theorem indexed by the ambient dimension, without assuming that the affine hull of the generating set is full-dimensional.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-Dimension Carathéodory Witness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional convex-hull witness bound indexed by the ambient dimension \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An ambient-dimension Carathéodory witness for \(x\) is a tuple
\[(m;x_1,\ldots,x_m;\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m)\]
such that
\[1\leq m\leq n+1,\qquad x_i\in S,\qquad \lambda_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1,\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i.\]
Carathéodory's theorem asserts that every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) has such a witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambient-dimension Carathéodory witness represents a point \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) as a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) points of \(S\). Every hull point has such a witness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x\in\operatorname{conv}S\ \exists m\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\},\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0:\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\1\leq |T|\leq n+1}}\operatorname{conv}T.\]
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), every hull point is a convex combination of at most two points of \(S\).
In \(\mathbb R^2\), every hull point belongs to the convex hull of at most three points of \(S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull membership in \(\mathbb R^n\) admits an exact certificate with at most \(n+1\) support points.
boundary_notes: The support may depend on \(x\); the theorem does not provide one fixed subset representing the entire hull.
The ambient bound may be sharpened when \(S\) lies in a lower-dimensional affine subspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-dimensional Carathéodory witness regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional regime indexed by the surrounding dimension n, whether or not S is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ambient-dimensional Carathéodory regime is the hull-membership witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq n+1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in S,\ \exists\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0:\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Zero coefficients may be deleted, so the active generators can be taken to have positive coefficients. Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{F\subseteq S\\1\leq |F|\leq n+1}}\operatorname{conv}F.\] The bound is uniform over all points of the hull but the witnessing subset \(F\) may vary with \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the ambient-dimensional Carathéodory regime, every point in the convex hull of a nonempty subset of R^n can be represented as a convex combination of at most n+1 points from that subset. Equivalently, the full convex hull is the union of the hulls of all subsets with at most n+1 elements. The supporting subset may depend on the point being represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) admits a convex-combination witness using at most \(n+1\) generators from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{F\subseteq S,\ 1\leq|F|\leq n+1}\operatorname{conv}F\).
Any initially finite convex representation can be replaced by one with support cardinality at most \(n+1\).
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}\), at most two generators are required.
In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), at most three generators are required.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull membership in fixed dimension has a bounded-size certificate independent of the cardinality of \(S\).
For compact \(S\), sequences in \(\operatorname{conv}S\) may be represented using a fixed maximum of \(n+1\) coefficient-generator pairs.
boundary_notes: The ambient bound can be reduced to \(d+1\) when \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S<n\).
The theorem does not provide one common subset of \(n+1\) generators for every point of the hull.

notation.meaning: cardinality of the finite witness subset F

children.title: Affine-Dimension Caratheodory Regime
children.top_down_role: Finite witnesses indexed by effective affine dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Affine-Dimension Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior point of an r-simplex needs all r+1 vertices, so the affine-dimensional bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(r\geq0\), let \(v_0,\ldots,v_r\) be affinely independent and let \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_r\})\). Every convex representation of \(x\) using these generators has all \(r+1\) coefficients positive. Thus the affine-dimensional Caratheodory bound \(r+1\) cannot be uniformly reduced.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is worst-case sharpness; particular points or generating sets may admit smaller supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dimension Caratheodory Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the affine hull of the generating set has dimension r, every point of its convex hull is a convex combination of at most r+1 affinely independent generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and set \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\). If \(x\in \operatorname{conv}(S)\), then there exist an integer \(m\le r+1\), affinely independent points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m>0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\), and let \(x\in \operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist an integer \(m\le r+1\), affinely independent points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m>0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the affine-dimension refinement of Caratheodory's theorem. Zero coefficients are omitted, so the retained coefficients are positive and the retained points may be chosen affinely independent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intrinsic affine-dimensional Carathéodory regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(d:=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic regime indexed by effective affine dimension d rather than ambient dimension n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-dimensional Carathéodory regime is the witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq d+1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in S,\ \exists\lambda_i\geq0:\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{F\subseteq S\\1\leq|F|\leq d+1}}\operatorname{conv}F.\] The dimension \(d\) is the dimension of the direction space parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}S\), so this formulation is invariant under affine embeddings and removes unused ambient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the affine hull of S has dimension d, every point in the convex hull of S is a convex combination of at most d+1 points of S. Equivalently, the hull is the union of the hulls of all subsets of size at most d+1. This intrinsic form can be sharper than the ambient n+1 bound and is unchanged by placing the same affine geometry in a larger surrounding space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) has a convex witness supported on at most \(d+1\) points, where \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{F\subseteq S,\ 1\leq|F|\leq d+1}\operatorname{conv}F\).
The bound is the ambient-dimensional Carathéodory bound computed in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(d=0\), \(S\) is contained in a singleton affine space and one generator suffices.
For \(d=1\), every hull point lies on a segment joining at most two points of \(S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Embedding \(S\) affinely into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space does not enlarge the intrinsic witness bound.
Any convex representation with more than \(d+1\) active generators can be replaced by a representation with at most \(d+1\) active generators.
boundary_notes: The number \(d+1\) is a universal upper bound and need not be the smallest possible bound for a particular set.
Affine dimension, not topological dimension of a nonconvex generating set, controls this regime.

notation.meaning: effective affine dimension of the generating set

children.title: Conic Caratheodory Regime
children.top_down_role: Finite generator reduction for conic hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Dependence-Elimination Algorithm
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear dependence determines a maximal coefficient step that preserves the represented vector and nonnegativity while deleting at least one generator; repetition produces independent support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\) with \(s_i\in S\) and \(\lambda_i>0\). If the active generators are linearly dependent, choose \(\beta\neq0\) with \(\sum_i\beta_i s_i=0\), changing its sign if necessary so that some \(\beta_i>0\). Set \[t=\min_{\beta_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\beta_i},\qquad \lambda_i'=\lambda_i-t\beta_i.\] Delete generators whose updated coefficient is zero and repeat while the active generators remain dependent. Every update preserves \(x\) and coefficient nonnegativity and removes at least one active generator; the procedure terminates with linearly independent positive support.
assumptions_latex: The active generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update preserves \(x\), keeps all coefficients nonnegative, removes at least one active generator, and finite repetition yields linearly independent positive support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the constructive finite-support reduction underlying conic Caratheodory; it specifies the coefficient update without duplicating the theorem statement.

notation.meaning: A nonzero coefficient vector witnessing linear dependence among the active generators.
The maximal dependence step preserving coefficient nonnegativity.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Span-Dimension Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the coordinate vectors requires all \(r\) coordinate rays, so the span-dimension bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\ge1\), let \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^r\) and \(x=e_1+\cdots+e_r\). Then \(\dim(\operatorname{span}S)=r\), and every representation \(x=\sum_{s\in S}\mu_s s\) with \(\mu_s\ge0\) has \(\mu_{e_i}=1\) for every \(i\). Thus every such representation has support size exactly \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every conic representation of \(x\) using generators from \(S\) has support size \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The coordinate-ray family establishes that the intrinsic generator bound is sharp.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Caratheodory Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Carathéodory theorem with an ambient-dimension support bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\in\mathbb N_0\), let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and suppose \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\). If \(x\ne0\), then there exist an integer \(m\) with \(1\le m\le d\), linearly independent points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m>0\) such that
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i s_i.
\]
If \(x=0\), the empty conic combination is a representation with support size zero. Thus every element of \(\operatorname{cone}S\) has a conic representation using at most \(d\) linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero point in a conic hull in Rᵈ can be generated by at most d linearly independent points with positive coefficients; zero has the empty representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) has a conic representation supported on at most \(d\) linearly independent elements of \(S\), with the empty representation used when \(x=0\).

notation.meaning: set of finite nonnegative linear combinations from S, including the empty combination for zero
positive conic coefficients in the nonzero case

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Carathéodory generator-reduction regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\setminus\{0\}\), where \(\operatorname{cone}S\) consists of finite nonnegative combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonzero conic representations; coefficients are nonnegative and are not normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic Carathéodory regime is the witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{cone}S\setminus\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq n,\ \exists s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S,\ \exists\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m>0:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i s_i,\] where the active generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) may be chosen linearly independent. More intrinsically, if \(r=\dim\operatorname{span}S\), then \(m\leq r\). Thus conic normalization removes the additional affine coordinate responsible for the \(n+1\) convex-hull bound: a nonzero conic point needs at most the dimension of the relevant linear span many active rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero point in the conic hull of a subset of R^n can be expressed as a positive combination of at most n generators from the set, and the active generators can be chosen linearly independent. If the generators span only an r-dimensional linear subspace, at most r are needed. Unlike a convex combination, the conic coefficients are not required to sum to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonzero \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\) has a positive representation using at most \(\dim\operatorname{span}S\leq n\) linearly independent generators from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}S=\bigcup\{\operatorname{cone}F:F\subseteq S,\ F\text{ linearly independent}\}\), with the origin included by convention.
Any conic representation with linearly dependent active generators can be replaced by one with fewer active generators.
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), every nonzero conic-hull point needs at most two linearly independent generators.
If \(S\) lies in a one-dimensional subspace, every nonzero conic-hull point uses one active generator whenever it is representable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonzero conic-hull membership has a certificate supported on at most \(n\) generators.
The selected positive generators determine a simplicial cone containing the represented point.
boundary_notes: The zero vector may be represented by all-zero coefficients; requiring strictly positive coefficients is therefore restricted to nonzero points.
The conic hull need not be closed, even when the generating set is compact.

notation.meaning: effective linear dimension of the generators

children.title: Sparse Hull-Membership Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Small-support certificates associated with convex-hull membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Verification Cost of a Sparse Hull Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse convex-combination certificate is verifiable in time linear in dimension times support size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and suppose a certificate lists indices \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and coefficients \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\). The conditions \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i s_i\) can be verified in \(O(d|I|)\) arithmetic operations. If \(|I|\leq r+1\leq d+1\), the cost is \(O(d(r+1))\), hence at most \(O(d^2)\).
assumptions_latex: The points, target, indices, and coefficients use an exact-arithmetic representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This counts exact real-arithmetic operations; bit complexity depends additionally on numeric encoding.

notation.meaning: Support of the sparse coefficient vector

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Hull-Membership Witnesses
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite generating set, convex-hull membership is certified by nonnegative coefficients that sum to one, reproduce the point, and have at most r+1 positive entries, where r is the affine dimension of the generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\), and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Then \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i s_i\), and \(|\{i:\lambda_i>0\}|\le r+1\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\), and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) holds if and only if there is a vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i s_i\), and \(|\{i:\lambda_i>0\}|\le r+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed coefficients form a directly checkable convex-hull membership certificate whose support obeys the affine-dimension Caratheodory bound.

notation.meaning: effective affine dimension of the finite generating set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Carathéodory-Sparse Convex-Hull Witness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). A finite family may repeat points, although zero coefficients and repetitions may always be removed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convex hulls; the bound used here is the ambient-dimension bound \(n+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sparse hull-membership witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}X\) is a tuple \(W=((x_i)_{i=1}^m,(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m)\) such that \[1\le m\le n+1,\qquad x_i\in X,\qquad \lambda_i>0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Its support is \(\operatorname{supp}W=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), and its support size is \(m\). Thus the witness is an explicitly checkable certificate consisting of at most \(n+1\) generating points and their convex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a sparse witness certifying that \(x\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}X\) consists of at most \(n+1\) points of \(X\) and positive coefficients summing to one whose weighted sum is \(x\). The number of positive coefficients is the witness support size.
equivalent_formulations_latex: After removing zero coefficients, the certificate is equivalently a finitely supported probability vector \(\lambda:X\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(|\operatorname{supp}\lambda|\le n+1\) and \(x=\sum_{u\in X}\lambda(u)u\).
The lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}\) may be chosen linearly independent; consequently, the selected points are affinely independent.
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), every hull point has a witness supported on at most two points.
If \(x\in X\), the singleton witness \(m=1\), \(x_1=x\), and \(\lambda_1=1\) is valid.
immediate_consequences_latex: Hull membership in \(\mathbb R^n\) always has a certificate whose support cardinality is bounded independently of the cardinality of \(X\).
boundary_notes: The definition is finite-dimensional; no uniform finite support bound follows in a general infinite-dimensional space.
The sharper affine-dimension bound is a neighboring regime and is not asserted as the defining bound in this record.
The representation need not be unique.

notation.meaning: selected generating points with positive weight

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology Relative to the Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, put \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and equip \(A\) with the subspace topology inherited from \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(B(x,r)=\{y:\|y-x\|<r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative topology in the effective affine ambient space \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative topology of \(C\) is the topology induced on \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\). Its intrinsic topological objects are \[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists r>0,\ B(x,r)\cap A\subseteq C\},\] \[\operatorname{cl}_A C=\{x\in A:\forall r>0,\ B(x,r)\cap C\ne\varnothing\},\qquad \operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_A C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] A set \(U\subseteq A\) is relatively open when \(U=A\cap O\) for some open \(O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relevant ambient space for a nonempty convex set \(C\) is its affine hull \(A\). Relative interior, closure, and boundary are respectively the interior, closure, and boundary computed in the subspace topology of \(A\). A relative neighborhood of \(x\) is obtained by intersecting an ordinary open ball about \(x\) with \(A\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if \(x\in C\) and some neighborhood of \(x\) in \(A\) is contained in \(C\).
Because \(A\) is closed in finite dimensions and contains \(C\), the relative closure \(\operatorname{cl}_A C\) equals the ordinary Euclidean closure \(\operatorname{cl}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=A\) is affine, then \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\) and \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\varnothing\).
If \(C\) is a nondegenerate line segment, its relative interior is the open segment and its relative boundary consists of its endpoints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative topological notions do not become degenerate merely because \(C\) lies in a proper affine subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: Ambient interior and ambient boundary are different objects when \(A\ne\mathbb R^n\).
The finite-dimensional equality between relative and ambient closures can fail in nonclosed affine subspaces of more general topological vector spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Characterization of Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \[z\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff \forall x\in C\;\exists\mu>1:\ (1-\mu)x+\mu z\in C.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign-invariant set and convex box characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coordinatewise sign invariance and records its equivalent order-box condition in the convex case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set C\subset\mathbb{R}^n is sign-invariant if, for every g\in C and every \sigma\in\{\pm1\}^n, one has \sigma\odot g\in C, where (\sigma\odot g)^{(i)}=\sigma_i g^{(i)}. If C is convex, this is equivalent to requiring that B(g):=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:-g\le s\le g\}\subseteq C for every g\in C\cap\mathbb{R}_+^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is sign-invariant when independently changing the signs of any coordinates preserves membership. For a convex set, this is equivalently characterized by containment of the coordinate box from −g to g for every nonnegative member g.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is sign-invariant}\iff \bigl(\forall g\in C\cap\mathbb{R}_+^n,\ B(g)\subseteq C\bigr)\quad\text{when }C\text{ is convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology and dimension of strict and non-strict convex level sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-topological comparison of level sets above the infimum of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n	o(-\infty,+\infty] be proper and convex, let \alpha\in\mathbb{R} satisfy \alpha>\inf f, and define L_{\leq}=\{x\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\} and L_{<}=\{x\mid f(x)<\alpha\}. Then
\[\operatorname{cl}L_{\leq}=\operatorname{cl}L_{<}=\{x\mid(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)\leq\alpha\},\]
\[\operatorname{ri}L_{\leq}=\operatorname{ri}L_{<}=\{x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\mid f(x)<\alpha\},\]
and
\[\dim L_{\leq}=\dim L_{<}=\dim(\operatorname{dom}f)=\dim f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every finite level strictly above the infimum of a proper convex function, its strict and non-strict level sets have the same closure, the same relative interior, and the same dimension as the effective domain. Their common closure is the corresponding closed level set of the closure of f, and their common relative interior consists of relative-interior domain points satisfying the strict inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Summation bound and asymptotic rounding coefficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate convergence consequence of the determinant-progress estimate for Algorithm 7.6.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{G_k\}\) be generated by Algorithm 7.6, let
\[
r_k:=\max_{g\in\mathcal C}\sqrt{g^\top G_k^{-1}g},
\]
and suppose \(r_k\ge\sqrt n\) and the determinant-progress estimate yields
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N}\left(1-\frac{\sqrt n}{r_k}\right)^2\le 2n\ln R\qquad\forall N\ge0.
\]
For \(r_N^*:=\min_{0\le k\le N}r_k\),
\[
\frac{\sqrt n}{r_N^*}\ge 1-\left(\frac{2n\ln R}{N+1}\right)^{1/2},
\]
and \(r_N^*\to\sqrt n\) as \(N\to\infty\). If \(\{G_k\}\) is compact, it has a limiting matrix \(G_*\) with rounding coefficient \(\beta=\sqrt n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming the determinant-progress summation estimate and the lower bound r_k at least square root n, the best radius among the first N+1 iterates satisfies the stated explicit estimate and converges to square root n. If the generated matrices form a compact set, a limiting matrix attains rounding coefficient square root n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\sqrt n}{r_N^*}\ge 1-\sqrt{\frac{2n\ln R}{N+1}},\qquad r_N^*\to\sqrt n;\quad \{G_k\}\text{ compact}\implies\exists G_*\text{ with }\beta(G_*)=\sqrt n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Termination bound from log-determinant progress
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional complexity theorem for an ellipsoidal update scheme satisfying the displayed continuation and determinant-growth conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n\in\mathbb{N}, \gamma>1, R\geq1, G_0\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n, and let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be measurable and convex with W_1(G_0)\subseteq C\subseteq W_R(G_0), where W_r(G)=\{x:x^\top G^{-1}x\leq r^2\}. Suppose an iterative scheme produces G_k\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n and, at every continued iteration, quantities satisfying \alpha_k=\frac1n r_k^2-1\geq\gamma^2-1 and \log\det G_{k+1}\geq\log\det G_k+2\log\gamma-\frac{\gamma^2-1}{\gamma^2}. Then the scheme terminates after at most 2n\frac{\gamma^2}{(\gamma-1)^2}\log R iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a measurable convex set lies between the unit and radius-R ellipsoids of the initial metric, and every continued iteration has the stated normalized violation and minimum log-determinant increase, then the scheme terminates within the displayed number of iterations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict concavity and maximizer of the ellipsoidal rounding potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the scalar potential used to choose a determinant-maximizing rank-one update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For n\geq2 and \sigma>0, define V:[0,1)\to\mathbb{R} by V(\alpha)=\log(1+\alpha(n(1+\sigma)-1))+(n-1)\log(1-\alpha). Then V is strictly concave and has the unique maximizer \alpha^*=\frac{\sigma}{n(1+\sigma)-1}. This maximizer satisfies \frac{n-1}{1-\alpha^*}=\frac{n(1+\sigma)-1}{1+\alpha^*(n(1+\sigma)-1)}, and V(\alpha^*)=\log(1+\sigma)+(n-1)\log\frac{(n-1)(1+\sigma)}{n(1+\sigma)-1}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For dimension at least two and positive sigma, the stated logarithmic potential is strictly concave on its domain. Its unique maximizer, first-order characterization, and attained value have the displayed closed forms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trace identity and lower bound for the rounding radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural identity and radius bound for a positive-definite iterate of Algorithm 7.6.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\). Suppose Algorithm 7.6 generates a positive-definite matrix
\[
G_k=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}a_i a_i^\top,
\qquad \lambda_k\in\mathbb R_+^m,
\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}=1.
\]
Define
\[
r_k:=\max_{g\in\mathcal C}\|g\|_{G_k}^*,\qquad \|a\|_{G_k}^*:=\sqrt{a^\top G_k^{-1}a}.
\]
Then
\[
I_n=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}G_k^{-1/2}a_i a_i^\top G_k^{-1/2},
\]
and consequently
\[
n=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}\bigl(\|a_i\|_{G_k}^*\bigr)^2\le r_k^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite Algorithm 7.6 iterate represented by simplex weights over a_i a_i transposed, congruence scaling by G_k inverse square root gives a decomposition of the identity. Taking traces shows that n is the weighted mean of the squared dual G_k-norms and is at most r_k squared.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Containment and log-determinant gain under a rank-one ellipsoid update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source-defined ellipsoid notation W_r(G), cut set C_{\pm g}(G), and dual G-norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n, g\in\mathbb{R}^n, and G(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)G+\alpha gg^\top for \alpha\in[0,1). Then W_1(G(\alpha))\subseteq C_{\pm g}(G). If \sigma=\frac1n(\|g\|_G^*)^2-1>0 and V(\alpha)=\log\frac{\det G(\alpha)}{\det G}=\log(1+\alpha(n(1+\sigma)-1))+(n-1)\log(1-\alpha), then V is maximized over [0,1) at \alpha^*=\frac{\sigma}{n(1+\sigma)-1}, and V(\alpha^*)=\log(1+\sigma)+(n-1)\log\frac{(n-1)(1+\sigma)}{n(1+\sigma)-1}\geq\log(1+\sigma)-\frac{\sigma}{1+\sigma}\geq\frac{\sigma^2}{(1+\sigma)(2+\sigma)}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite ellipsoidal metric, the specified rank-one convex update preserves containment in the source-defined symmetric cut set. When the normalized squared dual norm exceeds one, the associated log-determinant ratio is maximized at the stated step size and satisfies the two stated lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower bound for the maximum leverage radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dimension lower bound for the largest quadratic leverage score of vectors generating an invertible weighted second-moment matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\lambda_k^{(i)}\ge 0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}=1\). If \(G_k=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}a_i a_i^T\) is invertible, define \(H_k=G_k^{-1}\) and \(r_k^2=\max_{1\le i\le m}\langle a_i,H_k a_i\rangle\). Then \(r_k^2\ge n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For vectors whose weighted outer products form an invertible matrix, the largest quadratic leverage score with respect to the inverse matrix is at least the ambient dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective-Domain Invariants Under Convex Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-topological relationship between the effective domains of a proper convex function and its lower-semicontinuous closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a proper convex function. Then \(\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{cl}f)\) and \(\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{cl}f)\setminus\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{cl}f))=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{cl}f))=\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and \(\dim(\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{cl}f))=\dim(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a proper convex function can add effective-domain points only on the original domain's relative boundary; the original and enlarged domains therefore have the same closure, relative interior, and dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conversion of a Box Sandwich to an Ellipsoid Sandwich
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded containment lemma for axis-aligned boxes and their associated diagonal ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\hat a^{(i)}>0\) for all \(i\), set \(\hat D:=\operatorname{diag}((\hat a^{(1)})^2,\ldots,(\hat a^{(n)})^2)\), and for \(r>0\) define \[W_r(\hat D):=\left\{x:\langle\hat D^{-1}x,x\rangle\le r^2\right\}=\left\{x:\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x^{(i)}}{r\hat a^{(i)}}\right)^2\le1\right\}.\] Define \(B(\alpha\hat a):=\{x:|x^{(i)}|\le\alpha\hat a^{(i)}\ \forall i\}\). If \(m\ge1\) and \(B(\hat a)\subseteq C\subseteq B(m\hat a)\), then \[W_1(\hat D)\subset C\subset W_{m\sqrt n}(\hat D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly positive axis vector, any set lying between its unit box and the box enlarged by m also lies between the associated diagonal unit ellipsoid and its enlargement by m times square root n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_1(\hat D)\subset C\subset W_{m\sqrt n}(\hat D).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-combination invariant of the rounding matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant maintained by Algorithm 7.6, whether or not its stopping test is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\{G_k\}_{k\ge0}\) be generated by Algorithm 7.6, with or without its stopping test. If
\[
G_0=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_0^{(i)}a_i a_i^\top,\qquad \lambda_0\in\mathbb R_+^m,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_0^{(i)}=1,
\]
then for every \(k\ge0\) there exists \(\lambda_k\in\mathbb R_+^m\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}=1\) such that
\[
G_k=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_k^{(i)}a_i a_i^\top.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If Algorithm 7.6 starts from a convex combination of the rank-one matrices a_i a_i transposed, every generated matrix G_k remains a convex combination of those same matrices, regardless of whether the stopping test is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign-Symmetric Box Hull and Average Diagonal Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definitions for a finite family of nonzero nonnegative vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\{0\}\). For \(a\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\{0\}\), define \[B(a):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:|x_j|\le a_j,\ j=1,\ldots,n\},\qquad C:=\operatorname{Conv}\{B(a_i):i=1,\ldots,m\}.\] Define \(\hat a:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\) and assume \(\hat a>0\) componentwise. With \(D(\hat a):=\operatorname{diag}(\hat a)\), define \[\hat D:=D(\hat a)^2=\operatorname{diag}(\hat a)^2=\operatorname{diag}(\hat a\circ\hat a).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each nonzero nonnegative vector defines an axis-aligned sign-symmetric box. Their convex hull is a sign-symmetric convex set. If their componentwise average is strictly positive, that average defines a positive diagonal scaling matrix and its squared diagonal matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(a)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:|x_j|\le a_j,\ j=1,\ldots,n\},\quad C=\operatorname{Conv}\{B(a_i):i=1,\ldots,m\},\quad D(\hat a)=\operatorname{diag}(\hat a),\quad \hat D=D(\hat a)^2=\operatorname{diag}(\hat a\circ\hat a).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-radius estimate from cumulative deviations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The finite-horizon estimate is faithfully preserved. The stated convergence clause appears to rely on the additional lower bound \(r_k\ge\sqrt n\) supplied by the surrounding rounding construction but absent from this isolated extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\ge1\) and let \((r_k)_{k\ge0}\) be positive reals such that \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}(1-\sqrt n/r_k)^2\le2n\ln R\) for every \(N\ge0\). With \(r_N^*=\min_{0\le k\le N}r_k\), the proposition states that, for every \(N\ge0\), \(\sqrt n/r_N^*\ge1-\sqrt{2n\ln R/(N+1)}\), and that \(r_N^*\to\sqrt n\) as \(N\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all cumulative squared deviations of sqrt(n)/r_k from one are bounded by 2n log R, then the smallest radius through iteration N satisfies the displayed finite-horizon estimate; the proposition also states convergence of that smallest radius to sqrt(n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Simplicial Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a local geometric class and records its stated inclusion and boundary regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is locally simplicial if, for every \(x\in S\), there exist simplices \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq S\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) such that \(U\cap S=U\cap\bigl(S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_m\bigr)\). Such a set need be neither convex nor closed. The class includes simplices, line segments, polytopes, polyhedral convex sets, and relatively open convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset S of Euclidean space is locally simplicial when, near each of its points, it agrees with a finite union of simplices contained in S. Local simpliciality requires neither convexity nor closedness; examples include simplices, line segments, polytopes, polyhedral convex sets, and relatively open convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is locally simplicial}\iff \forall x\in S\ \exists m,U,S_1,\ldots,S_m:\ S_i\subseteq S\text{ are simplices and }U\cap S=U\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^m S_i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterative scheme for a gamma-n ellipsoidal rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the iteration and stopping rule; it does not by itself assert termination or an iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex with nonempty interior, \gamma>1, n\ge 2, v_0\in\mathbb{R}^n, and G_0\succ0. For k=0,1,\ldots, set r_k=\max_{g\in C}\|g-v_k\|_{G_k}^* and choose g_k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{g\in C}\|g-v_k\|_{G_k}^*. If r_k\le\gamma n, stop and output (v_k,G_k). Otherwise set \alpha_k=\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{r_k-n}{r_k-1} and \beta_k=\frac{\alpha_k}{r_k}+\left(\frac{r_k-1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{\alpha_k}{r_k}\right)^2, and update v_{k+1}=v_k+\alpha_k\frac{r_k-1}{2r_k}(g_k-v_k) and G_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)G_k+\beta_k(g_k-v_k)(g_k-v_k)^T.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, find a point of the convex set farthest from the current center in the current dual metric. Stop when its radius is at most gamma times n; otherwise update the center and metric using the stated coefficients.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is convex with nonempty interior}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_k\le\gamma n\Rightarrow\operatorname{output}(v_k,G_k);\quad r_k>\gamma n\Rightarrow (v_{k+1},G_{k+1})\text{ is given by the stated updates}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariance ellipsoid sandwich for a finite convex hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs explicit inner and outer ellipsoids for a full-dimensional finite convex hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional convex hull of finitely many points, the empirical-center covariance metric defines a unit ellipsoid inside the hull and a concentric ellipsoid of radius square root of m(m−1) containing it.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contained update ellipsoid and determinant progress
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the preceding definitions of \(C_g(G)\), \(r\), and \(G(\alpha)\). The printed optimizer formula is singular at the boundary \(r=1\), which can occur when \(n=1\); the extract provides no separate convention for that case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\succ0\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(r=\|g\|_G^*\), and let \(C_g(G)\) and \(G(\alpha)\) be as defined above. For every \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), \(E_\alpha=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|s-\frac{r-1}{2r}\alpha g\|_{G(\alpha)}^*\le1\}\subseteq C_g(G)\). If \(r\ge n\), then \(V(\alpha)=\ln\frac{\det G(\alpha)}{\det G(0)}=2\ln(1+\alpha\frac{r-1}{2})+(n-1)\ln(1-\alpha)\) attains its maximum at \(\alpha^*=\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{r-n}{r-1}\). With \(\sigma=\frac{r-n}{n+1}\), the maximum satisfies \(V(\alpha^*)=2\ln\frac{r-1}{n+1}+(n-1)\ln\frac{(n-1)(r+1)}{(n+1)(r-1)}\ge2[\ln(1+\sigma)-\frac{\sigma}{1+\sigma}]\ge\frac{2\sigma^2}{(1+\sigma)(2+\sigma)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every update ellipsoid with alpha below one is contained in the one-point convex-hull extension. When r is at least n, the log-determinant gain has the stated maximizing alpha and admits explicit logarithmic and rational lower bounds in terms of sigma.
assumptions_latex: r\ge n\text{ for the maximization and progress bounds}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set, let \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and let \(L=A-A\) be the linear space parallel to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, including lower-dimensional and nonclosed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative interior of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ x+(B(0,\varepsilon)\cap L)\subseteq C\}.\] Thus \(x\) is a relative interior point precisely when \(C\) contains an open neighborhood of \(x\) in its own affine hull. The relative dimension of \(C\) is \(\dim C=\dim A=\dim L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point \(x\) lies in the relative interior of a nonempty convex set \(C\) when a sufficiently small ball around \(x\), restricted to directions parallel to the affine hull of \(C\), remains inside \(C\). This definition measures interior intrinsically and therefore remains meaningful for lower-dimensional convex sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is the ordinary interior of \(C\) in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
Using any norm on \(\mathbb R^n\) gives the same relative interior because all finite-dimensional norms induce the same topology.
special_cases_latex: For a singleton \(C=\{x\}\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).
For an affine set \(C\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).
For a nonempty full-dimensional convex set, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is nonempty and convex, and \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{aff}C\).
boundary_notes: Convexity is not needed to write the subspace-interior definition, but it is essential for the listed structural consequences.
Relative interior does not require \(C\) to be closed.
Ambient interior may be empty even when relative interior is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of the Convex Hull of a Finite Union
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the relative interior using strictly positive convex combinations involving the relative interior of every constituent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $m\ge 1$, let $C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty convex sets, and set $C_0=\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_m)$. Then
\[
\operatorname{ri} C_0
=
\bigcup_{\substack{\lambda_i>0\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1}}
\left(\lambda_1\operatorname{ri}C_1+\cdots+\lambda_m\operatorname{ri}C_m\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many nonempty convex subsets of Euclidean space, the relative interior of the convex hull of their union is exactly the union of the weighted Minkowski sums of their relative interiors over all strictly positive weights summing to one.
assumptions_latex: C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty and convex for every }i=1,\ldots,m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and affine-hull preservation under closure and relative interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational structural properties of finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the sets \(\operatorname{cl}C\) and \(\operatorname{ri}C\) are convex and
\[
\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{aff}C.
\]
Consequently, both have the same dimension as \(C\), and \(C\ne\varnothing\) implies \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure and relative interior of a finite-dimensional convex set are convex and have the same affine hull and dimension as the original set. In particular, every nonempty convex set has nonempty relative interior.
