knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Intrinsic Interior and Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. The definition uses only segments inside \(C\), while the equivalent relative-interior formulation uses the topology of \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine geometry; the stated equivalence is for nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the intrinsic algebraic interior of \(C\) by \[\operatorname{aint}C=\{x\in C:\forall y\in C\ \exists\gamma>0\text{ such that }x+\gamma(x-y)\in C\}.\] A point in \(\operatorname{aint}C\) is therefore an endpoint from which every segment \([y,x]\subseteq C\) can be prolonged a positive distance beyond \(x\) without leaving \(C\). In finite-dimensional convex geometry, \[\operatorname{aint}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic algebraic interior consists of those points \(x\in C\) for which every segment joining another point \(y\in C\) to \(x\) can be extended beyond \(x\) while staying in \(C\). For a nonempty convex subset of finite-dimensional space, this segment-based notion is exactly the relative interior.
assumptions_latex: All quantifiers over directions are restricted to the effective affine space of \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(z=x+\gamma(x-y)\), the condition says that \(x\) lies in the open segment \((y,z)\) for some \(z\in C\), for every \(y\in C\).
The same points are characterized by the existence of an affine-hull neighborhood \(B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is affine, every point satisfies the prolongation condition.
If \(C=[a,b]\) with \(a\ne b\), exactly the points of \((a,b)\) satisfy it.
immediate_consequences_latex: The intrinsic-interior notion is affine invariant: for an affine bijection \(T\), \(T(\operatorname{aint}C)=\operatorname{aint}(T(C))\).
boundary_notes: The parameter \(\gamma\) may depend on \(y\); no uniform positive prolongation length is required.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, algebraic interior and topological relative interior need not coincide.
Convexity is part of the equivalence.

notation.meaning: intrinsic algebraic interior defined by segment prolongation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative interior of a finite-dimensional convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative interior measured in the affine hull, including its basic containment and full-dimensional specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Its relative interior is
\[
\operatorname{ri}C=\left\{x\in\operatorname{aff}C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ (x+\varepsilon B)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C\right\},
\]
where \(B=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\|z\|\le 1\}\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\), and if \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a convex set is its interior when the set is viewed inside its affine hull. It lies in the set, and for a full-dimensional convex set it equals the ordinary interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Invariance of the Algebraic Core
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine change of coordinates maps the intrinsic algebraic core exactly onto the intrinsic algebraic core of the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\operatorname{aff}C\to A'\) be an affine bijection. Then \[T\!\left(\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\right)=\operatorname{core}_{A'}T(C).\] Thus intrinsic-core membership is independent of affine coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a real vector space.
\(T:\operatorname{aff}C\to A'\) is an affine bijection onto an affine space \(A'\).
The cores are computed intrinsically in their respective affine hulls.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bijectivity on the affine hull is essential for the stated equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Core Segment Absorption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving from an intrinsic-core point toward any point of a convex set stays in the core until the possible endpoint; hence the intrinsic core is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\) and \(y\in C\), then \[(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\qquad(0\le t<1).\] Consequently, the intrinsic algebraic core of a convex set is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
The core is computed relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is purely algebraic and requires no topology or finite-dimensional assumption. The endpoint need not be a core point.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional and Radial Characterizations of the Intrinsic Core
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the intrinsic algebraic core exactly when the radial cone there is the full direction space, equivalently when every chord to the point can be extended beyond it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty and convex, let \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\), and let \(x\in C\). Then \[x\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{cone}(C-x)=L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall y\in C\ \exists\varepsilon>0:\ x+\varepsilon(x-y)\in C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
The core is computed intrinsically in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These equivalences are purely algebraic. Convexity converts the two-sided directional definition into the cone and chord-extension forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Failure of Intrinsic Interior Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A halfspace defined by a discontinuous linear functional has nonempty algebraic core but empty relative interior, so the finite-dimensional equivalence can fail in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an infinite-dimensional normed real vector space admitting a discontinuous linear functional \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and set \(C=\{x\in X:f(x)\le 1\}\). Then \(C\) is convex, \(\operatorname{aff}C=X\), and
\[
\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in X:f(x)<1\}\ne\varnothing,
\qquad
\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example uses a discontinuous algebraic linear functional. It shows that finite dimensionality is essential in general normed spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Boundary Partition and Degenerate Case
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set's closure is the disjoint union of its relative interior and relative boundary, and the relative boundary is empty exactly for affine sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Then \(\operatorname{rbd}C\) is closed relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\), and \[\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{ri}C\,\dot\cup\,\operatorname{rbd}C.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\varnothing\) if and only if \(C=\operatorname{aff}C\), equivalently, \(C\) is an affine set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic intrinsic-topological structure of the relative boundary for a convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary is the relative closure of a set minus its relative interior, with both topological operations performed inside the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed real vector space and set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\). The relative boundary of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\), where \(\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\) denotes closure in the topology induced on \(A\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed real vector space and set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative boundary of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\), where \(\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\) is closure in the topology induced on \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Access from a Relative-Interior Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, choose \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the target may be a missing limit point of a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\) is radially accessible from \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) when every point before \(y\) on the segment from \(x\) to \(y\) remains in the relative interior: \[x_t=(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\qquad(0\le t<1).\] The radial-access set from \(x\) is \[\operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\{y\in\operatorname{cl}C:\forall t\in[0,1),\ (1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\}.\] For a nonempty convex \(C\), every closure point is accessible, so \(\operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix a relative-interior point \(x\) of a convex set \(C\). A closure point \(y\) is radially accessible from \(x\) if the half-open segment from \(x\) to \(y\) is contained in the relative interior of \(C\). Convexity implies that every point of the closure is accessible in this sense, even when the endpoint itself is absent from \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the point \(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
The half-open segment \([x,y)\) is contained in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(y\in C\), accessibility holds along an ordinary segment contained in \(C\).
If \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), every point before the missing endpoint still lies in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every closure point is the limit of a one-dimensional path lying entirely in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
Consequently, \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C\).
boundary_notes: No assertion is made that the endpoint \(y\) itself belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) or even to \(C\).
The starting point must lie in the relative interior; an arbitrary boundary starting point need not provide this access.

notation.meaning: point at parameter t on the segment from x to y
closure points radially accessible from x

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Reachability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to any fixed relative-interior point x, a point y of C is itself relatively interior exactly when the ray from x through y can be extended beyond y while remaining in C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space and fix \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\). For \(y\in C\), one has \(y\in\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\in C\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, fix \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(y\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This characterizes relative-interior points by extendability of the ray from one fixed relative-interior base point beyond the candidate point.

notation.meaning: a point beyond y on the ray from x through y

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Accessibility Limits
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-boundary point is approached by relative-interior points along every segment from a relative-interior base point, but the ray through that boundary point cannot be extended farther while staying in the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space. If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and \(y\in\operatorname{rbd}C\), then \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\) for every \(t\in[0,1)\), and \(\lim_{t\uparrow1}((1-t)x+ty)=y\). Furthermore, \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\notin C\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, let \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in\operatorname{rbd}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\in[0,1)\), one has \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(\lim_{t\uparrow1}((1-t)x+ty)=y\); moreover, \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\notin C\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The statement distinguishes approach to a relative-boundary point from radial extension beyond it: the open segment is relatively interior, but the ray cannot remain in the set past the boundary point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Dimensional and Lower-Dimensional Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Ambient interior is computed in \(\mathbb R^n\), whereas relative interior is computed in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ambient-relative interior regime of \(C\) is determined by \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\). It is full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\), and lower-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\). Precisely, \[\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\iff\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n,\] and in the full-dimensional regime \[\operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\] In the lower-dimensional regime, \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set is in the full-dimensional regime when its affine hull is all of the ambient space. Exactly in that regime its ambient interior is nonempty and equals its relative interior. If the affine hull is proper, the ambient interior is empty, but the relative interior remains nonempty because it is measured inside the affine hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The full-dimensional regime is equivalently \(\dim C=n\).
The lower-dimensional regime is equivalently \(\dim C<n\), in which case every point of \(C\) is an ambient boundary point.
special_cases_latex: A line segment in \(\mathbb R^2\) has empty ambient interior but a nonempty relative interior.
An affine space \(A\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(\operatorname{ri}A=A\) and \(\operatorname{int}A=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For lower-dimensional convex sets, statements requiring an interior point must be formulated with \(\operatorname{ri}C\), not \(\operatorname{int}C\).
boundary_notes: Nonemptiness is essential: conventions for the affine hull and relative interior of the empty set vary.
The equivalence uses convexity for the implication from full affine hull to nonempty interior.

notation.meaning: interior relative to the affine hull

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Dimensional Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex subset of Euclidean space is full-dimensional exactly when it has nonempty ambient interior; in that regime its relative interior equals its ordinary interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and convex. Then \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^d\) if and only if \(\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\). Under these equivalent conditions, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The following are equivalent: \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^d\); \(\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\). Whenever these conditions hold, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional Euclidean regime in which the affine hull is the entire ambient space, so relative and ambient topology agree on the set.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for Nonempty Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct points in the plane form a nonempty lower-dimensional set with empty relative interior, showing that convexity is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(-1,0),(1,0)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^2\). Then \(C\) is nonempty and \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\), so \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)=1<2\), while \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\). Thus convexity cannot be omitted from the lower-dimensional nonempty-relative-interior assertion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite example isolates the necessity of convexity in the assertion that every nonempty lower-dimensional convex set has nonempty relative interior.

notation.meaning: interior relative to the affine hull of C

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty lower-dimensional convex set has empty ambient interior but nonempty relative interior in its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set. If \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)<n\), then \[\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing.\] Thus the intrinsic interior is taken in \(\operatorname{aff}C\), where it is nonempty, even though no ambient open ball lies in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean regime; nonemptiness is essential for the asserted nonempty relative interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for the Affine-Hull Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit circle spans the plane affinely but has empty ambient interior, showing that convexity is essential to the affine-hull criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\|x\|_2=1\}\). Then \(C\) is nonempty and \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^2\), but \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\). Hence the equivalence \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\iff\operatorname{aff}C\ne\mathbb{R}^2\) fails if convexity is omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Interior Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set has empty ambient interior exactly when its affine hull is a proper affine subspace of the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{aff}C\neq\mathbb{R}^n.\] Equivalently, \(C\) has nonempty ambient interior exactly when it is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This gives the exact finite-dimensional boundary between empty and nonempty ambient interior for a nonempty convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior-Compatible Set Operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be an operation taking one or more nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-set operations; qualifications are part of compatibility where required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) is relative-interior compatible on inputs \((C_1,\ldots,C_m)\) when \[\operatorname{ri}\Phi(C_1,\ldots,C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{ri}C_1,\ldots,\operatorname{ri}C_m),\] with the right side interpreted using the same set operation. Cartesian products, Minkowski sums, and affine images are compatible without a constraint qualification. Finite intersections are compatible under \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\); affine preimages are compatible when the preimage meets the target relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior calculus records when taking relative interiors commutes with a convex-set construction. Products, sums, and affine images commute unconditionally. Intersections and affine preimages require a nonempty relative-interior feasibility condition. The qualification is part of the operation's declared domain of compatibility.
assumptions_latex: All participating sets are nonempty and convex in finite-dimensional spaces.
Any intersection or affine-preimage identity is invoked only under its stated relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ri}\Phi(C_1,\ldots,C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{ri}C_1,\ldots,\operatorname{ri}C_m)\] for each operation on its qualified domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Compatibility means that intrinsic neighborhoods are transported exactly by the set operation, rather than yielding merely one-sided inclusion.
For an affine map \(T\), image compatibility reads \(T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C))\).
special_cases_latex: For products, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1\times\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
For sums, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A compound construction may be evaluated by propagating relative interiors through successive compatible operations while retaining every necessary qualification.
boundary_notes: Closure does not share all of these unconditional commutation properties.
Without a common relative-interior point, the intersection identity can fail.
The definition concerns exact equality, not merely inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Common Relative-Interior Point
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite closed halfplanes have disjoint relative interiors, while their intersection is a line with nonempty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge0\}\) and \(C_2=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\le0\}\). Then \(\operatorname{ri}C_1=\{y>0\}\), \(\operatorname{ri}C_2=\{y<0\}\), and \(C_1\cap C_2=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). Therefore \[\operatorname{ri}(C_1\cap C_2)=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\ne\varnothing=\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are the upper and lower closed halfplanes in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that the standard compatibility condition cannot simply be omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors of Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a positive finite family of convex sets has a common relative-interior point, the relative interior of its intersection equals the intersection of the sets' relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive, and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets satisfying \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Then \[\operatorname{ri}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersection rule under the standard relative-interior compatibility condition.

notation.meaning: A positive finite number of sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior-Regular Intersection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets, where \(m\ge1\), and put \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections of finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((C_i)_{i=1}^m\) is relative-interior regular when \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing.\] For such a family, the intersection calculus is exact: \[\operatorname{ri}\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{cl}\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}C_i.\] Relative-interior regularity is therefore a geometric constraint qualification for commuting both intrinsic interior and closure with intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of convex sets is relative-interior regular when all sets share a point that lies in each of their relative interiors. Under this qualification, the relative interior of the intersection is the intersection of the relative interiors, and closure also commutes with the intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regularity means that there exists \(\bar x\) and radii \(r_i>0\) such that \(B(\bar x,r_i)\cap\operatorname{aff}C_i\subseteq C_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=1\), regularity is automatic because a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set has nonempty relative interior.
For two sets, the qualification is \(\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2\ne\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The qualified intersection is nonempty, and its relative interior contains every common relative-interior point.
boundary_notes: Without the qualification, equality may fail even when the intersection is nonempty; for example, opposite closed half-lines can meet at one point while their relative interiors are disjoint.
For arbitrary infinite families, finite-family induction does not establish the same identities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product and Minkowski-Sum Relative-Interior Rules
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be nonempty convex sets. When forming a Minkowski sum, assume all summands lie in a common vector space \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products and finite Minkowski sums in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cartesian product and Minkowski sum are \[\prod_{i=1}^m C_i=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):x_i\in C_i\},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m C_i=\{x_1+\cdots+x_m:x_i\in C_i\}.\] Their relative-interior calculus is \[\operatorname{ri}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\] No common-interior qualification is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a finite Cartesian product is the product of the relative interiors. For convex sets in a common vector space, the relative interior of their Minkowski sum is the sum of their relative interiors. Both identities hold without an intersection-type constraint qualification.
assumptions_latex: For the sum identity, \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) for all \(i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The sum identity is the affine-image rule applied to the addition map \(A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i x_i\) on \(\prod_i C_i\).
special_cases_latex: For two sets, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
For a scalar \(\alpha>0\), \(\operatorname{ri}(\alpha C)=\alpha\operatorname{ri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vector \(z\in\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)\) admits a decomposition \(z=x_1+x_2\) with \(x_i\in\operatorname{ri}C_i\).
boundary_notes: For multiplication by \(\alpha=0\), the image is the singleton \(\{0\}\), whose relative interior is itself.
Analogous closure equality for sums can fail when both summands are unbounded, even if they are closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Product Formula Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior commutes with every nonempty finite Cartesian product, even for nonconvex factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) be nonempty for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then \[\operatorname{aff}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m S_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{aff}S_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m S_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}S_i.\] No convexity assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite topological-product formulation; convexity is unnecessary for the identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors of Cartesian Products
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a Cartesian product of nonempty convex sets is the Cartesian product of their relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), \[\operatorname{ri}(C\times D)=\operatorname{ri}C\times\operatorname{ri}D.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The product is regarded as a subset of the product Euclidean space.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for Minkowski-Sum Equality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, a Minkowski sum can acquire interior even though one summand has empty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{0,1\}\) and \(D=[0,1]\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\), whereas \(C+D=[0,2]\). Hence \[\operatorname{ri}(C+D)=(0,2)\ne\varnothing=\operatorname{ri}C+\operatorname{ri}D.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional failure when a summand is nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Minkowski-Sum Relative Interiors
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a finite Minkowski sum of nonempty convex sets is the sum of their relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m\ge1\) and \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \[\operatorname{ri}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the binary sum formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors of Minkowski Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of the Minkowski sum of two nonempty convex sets equals the Minkowski sum of their relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(C+D=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}\). Then \[\operatorname{ri}(C+D)=\operatorname{ri}C+\operatorname{ri}D.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Minkowski-sum calculus for nonempty convex sets.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior and Closure of a Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior equality and closure inclusion for the Minkowski sum of two finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n are convex, then \operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2 and \operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2)\supseteq \operatorname{cl}C_1+\operatorname{cl}C_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of the Minkowski sum of two convex sets is the sum of their relative interiors. The closure of the sum contains the sum of their closures; equality is not asserted.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Product or Sum Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With relative interior of the empty set defined as empty, empty factors or summands give empty results, while singleton factors and summands preserve the usual product and translation formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt \(\operatorname{ri}\varnothing=\varnothing\). Products and Minkowski sums involving an empty set are empty. For every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and every \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{ri}(C\times\{d\})=\operatorname{ri}C\times\{d\},\qquad \operatorname{ri}(C+\{a\})=\operatorname{ri}C+\{a\}.\] Hence zero-dimensional factors and summands do not invalidate the relative-interior formulas.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the empty-set and singleton degeneracies of product and sum calculus.

children.title: Relative Interiors Under Affine Maps
children.top_down_role: Transport of intrinsic interiors through affine images and preimages.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Preimage Formula Can Fail Without Range Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an affine range is tangent to a convex set and misses its relative interior, the relative-interior preimage identity can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\) by \(T(t)=(t,0)\), and let \(D=\{(x,y):y\ge x^2\}\). Then \(D\) is closed and convex, \(\operatorname{ri}D=\{(x,y):y>x^2\}\), and \(T^{-1}(D)=\{0\}\). Thus \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}D)=\{0\}\ne\varnothing=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional failure when the affine range only touches the target boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors Under Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine images carry the relative interior of a nonempty convex set onto the relative interior of its image. An affine preimage has the analogous formula when the affine range meets the target's relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine, with \(T(x)=Ax+b\). For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C)).\] If \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty and convex and \(T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\neq\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C))\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\) under the stated preimage qualification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The image identity is unconditional for a nonempty convex set; the preimage identity requires the affine range to meet the relative interior of the target set.

notation.meaning: Affine mapping with linear part A and translation b

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Image and Qualified Preimage Calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine, \(T(x)=Ax+b\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine images and preimages; preimages require relative-interior feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine images transport relative interiors exactly: \[T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C)).\] For a target set \(D\), define \(T^{-1}(D)=\{x:T(x)\in D\}\). If \[T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\ne\varnothing,\] then the affine preimage is relative-interior regular and \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D),\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map sends the relative interior of a nonempty convex set onto the relative interior of its image. A preimage obeys the corresponding relative-interior and closure identities provided at least one point maps into the relative interior of the target set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The preimage qualification says \(T(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing\).
Translations do not affect the rule, so the linear-map statements apply to affine maps after translating the image.
special_cases_latex: If \(T\) is an affine bijection, both image and preimage formulas hold without an additional qualification.
Coordinate projection satisfies the unconditional image formula.
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative interior is invariant under invertible affine changes of coordinates.
Minkowski-sum calculus follows by applying the image formula to the addition map.
boundary_notes: The image \(T(C)\) need not be closed when \(C\) is closed and unbounded.
Without preimage feasibility in \(\operatorname{ri}D\), the preimage relative-interior equality can fail.
The notation \(T^{-1}(D)\) denotes set preimage, not an inverse affine map.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the preimage of the relative interior of a convex set under a linear map is nonempty, relative interior and closure both commute exactly with taking the preimage.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, with the Euclidean topology on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, possibly nonclosed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closure of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{cl}C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\forall\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap C\ne\varnothing\}.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\) exactly when there is a sequence \((x_k)\subseteq C\) with \(x_k\to x\). For convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{cl}C\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(C\), and \[\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{aff}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of \(C\) consists of all points whose every neighborhood meets \(C\), equivalently all limits of sequences from \(C\). If \(C\) is convex, its closure remains convex and is the smallest closed convex superset of \(C\). Closing a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set does not change its affine hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}C\) is the intersection of all closed subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) containing \(C\).
Because closure preserves convexity, it is also the intersection of all closed convex sets containing \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}C=C\).
For an open segment \((a,b)\), \(\operatorname{cl}C=[a,b]\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point missing solely because of nonclosedness belongs to \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\).
The relative topology of \(C\) and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) uses the same affine ambient space.
boundary_notes: Closure does not imply boundedness or compactness.
Affine images of closed unbounded convex sets need not be closed.
The empty-set convention is excluded by the stated nonemptiness assumption.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative interior is dense in the closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient-open-set formulation of density for the relative interior of a finite-dimensional convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. For every open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[
U\cap\operatorname{cl}C\ne\varnothing
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
U\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every ambient open set that meets the closure of a convex set also meets its relative interior. Equivalently, the relative interior is dense in the closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent closure, relative-interior, and sandwich conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of convex sets belonging to the same closure and relative-interior class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Then
\[
\operatorname{cl}C_1=\operatorname{cl}C_2
\iff
\operatorname{ri}C_1=\operatorname{ri}C_2
\iff
\operatorname{ri}C_1\subseteq C_2\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C_1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex sets have the same closure exactly when they have the same relative interior. Equivalently, the second set lies between the relative interior and closure of the first.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure–relative-interior invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutual invariance of closure and relative interior for finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking relative interior does not change the closure of a convex set, and taking closure does not change its relative interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Failure of the Pairing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative cone in l2 is closed and convex but has empty relative interior, so its closure is not generated by its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the Hilbert space \(\ell^2\), let \(C=\{x=(x_k):x_k\ge 0\text{ for every }k\}\). Then \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(\operatorname{aff}C=\ell^2\), and \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\). Hence \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\varnothing\ne C=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that the finite-dimensional hypothesis in the seed cannot be removed in general.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure–Relative-Interior Equivalence Class
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, without a closedness assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\) when \(C\) and \(D\) have the same closure-relative-interior data. For nonempty convex sets, the following equivalent conditions define this relation: \[\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{cl}D,\qquad \operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{ri}D,\] or, after possibly exchanging \(C\) and \(D\), \[\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C.\] Each set satisfies the canonical pairing identities \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C,\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty finite-dimensional convex sets, closure and relative interior determine one another. Two such sets have the same closure exactly when they have the same relative interior. Any convex set lying between the relative interior of \(C\) and the closure of \(C\) belongs to the same closure–relative-interior equivalence class.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\) if and only if both sets lie between their common relative interior and common closure.
For a convex \(D\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\) implies \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\).
special_cases_latex: \(C\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) all belong to the same equivalence class.
An open convex set relative to its affine hull and its closure have the same relative interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Adding or deleting only non-interior boundary points while remaining convex does not change either canonical datum.
boundary_notes: Convexity is essential; arbitrary sets with the same closure need not have the same interior.
Nonemptiness avoids exceptional conventions for relative interior.
Equality of closures does not imply equality of the underlying sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-Exact Convex-Set Operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be an operation on nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional spaces. Write \(\overline C=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian products and Minkowski addition, with explicit boundedness conditions for exact closure of sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) is closure exact at \((C_1,	ext{\ldots},C_m)\) when \[\operatorname{cl}\Phi(C_1,	ext{\ldots},C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{cl}C_1,	ext{\ldots},\operatorname{cl}C_m).\] Cartesian product is always closure exact: \[\operatorname{cl}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1\times\operatorname{cl}C_2.\] Minkowski addition always satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}C_1+	ext{\operatorname{cl}}C_2\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2),\] and it is closure exact when at least one summand is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-set operation is closure exact when closing its inputs before applying the operation gives the same set as closing its output. Cartesian products are always closure exact. Minkowski sums have a general one-sided inclusion and become closure exact when at least one of the two convex summands is bounded.
assumptions_latex: For exactness of Minkowski addition, at least one of \(C_1,C_2\) is bounded.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For Minkowski addition, closure exactness means every limit of sums can be written as a sum of one point from each input closure.
special_cases_latex: If both summands are compact, their sum is compact and hence closed.
If \(C_1\) is bounded and \(C_2\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1+C_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closure calculus for a product followed by addition is exact whenever the boundedness condition is retained at the addition stage.
boundary_notes: The boundedness condition cannot simply be discarded: sums of closed unbounded convex sets may be nonclosed.
Closure exactness is operation- and input-dependent; it is not implied merely by convexity.
The inserted null markers in the displayed tuple notation carry no mathematical meaning and should be removed during normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Invariance of Convex Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is unchanged if the generating set is first replaced by its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cl}S)).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closing the generators before convexification does not alter the resulting closed convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Carathéodory Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed convex hull exactly when it is a limit of convex combinations using at most n+1 generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) if and only if, for every \(m\), there are \(s_{m,0},\ldots,s_{m,n}\in S\) and \(\lambda_{m,i}\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_{m,i}=1\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_{m,i}s_{m,i}\longrightarrow x.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\iff x\text{ is a limit of convex combinations of at most }n+1\text{ points of }S.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional sequential membership form of the closed convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of the convex hull of a set is exactly the intersection of all closed convex sets containing it, hence its smallest closed convex superset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its closed convex hull satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\bigcap\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:S\subseteq K,\ K\text{ is closed and convex}\}.\] Thus \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) is the unique smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of the closed convex hull in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

source_witnesses.locator: III.1.4, Closed Convex Sets and Hulls, p. 99

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 1.4 Closed Convex Sets and Hulls p. 99

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Finite Unions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure commutes with finite unions, while infinite unions may have additional limit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) in a Euclidean space, \[\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i\right)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}A_i.\] For an arbitrary family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\), only \[\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{cl}A_i\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\right)\] is automatic.
assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are subsets of a Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equality is restricted to finite unions; infinite unions may acquire additional limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Sum Closure Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the summands does not change the closure of their Minkowski sum; compact-plus-closed sums are closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(A+B)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}A+\operatorname{cl}B).\] If one summand is compact and the other is closed, then \(A+B\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The outer closure is essential in general, even for closed convex summands.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of A and B

knowledge_statements.title: Closure and Continuous Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous linear map sends closure into the closure of the image, and closing before mapping does not change the final closed image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear map \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and any \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[L(\operatorname{cl}A)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(L(A)),\qquad \operatorname{cl}(L(A))=\operatorname{cl}(L(\operatorname{cl}A)).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A linear image need not be closed, so equality is asserted only after closure in the codomain.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Set Operations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure always commutes with Cartesian products. For a positive finite family of convex sets, it also commutes with intersection when their relative interiors have a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary sets \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), \[\operatorname{cl}(A\times B)=\operatorname{cl}A\times\operatorname{cl}B.\] Let \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive. If \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are convex and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^k\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^k C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}C_i.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines unconditional product closure with the qualified finite-intersection rule for convex sets.

source_witnesses.locator: III.1.4, Closed Convex Sets and Hulls, p. 99; III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 1.4 Closed Convex Sets and Hulls p. 99

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polars of Linear Images and Preimages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polar-set calculus for arbitrary convex sets, not only cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be linear. For every convex C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, (AC)^\circ=(A^*)^{-1}(C^\circ). For every convex D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m, \bigl(A^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}D)\bigr)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(A^*(D^\circ)\bigr). If \operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}D\neq\varnothing, then \bigl(A^{-1}D\bigr)^\circ=A^*(D^\circ).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a linear image is the inverse adjoint image of the original polar. The polar of the inverse image of a set's closure is the closure of the adjoint image of its polar. If the linear map's range meets the relative interior of the set, the latter closure is unnecessary.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Sets Can Have a Nonclosed Sum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets can have a nonclosed Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\},\qquad V=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.\] Both \(C\) and \(V\) are closed and convex, but \[C+V=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\] is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional failure of closedness under Minkowski addition.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull of a Closed Set Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the origin to the closed epigraph of 1/x produces a closed set whose convex hull approaches but does not contain the positive horizontal axis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\},\qquad S=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(S\) is closed, but for every \(r>0\), \[(r,0)\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\setminus\operatorname{conv}S.\] Hence \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is closed but }\operatorname{conv}S\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This demonstrates why the outer closure in the definition of the closed convex hull cannot generally be omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Images Need Not Preserve Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\}\) and let \(L(x,y)=x\). Then \(C\) is closed and convex, whereas \[L(C)=(0,\infty)\] is not closed. Thus \(L(\operatorname{cl}C)\neq\operatorname{cl}(L(C))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional closed-convex counterexample; compactness of the domain set would restore closedness of the image.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncommuting Closure Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convex examples showing closure need not commute with intersection or Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Closure need not commute with intersection: for \(C=\{(x,y):y>0\}\) and \(D=\{(x,y):y<0\}\), both sets are convex, yet \(\overline{C\cap D}=\varnothing\) while \(\overline C\cap\overline D=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). It also need not commute with Minkowski addition. Let
\[
E=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y\geq 1/x\},
\qquad
L=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}.
\]
Both are closed and convex, but \(E+L=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\) is not closed. Thus \(\overline E+\overline L\neq\overline{E+L}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex half-planes show failure for intersections, while a closed epigraph plus a line shows that a Minkowski sum of closed convex sets need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closure fails to commute with both intersection and Minkowski addition, even for convex sets.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of E and L

children.title: Nonclosed Convex-Set Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Attainment, representation, and separation failures caused by missing limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Separation Detects Only Points Outside the Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is strongly separable from a convex set exactly when it lies outside the closure; omitted boundary points cannot be strongly separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle<\alpha\le\langle a,c\rangle\) for every \(c\in C\) if and only if \(x\notin\operatorname{cl}C\). Thus every \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) is a nonmember admitting no strong separator from \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the separation obstruction at an omitted boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Attainment Is Determined by Missing Closure Minimizers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a set does not change the infimum of a continuous linear objective, but it can add all of the minimizers and thereby restore attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+\beta\). Then \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{cl}C}f(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f=C\cap\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{cl}C}f.\] Consequently, if the infimum is attained on \(\operatorname{cl}C\) only at points omitted from \(C\), it is not attained on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the exact mechanism by which omitted limit points can destroy attainment without changing an optimal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Halfspace Hull of a Nonclosed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-halfspace inequalities cannot distinguish a convex set from its closure and represent the original set exactly precisely when it is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing \(C\) is \(\operatorname{cl}C\). Hence \(C\) is representable exactly as an intersection of closed halfspaces if and only if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap\{H:H\text{ is a closed halfspace and }C\subseteq H\}=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional representation loss caused by omitted limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex-Set Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missing boundary points obstruct attainment and strict separation despite convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|_2<1\}\), and choose \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\|p\|_2=1\). Then \(C\) is convex but not closed, \(p\notin C\), and \(p\in\overline C\). The linear optimization problem
\[
\inf_{x\in C}-\langle p,x\rangle=-1
\]
has no minimizer. Moreover, no affine hyperplane strictly separates \(p\) from \(C\): there are no \(a\neq0\) and \(\alpha<\beta\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle\leq\alpha<\beta\leq\langle a,p\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open ball is convex, yet a boundary-directed linear objective has no minimizer and its missing boundary point cannot be strictly separated from the ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infimum is unattained, and \(p\) cannot be strictly separated from \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Missing Boundary and Attained Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, not necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonclosed convex sets and their relative boundary decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative boundary is \[\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Its missing-boundary part and attained-boundary part are respectively \[\operatorname{mbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C,\qquad \operatorname{abd}C=C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Since \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\), these sets form the disjoint decomposition \[\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{abd}C\mathbin{\dot\cup}\operatorname{mbd}C.\] The set is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary of a possibly nonclosed convex set splits into boundary points that belong to the set and missing limit points that do not. The missing boundary is \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\); it is empty exactly when \(C\) is closed. Both types lie outside the relative interior.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in\operatorname{mbd}C\) if and only if \(y\notin C\) and some sequence in \(C\) converges to \(y\).
special_cases_latex: For a relatively open convex set, \(\operatorname{abd}C=\varnothing\), so all relative-boundary points are missing.
For a closed convex set, \(\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing\), so every relative-boundary point is attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: An optimization value approached only through a point of \(\operatorname{mbd}C\) need not be attained over \(C\).
Affine images and sums can create missing boundary points even from closed unbounded convex inputs.
boundary_notes: The decomposition classifies topological membership only; it does not by itself assert existence or nonexistence of an optimizer.
Ambient boundary can be larger than relative boundary for lower-dimensional sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Cone and Lineality Data
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global asymptotic geometry of closed finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic cone geometry of \(C\) is the pair \((C^\infty,\operatorname{lin}_\infty C)\), where \[C^\infty=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\forall x\in C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x+td\in C\}\] and \[\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=C^\infty\cap(-C^\infty).\] The cone \(C^\infty\) records directions retained indefinitely by \(C\), while \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty C\) records two-sided directions along which every point of \(C\) lies on a complete line contained in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global asymptotic geometry of a nonempty closed convex set consists of its recession cone and the lineality subspace inside that cone. A recession direction can be followed indefinitely from every point of the set. A lineality direction and its negative are both recession directions, so entire parallel lines remain in the set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\infty\text{ is a closed convex cone},\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty C=C^\infty\cap(-C^\infty)\text{ is a linear subspace}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{lin}_\infty C\) if and only if \(x+td\in C\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(t\in\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(C^\infty=\{0\}\).
If \(C\) is an affine space \(x_0+L\), then \(C^\infty=\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=L\).
If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^\infty=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(C\) is unbounded exactly when \(C^\infty\) contains a nonzero vector.
The asymptotic cone is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=\{0\}\).
boundary_notes: Closedness is required for the stated closed-cone and unboundedness characterizations.
For nonclosed convex sets, the recession cone may fail to be closed and may fail to detect unboundedness.
This record treats set asymptotics, not recession functions of convex functions.

notation.meaning: asymptotic or recession cone of C
lineality subspace of the asymptotic cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Direction and Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. The basic definition applies without closedness; the one-base-point characterization requires \(C\) to be closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, with closedness explicitly separated from the general definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) is a recession direction of \(C\) when \[x+td\in C\qquad\text{for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\ge0.\] The recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:\forall x\in C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x+td\in C\}.\] If \(C\) is also closed, membership can be tested from one base point: \[d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff\exists x_0	ext{\in}C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x_0+td\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction of a convex set is a direction that can be followed indefinitely from every point without leaving the set. All such directions form the recession cone. For a nonempty closed convex set, it is enough to exhibit one complete ray with base point in the set; the same direction then works from every point.
assumptions_latex: For the one-base-point equivalence and closed-cone conclusions, \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:x+td\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ t\ge0\},\quad d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff\exists x_0\in C\ \forall t\ge0:\ x_0+td\in C\] when \(C\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For closed convex \(C\), any single ray \(x_0+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\) certifies \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\).
The defining condition is equivalently \(C+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\).
special_cases_latex: The zero vector always belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
For a closed halfspace \(C=\{x:a^Tx\le b\}\), \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:a^Td\le0\}\).
For bounded closed convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a closed convex cone.
Such a set is unbounded if and only if its recession cone contains a nonzero direction.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed convex set, one ray from one base point need not certify recession from every point.
An unbounded nonclosed convex set may have no nonzero recession direction.
Recession directions describe infinite rays, not merely feasible infinitesimal directions.

notation.meaning: base point of a recession ray

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Recession Cone and Lineality of Convex Sublevel Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the recession cone and lineality space shared by all nonempty sublevel sets of a closed proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a closed proper convex function. For each \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), define \(L_\alpha=\{x\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}\). All nonempty sets \(L_\alpha\) have the same recession cone and the same lineality space, namely the recession cone of \(f\) and the constancy space of \(f\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty sublevel set of a closed proper convex function has the same recession cone and the same lineality space. These equal the function's recession cone and constancy space, respectively.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}

Then \[\bigl(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr)^\circ=\operatorname{rec}(f^*).\] If, in addition, \(f\) is closed, then \[\bigl(\operatorname{rec}f\bigr)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\!\bigl(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\bigr).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession directions and the recession cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set, and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) denote a direction vector.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The defining all-base-point condition applies to every nonempty convex set. The equivalent one-base-point test and closedness of the recession cone are stated only for closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(d\) is a recession direction of \(C\) precisely when every ray in direction \(d\) starting in \(C\) remains in \(C\). The recession cone is
\[
\operatorname{rec}C:=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall x\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x+td\in C\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(C+\operatorname{rec}C\subseteq C\). If \(C\) is also closed, then for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
d\in\operatorname{rec}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\exists x_0\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x_0+td\in C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction is a vector along which one may move indefinitely from every point of the set without leaving it. The recession cone is the set of all such vectors. For a nonempty closed convex set, it is enough to verify the entire ray condition from one point of the set; without closedness, that one-point test need not be valid.
assumptions_latex: For the one-base-point equivalence, \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:(\forall x\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x+td\in C\}\), and when \(C\) is closed, \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff(\exists x_0\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x_0+td\in C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff C+\mathbb{R}_+d\subseteq C\).
\(C+\operatorname{rec}C=C\), because \(0\in\operatorname{rec}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone containing \(0\), then \(\operatorname{rec}K=K\).
The zero vector always belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a convex cone.
If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is closed.
boundary_notes: The empty set is excluded because the universal condition would otherwise be vacuous.
For a convex set that is not closed, its recession cone need not be closed, and a ray from one base point need not establish recession from every base point.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the set C.
The ray consisting of all nonnegative scalar multiples of d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior and Closure Invariance of Recession Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the recession cones of a convex set's relative interior and closure and gives a relative-interior base-point test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex set. Then
\[
0^+(\operatorname{ri}C)=0^+(\operatorname{cl}C).
\]
Moreover, for every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and every vector \(y\),
\[
y\in0^+(\operatorname{cl}C)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x+\lambda y\in C\quad\text{for every }\lambda>0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonempty convex set, the relative interior and closure have the same recession cone. From any relative-interior point, a vector belongs to that cone exactly when every strictly positive displacement along the vector remains in the original set.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Base Direction Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infinite-ray directions from a fixed point of a convex set form a convex cone, which is closed when the set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and \(\bar x\in C\). Then \[D_C(\bar x):=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\bar x+td\in C\text{ for every }t\geq0\}\] is a convex cone. If \(C\) is closed, then \(D_C(\bar x)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_C(\bar x)\) is a convex cone, and it is closed if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This concerns directions from one specified base point, not the all-base-points recession cone.

notation.meaning: The set of recession directions based at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Ray Sequence Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set, an entire ray is feasible from a fixed point exactly when feasible points occur arbitrarily far along that ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, \(\bar x\in C\), and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\). Then \(d\) is a recession direction from \(\bar x\) if and only if there exists a sequence \(t_k\geq0\) with \(t_k\to+\infty\) and \(\bar x+t_kd\in C\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in D_C(\bar x)\iff \exists(t_k)\subseteq[0,\infty),\ t_k\to\infty,\ \bar x+t_kd\in C\text{ for every }k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This fixed-base criterion uses convexity and does not assert base-point independence.

notation.meaning: An unbounded sequence of nonnegative ray parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a recession direction from a base point when the entire ray starting at that point in the vector's direction remains in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(\bar x\in C\). A vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a recession direction of \(C\) from \(\bar x\) if \[\bar x+t d\in C\qquad\text{for every }t\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is a recession direction of \(C\) from \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\bar x+t d\in C\) for every \(t\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the ray-from-a-base-point definition; independence of the base point requires additional convexity and closedness assumptions.

notation.meaning: A chosen base point in the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Ray Criterion for a Recession Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Promotes the existence of one contained ray to recession from every base point, including relative-interior base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex set and let \(y\neq0\). If there exists \(x\) such that
\[
\{x+\lambda y\mid \lambda\geq0\}\subseteq C,
\]
then \(y\in0^+C\); equivalently,
\[
\{z+\lambda y\mid \lambda\geq0\}\subseteq C
\quad\text{for every }z\in C.
\]
Moreover, for every \(z\in\operatorname{ri}C\),
\[
\{z+\lambda y\mid \lambda\geq0\}\subseteq\operatorname{ri}C,
\]
so \(y\in0^+(\operatorname{ri}C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set and a nonzero vector y, if one entire forward ray in direction y lies in the set, then y is a recession direction from every point of the set. Rays starting in the relative interior remain in the relative interior, so y is also a recession direction of the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in0^+C,\quad \forall z\in C\ \forall\lambda\geq0:\ z+\lambda y\in C,\quad \forall z\in\operatorname{ri}C\ \forall\lambda\geq0:\ z+\lambda y\in\operatorname{ri}C,\quad y\in0^+(\operatorname{ri}C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-Exception Replacement of a Common-Recession Hypothesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A hypothesis-replacement theorem whose inherited feasibility conclusions are those of the referenced convex-system results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the full-space case \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), the original common-recession-direction hypothesis may be replaced by the existence of a finite set \(I_0\subset I\) such that every \(f_i\) with \(i\in I_0\) is affine and every common recession direction of \(\{f_i\}_{i\in I}\) is a direction of constancy of each \(f_i\) with \(i\in I\setminus I_0\). Under this replacement, the conclusions of the underlying convex-system theorem and its corollary remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex-function system on all of R^n, the usual common-recession hypothesis can be weakened: finitely many functions may be affine, while every common recession direction must leave all remaining functions constant. The conclusions of the underlying system results then remain valid.
assumptions_latex: f_i\text{ is affine for every }i\in I_0
\forall d\,\bigl[(\forall i\in I,\ d\text{ is a recession direction of }f_i)\Rightarrow(\forall i\in I\setminus I_0,\ d\text{ is a direction of constancy of }f_i)\bigr]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The original recession hypothesis may be replaced by these conditions without changing the inherited conclusions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every closed proper convex function, the conjugate at zero gives the infimum, while the conjugate's subdifferential, domain geometry, differentiability, and directional derivatives characterize attainment, bounded or unique minimizers, and finite nonattainment. All nonempty lower level sets share the function's recession cone, whose polar representation uses the conjugate domain; their support functions are generated by the conjugate and converge to its directional derivative at zero. Membership of zero in the closure of the conjugate domain is equivalent to nonnegativity of the recession function, with failure characterized by a uniform linear descent direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundedness Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set in finite dimensions is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, \(C\) is unbounded exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}C\) contains a nonzero vector.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closedness and convexity are essential for the reverse implication.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Boundary for Boundedness Detection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded nonclosed convex set may have a trivial recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[C=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a\geq0,\ 0\leq b<1\}\cup\{(0,1)\},\] the set \(C\) is convex and unbounded but \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\). Hence \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\) need not imply boundedness when closedness is omitted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The claim concerns failure of the recession cone to detect unboundedness for a nonclosed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cone of a Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of a nonempty convex cone is the cone itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex cone, then \[\operatorname{rec}K=K.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the fixed-point property of the recession operation on convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic and Closedness Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All-base-points recession vectors always form a convex cone, which is closed whenever the underlying set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a convex cone containing \(0\). If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a convex cone containing \(0\), and it is closed if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of the all-base-points recession cone does not require convexity of the underlying set.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone consists of all directions along which every point of the set can be moved by any nonnegative distance while remaining in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}C:=\bigl\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+t d\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\geq0\bigr\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses the all-base-points convention and is meaningful for any nonempty set; for a closed convex set it agrees with the single-base-point formulation.

notation.meaning: The recession cone of the set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5, Recession and Barrier Cones, p. 128

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality from Opposite Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This statement is mathematically sound but is canonically owned by the dedicated residual-lineality scope rather than this recession-cone leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and define \(\operatorname{lin}C:=\{d:C+d=C\}\). Then \[\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\bigl(-\operatorname{rec}C\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation-lineality consists exactly of recession directions whose negatives are also recession directions.

notation.meaning: The translation-lineality space of the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Cone of an Arbitrary Nonempty Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the recession-cone calculus rule for arbitrary families of closed convex sets having nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{C_i\mid i\in I\}\) be an arbitrary family of closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Then
\[
0^+\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i\in I}0^+C_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any family of closed convex subsets of Euclidean space having a nonempty common intersection, the recession cone of the intersection equals the intersection of their recession cones.
assumptions_latex: C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex for every }i\in I
