knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential and Homogenized-Cone Representations of a Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives closedness, a vanishing-scale sequential representation, and a homogenized-cone closure formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then \(0^+C\) is closed and consists precisely of all limits \(\lim_{i\to\infty}\lambda_i x_i\) for sequences \(x_i\in C\) and \(\lambda_i\downarrow0\) for which the limit exists. If
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}\{(1,x)\mid x\in C\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1},
\]
then
\[
\operatorname{cl}K=K\cup\{(0,y)\mid y\in0^+C\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex subset of Euclidean space, the recession cone is closed and is exactly the set of limits obtained by scaling points of the set by positive scalars decreasing to zero. The closure of the set's homogenized cone adds precisely the zero-height points whose spatial components belong to the recession cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0^+C\text{ is closed},\quad 0^+C=\left\{\lim_{i\to\infty}\lambda_i x_i\mid x_i\in C,\ \lambda_i\downarrow0\right\},\quad \operatorname{cl}K=K\cup\{(0,y)\mid y\in0^+C\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing-Dilation Representation of a Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the recession cone of an origin-containing closed convex set as the intersection of all its positive dilations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C\) is a closed convex set with \(0\in C\), then
\[
0^+C
=\{y\mid \varepsilon^{-1}y\in C\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}
=\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\varepsilon C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set containing the origin, a vector is in the recession cone exactly when its inverse rescaling belongs to the set for every positive scale; equivalently, the recession cone is the intersection of all positive dilations of the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Structure and Translation Characterization of the Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the recession cone of a nonempty convex set through translations that preserve the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex set. Then \(0^+C\) is a convex cone containing \(0\), and
\[
0^+C=\{y\mid C+y\subseteq C\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonempty convex set C, its recession cone is a convex cone containing the origin and consists exactly of the vectors whose translation maps C into itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0^+C\text{ is a convex cone containing }0,\qquad 0^+C=\{y\mid C+y\subseteq C\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Criterion for Closedness of a Polyhedral–Closed Convex Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient closedness condition expressed through recession directions and the lineality of the closed summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets, with \(C_1\) polyhedral and \(C_2\) closed. If \[\{d\in\operatorname{rec}C_1:-d\in\operatorname{rec}C_2\}\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C_2,\] then the Minkowski sum \(C_1+C_2\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of a nonempty polyhedral convex set and a nonempty closed convex set is closed if every recession direction of the first whose opposite is a recession direction of the second is a lineality direction of the second.
assumptions_latex: C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ are nonempty and convex}

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Failures Without Closedness or Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Base-point independence can fail for a convex set lacking closedness and for a closed set lacking convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[C_1=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a\geq0,\ 0\leq b<1\}\cup\{(0,1)\}.\] This set is convex but not closed. For \(d=(1,0)\), the ray \((0,0)+td\) lies in \(C_1\) for every \(t\geq0\), whereas \((0,1)+td\notin C_1\) for every \(t>0\). Likewise, \[C_2=\{(a,0):a\geq0\}\cup\{(0,1)\}\] is closed but not convex, and the same direction is recessionary from \((0,0)\) but not from \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two examples separately show that neither closedness nor convexity can simply be omitted from the seeded base-point-independence theorem.

notation.meaning: A nonclosed convex set exhibiting base-point dependence.
A closed nonconvex set exhibiting base-point dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point Independence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set, testing whether a ray remains in the set from any one fixed point gives the entire recession cone, so the answer does not depend on the chosen base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and fix any \(\bar x\in C\). Then \[\operatorname{rec}C=\bigl\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\bar x+t d\in C\text{ for every }t\geq0\bigr\}.\] Consequently, the set of recession directions obtained from a single base point is independent of the chosen point in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional closed-convex version. Closedness is essential for deriving an all-base-points recession direction from one infinite ray.

notation.meaning: An arbitrary fixed base point of the set.
The recession cone of the set.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.2, The Asymptotic Cone, p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Without Closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example shows that convexity alone does not promote a ray from one point to a direction valid from every point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a\ge0,\ 0\le b<1\}\cup\{(0,1)\}.\] Then \(C\) is nonempty and convex but not closed. For \(d=(1,0)\), the ray \((0,0)+td\) lies in \(C\) for every \(t\ge0\), whereas \((0,1)+td\notin C\) for every \(t>0\). Thus the fixed-base direction set depends on the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex set can contain an infinite ray from one point while the parallel ray from another point immediately leaves the set.

notation.meaning: The convex hull of a horizontal ray and the point \((0,1)\), written explicitly.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Equality for Sums and Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality-type qualifications make the recession inclusions for sums and linear images exact and guarantee closedness of the resulting set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. If \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}D)\) is a linear subspace, then \(C+D\) is closed and \[\operatorname{rec}(C+D)=\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D.\] If \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear, and \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace, then \(A(C)\) is closed and \[\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(\operatorname{rec}C).\]
assumptions_latex: For the sum assertion, \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}D)\) is a linear subspace.
For the image assertion, \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear, and \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In the respective regimes, \(C+D\) and \(A(C)\) are closed, \(\operatorname{rec}(C+D)=\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\), and \(\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(\operatorname{rec}C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These lineality qualifications provide standard sufficient conditions for the reverse inclusions omitted from the seed and also ensure closedness of the resulting sum or image.

notation.meaning: The reflection of the recession cone of \(D\) through the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictness of Sum and Image Inclusions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the vertical line to the exponential epigraph or projecting that epigraph horizontally produces recession directions not obtained from the original recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge e^x\},\qquad D=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R},\qquad A(x,y)=x.\] These are nonempty closed convex sets or maps of the required type, and \[\operatorname{rec}C=(-\mathbb{R}_+)\times\mathbb{R}_+,\qquad \operatorname{rec}D=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}.\] Moreover, \(C+D=\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(A(C)=\mathbb{R}\), whereas \[\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D=(-\mathbb{R}_+)\times\mathbb{R},\qquad A(\operatorname{rec}C)=-\mathbb{R}_+.\] Hence both corresponding recession inclusions are strict.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The same exponential-epigraph construction shows that both reverse inclusions in the seed may fail when suitable qualifications are absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Preimage Recession Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of a nonempty affine preimage is exactly the linear preimage of the target recession cone, so every kernel direction is recessionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, and let \(a\in\mathbb{R}^m\). If \[E=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax+a\in D\}\neq\varnothing,\] then \[\operatorname{rec}E=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\in\operatorname{rec}D\}=A^{-1}(\operatorname{rec}D).\] In particular, \(\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{rec}E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unlike a direct image, a nonempty affine inverse image has an exact recession formula without a closed-image qualification.

notation.meaning: The set \(\{d:Ad\in K\}\), not an inverse linear operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary-Intersection Recession Rule
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession cones commute with every nonempty intersection of closed convex sets, including intersections indexed by an arbitrary set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Then \[\operatorname{rec}\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{rec}C_i.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the arbitrary-family extension of the finite-intersection equality in the seed.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession cones commute exactly with nonempty finite intersections and Cartesian products. Sums of recession directions and linear images of recession directions always give recession directions of the corresponding sum or image, although the reverse inclusions need extra assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty closed convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\), \[\operatorname{rec}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{rec}C_i.\] For nonempty closed convex sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), \[\operatorname{rec}(C\times D)=\operatorname{rec}C\times\operatorname{rec}D.\] If \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), then \[\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D).\] For every linear map \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\), \[A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(A(C)).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty closed convex sets and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
\(A\) is a linear map of compatible finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The universally valid finite-dimensional rules are stated as equalities for intersections and products and as inclusions for sums and linear images; reverse inclusions need additional hypotheses.

notation.meaning: The Minkowski sum of two sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession calculus for basic set operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed and convex, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, and let \(W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty compact and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional calculus records unconditional intersection and product identities, a compact affine-preimage identity, and safe inclusions for sums and images. It does not assert generally false equality rules for arbitrary linear images or Minkowski sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession calculus associates set operations with the following directional rules:
\[
\operatorname{rec}\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{rec}C_i
\quad\text{when }\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing,
\]
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C_1\times\cdots\times C_r)=\operatorname{rec}C_1\times\cdots\times\operatorname{rec}C_r,
\]
and, for \(V:=\{x\in C:Ax\in W\}\neq\varnothing\),
\[
\operatorname{rec}V=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A.
\]
For nonempty convex \(C,D\), the universally valid directional inclusions are
\[
\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D),
\qquad A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(AC).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession calculus transports directions through common set operations. A nonempty intersection of closed convex sets has the intersection of their recession cones, and a Cartesian product has the product of the recession cones. Constraining a closed convex set by requiring its linear image to lie in a compact convex set retains exactly those recession directions lying in the kernel. Recession directions add under Minkowski sums and map to recession directions under linear maps, but these last two statements are inclusions unless additional hypotheses justify equality.
assumptions_latex: Every set used in the intersection identity is closed and convex, and their intersection is nonempty.
\(W\) is compact and convex, and \(V=\{x\in C:Ax\in W\}\) is nonempty.
Only nonemptiness and convexity are required for the two displayed inclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection, product, and compact-preimage recession formulas hold as displayed, while \(\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D)\) and \(A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(AC)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty affine section \(V=C\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\), \(\operatorname{rec}V=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\).
The product formula says that \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\) is a recession direction of the product exactly when \(d_i\in\operatorname{rec}C_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For two nonempty closed convex sets with nonempty intersection, \(\operatorname{rec}(C\cap D)=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\operatorname{rec}D\).
If \(A\) is injective, a nonempty compact-preimage constraint introduces no nonzero kernel direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(d_i\in\operatorname{rec}C_i\), then \(d_1+\cdots+d_r\in\operatorname{rec}(C_1+\cdots+C_r)\).
Common recession directions are precisely the directions preserved by every member of a nonempty closed-convex intersection.
boundary_notes: A linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
Equality in the image or Minkowski-sum inclusions requires additional regularity and is not part of this definition.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of C and D.
Linear image of C under A.
Nullspace of the linear map A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Minkowski Sum Under Exclusion of Opposing Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded two-set closedness and recession-calculus result for Minkowski sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty closed convex sets. Suppose there is no nonzero recession direction of C_1 whose negative is a recession direction of C_2, equivalently 0^+C_1\cap(-0^+C_2)=\{0\}. Then C_1+C_2 is closed and 0^+(C_1+C_2)=0^+C_1+0^+C_2. The hypothesis holds in particular if either C_1 or C_2 is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of two nonempty closed convex sets is closed, and its recession cone is the sum of their recession cones, when the sets have no nonzero mutually opposing recession directions. This sufficient condition is automatic if either set is bounded.
assumptions_latex: C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_1+C_2\text{ is closed},\qquad 0^+(C_1+C_2)=0^+C_1+0^+C_2;\qquad \left(C_1\text{ bounded or }C_2\text{ bounded}\right)\implies 0^+C_1\cap(-0^+C_2)=\{0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundedness characterized by the recession cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. Boundedness is with respect to the Euclidean norm, and compactness uses the usual finite-dimensional topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence is finite-dimensional and requires closedness and convexity. It distinguishes boundedness from the absence of visually apparent rays in a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession boundedness criterion classifies \(C\) by
\[
C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
C\text{ is unbounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\exists d\in\operatorname{rec}C)\;d\neq0.
\]
Since \(C\) is closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the same condition may be written
\[
C\text{ is compact}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded exactly when its only recession direction is zero. Thus unboundedness is equivalent to the existence of a nonzero direction along which every point of the set can be moved indefinitely. Because closed and bounded sets are compact in finite dimensions, trivial recession is also equivalent to compactness for this class of sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\); equivalently, \(C\) is unbounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C\) contains a nonzero vector.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((\forall d\in\operatorname{rec}C)\;d=0\iff C\) is bounded.
\(C\) is compact if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: Every nonempty compact convex set has recession cone \(\{0\}\).
A nonzero closed convex cone is unbounded and contains each of its nonzero elements as a recession direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: To certify unboundedness of a closed convex set, it suffices to exhibit one nonzero recession vector.
A closed convex feasible region with trivial recession cone is compact, so every continuous real-valued function on it attains its extrema.
boundary_notes: Closedness is essential: an unbounded convex set that is not closed can have no nonzero recession direction.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, closedness and boundedness do not imply compactness.

notation.meaning: The trivial cone consisting only of the zero vector.

For every bounded set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\),

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality space and orthogonal reduction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Let \(\operatorname{rec}C\) be its recession cone, and let orthogonality be defined by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lineality definition does not require closedness. The decomposition uses any subspace contained in the lineality space and provides a canonical reduction when that subspace is the full lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality space of \(C\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}C:=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)
 =\{d:(\forall x\in C)(\forall t\in\mathbb{R})\;x+td\in C\}.
\]
For every linear subspace \(S\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C\),
\[
C=S+(C\cap S^\perp).
\]
In particular, with \(L:=\operatorname{lin}C\), the lineality-reduced section is
\[
C_0:=C\cap L^\perp,
\qquad C=L+C_0,
\qquad \operatorname{lin}C_0=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions that are recession directions in both signs, or equivalently directions of complete affine lines contained in the set through every base point. Removing any lineality subspace by intersecting with its orthogonal complement loses no information: the original set is the Minkowski sum of that subspace and the orthogonal section. Using the entire lineality space produces a reduced convex set with no nontrivial reversible direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)\) and \(C=S+(C\cap S^\perp)\); for \(S=\operatorname{lin}C\), the orthogonal section has zero lineality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{lin}C\iff C+\mathbb{R}d=C\).
\(d\in\operatorname{lin}C\iff d,-d\in\operatorname{rec}C\).
special_cases_latex: For a convex cone \(K\), \(\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\).
If \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), then the reduction is trivial: \(C_0=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point of \(C\) admits an orthogonal decomposition \(x=\ell+x_0\) with \(\ell\in L\) and \(x_0\in C_0\).
Geometric questions invariant under translation along \(L\) can be studied on \(C_0\).
boundary_notes: Zero lineality does not imply boundedness; a pointed cone is generally unbounded.
The decomposition is orthogonal only after an inner product has been fixed.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal complement of the subspace S.

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Invariance along Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set is invariant under translation along its lineality space, which is the largest subspace with this invariance property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(L=\operatorname{lin}C\). Then \[C+L=C.\] Moreover, \(L\) is the largest linear subspace \(V\) satisfying \(C+V=C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C+L=C\), and \(C+V=C\) for a linear subspace \(V\) implies \(V\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic representation of a closed convex set as a union of affine cosets parallel to its lineality space.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the convex set.
The Minkowski sum of the set and its lineality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Spaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions along which the set extends indefinitely in both signs. It is the largest linear directional component of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}C:=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\bigl(-\operatorname{rec}C\bigr).\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{lin}C=\bigl\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+t d\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\}.\] The set \(\operatorname{lin}C\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C:=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)=\{d:x+t d\in C\ \text{for every }x\in C\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R}\}\), and this set is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lineality is defined directionally for a closed convex set; for a convex cone it is its largest contained linear subspace.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the convex set.

children.title: Lineality-Free Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Directional geometries without nontrivial reversible directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality-free sets and pointed cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. When \(C=K\) is a cone, assume \(0\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats general closed convex sets through their recession lineality and specializes to the standard pointedness condition for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality-free family in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is
\[
\mathfrak{LF}_n:=\{C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:C\neq\varnothing,\ C\text{ closed and convex},\ \operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(C\in\mathfrak{LF}_n\) exactly when \(C\) contains no affine line. For a closed convex cone \(K\), this condition becomes
\[
K\cap(-K)=\{0\},
\]
and such a cone is called pointed. Thus the pointed-cone family is
\[
\mathfrak{P}_n:=\{K:K\text{ is a closed convex cone and }K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set is lineality-free when its only reversible recession direction is zero. This is equivalent to the absence of every complete affine line in the set. In the conic case, the lineality space is the intersection of the cone with its negative, so lineality-free cones are exactly pointed cones.
assumptions_latex: For the pointed-cone specialization, \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is lineality-free iff \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), and a closed convex cone \(K\) is pointed iff \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\in\mathfrak{LF}_n\iff\nexists x\in C,\ d\neq0\text{ such that }x+\mathbb{R}d\subseteq C\).
For a cone, \(K\) is pointed iff \((d\in K\ \text{and}\ -d\in K)\Rightarrow d=0\).
special_cases_latex: The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is pointed.
Every linear subspace of positive dimension fails to be pointed when regarded as a cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: The orthogonal lineality reduction of any nonempty closed convex set belongs to a lineality-free regime.
A pointed cone has no nonzero subspace contained in it.
boundary_notes: Pointedness does not mean full dimensionality or nonempty interior.
A lineality-free closed convex set can still possess many nonzero recession directions, provided their negatives are absent.

notation.meaning: Family of nonempty closed convex sets with zero lineality.
Family of pointed closed convex cones.

source_refs.locator: §3.3, paragraph following Theorem 3.3.14 defining pointed closed convex cones by K∩(−K)={0}, and Theorem 3.3.15

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Cone Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is pointed when it contains no nonzero direction together with its negative, equivalently when its lineality space is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is pointed if \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, \(K\) contains no nonzero linear subspace and no line through the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness is the lineality-free condition for a convex cone.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Free Convex-Set Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set is line-free exactly when its lineality space is zero, or equivalently when its recession cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. The following conditions are equivalent: \[C\text{ contains no affine line},\qquad \operatorname{lin}C=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{rec}C\text{ is pointed}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) contains no affine line if and only if \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), equivalently if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An affine line means a set of the form \(x+\mathbb{R}d\) with \(d\neq0\).

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the set.
The recession cone of the set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111; 6.5, Recession and Barrier Cones, p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Lineality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Line-free geometry fails precisely when a nonzero recession direction and its negative are both present. The half-plane cone given by a free horizontal coordinate and a nonnegative vertical coordinate has the entire horizontal axis as residual lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the line-free regime fails exactly when \[\operatorname{lin}C\neq\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exists }d\neq0\text{ with }d\in\operatorname{rec}C\text{ and }-d\in\operatorname{rec}C.\] For example, if \(C=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_+\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), then \[\operatorname{rec}C=C,\qquad \operatorname{lin}C=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\},\] so \(C\) is not pointed despite retaining a pointed component in the second coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lineality is nontrivial exactly when there exists \(d\neq0\) with \(d,-d\in\operatorname{rec}C\); for \(C=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_+\), \(\operatorname{lin}C=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The record identifies the exact boundary where pointed or line-free geometry fails and includes a concrete closed convex cone with residual lineality.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111; 6.5, Recession and Barrier Cones, p. 128

children.title: Quotient Geometry by Lineality
children.top_down_role: Reduction from degenerate directional geometry to a pointed quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Quotients and the Proper-Subspace Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full lineality quotient of a closed finite-dimensional cone is closed. Removing only a proper subspace of lineality leaves precisely the remaining quotient lineality and does not produce a pointed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone with lineality space \(L\). Then \(K/L\) is closed. More generally, if \(M\subseteq L\) is a linear subspace and \(\pi_M:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/M\) is the quotient map, then \[\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(K))=L/M.\] Consequently, \(\pi_M(K)\) is pointed if and only if \(M=L\); quotienting by a proper subspace of \(L\) leaves nonzero lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K/L\) is closed, \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(K))=L/M\), and \(\pi_M(K)\) is pointed exactly when \(M=L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closedness of quotient cones and the exact failure of pointedness when less than the full lineality space is removed.

notation.meaning: A subspace of the lineality space used for a possibly incomplete quotient.
The residual lineality in the quotient by \(M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Quotient by Full Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a convex cone by all of its lineality produces a pointed cone, while the original cone is exactly the full inverse image of the quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone, let \(L=K\cap(-K)\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) be the quotient map. Then \[\pi^{-1}(\pi(K))=K,\qquad \pi(K)\cap(-\pi(K))=\{L\}.\] Thus \(K/L:=\pi(K)\) is a pointed convex cone and \(K\) is recovered as its full inverse image.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract quotient representation of a convex cone after identifying vectors differing by a lineality direction; closedness is not required.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the cone.
The canonical quotient map modulo lineality.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Geometry by Lineality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical reduction of a convex cone to a pointed cone in the quotient by its lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(L=K\cap(-K)\), and let \(\pi:V\to V/L\) be the quotient map. Then \(\pi(K)\) is a pointed convex cone and \[\pi(K)\cap\bigl(-\pi(K)\bigr)=\{0_{V/L}\},\qquad \pi^{-1}(\pi(K))=K.\] Thus quotienting by the maximal subspace \(L\) removes exactly the bidirectional component of \(K\), while \(K\) is recovered as the full inverse image of its pointed quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a convex cone by its lineality produces a pointed cone and retains the original cone as the quotient cone's full inverse image.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(\pi:V\to V/L\) is the canonical quotient map.

notation.meaning: canonical map from V to the quotient V/L
zero coset in the quotient space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quotient reduction by the lineality space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(L:=\operatorname{lin}C\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) be the canonical quotient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The quotient is finite-dimensional. Its concrete Euclidean realization uses the unique orthogonal representative in \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quotient geometry of \(C\) by its lineality is the image
\[
\overline C:=\pi(C)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n/L,
\qquad \pi(x)=x+L.
\]
Identifying \(\mathbb{R}^n/L\) isometrically with \(L^\perp\) by choosing the orthogonal representative of each coset gives
\[
\overline C\cong C_0:=C\cap L^\perp,
\qquad C=L+C_0.
\]
Under this identification,
\[
\operatorname{rec}C_0=\operatorname{rec}C\cap L^\perp,
\qquad \operatorname{lin}C_0=\{0\}.
\]
Thus quotienting collapses precisely the reversible directions and retains a lineality-free directional geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotient geometry identifies points of a closed convex set that differ by an element of its lineality space. Every coset has a unique representative orthogonal to that space, and the quotient set is therefore represented concretely by the intersection of the original set with the orthogonal complement. Its recession cone is the orthogonal part of the original recession cone, and it has no nonzero lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\operatorname{lin}C\), and \(\pi\) is the canonical quotient map.
The quotient is represented using the Euclidean orthogonal complement \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(C)\cong C\cap L^\perp\), \(C=L+(C\cap L^\perp)\), and the reduced set has lineality \(\{0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x,y\in C\) represent the same quotient point iff \(x-y\in L\).
The quotient class \(x+L\) is represented by \(P_{L^\perp}x\in C\cap L^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\{0\}\), then \(\mathbb{R}^n/L\cong\mathbb{R}^n\) and no reduction occurs.
If \(C=L\) is a subspace, then \(\pi(C)=\{0+L\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For a convex cone \(K\), the reduced cone \(K\cap L^\perp\) is pointed.
The dimension of the quotient ambient space is \(n-\dim L\).
boundary_notes: The quotient removes lineality but does not remove one-sided recession directions.
The concrete orthogonal section depends on the chosen inner product, although the abstract quotient does not.

notation.meaning: Canonical map to the quotient by L.
Image of C in the quotient space.
Orthogonal projection onto the complement of L.

children.top_down_role: Conic generation, dimensional regimes, and extremal directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural data of a convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). All spans, dimensions, closures, and interiors are taken in the finite-dimensional Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates conicity, convexity, dimensional structure, lineality, and extremal rays. Closedness is an additional property rather than part of the bare convex-cone definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(K\) is a convex cone when
\[
(\forall x,y\in K)(\forall\alpha,\beta\geq0)\quad \alpha x+\beta y\in K.
\]
Its structural data include
\[
\operatorname{span}K:=K-K,\qquad \dim K:=\dim(\operatorname{span}K),
\qquad \operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K).
\]
It is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{span}K=\mathbb{R}^n\), and proper when it is closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior. For \(u\in K\setminus\{0\}\), the ray \(R_u:=\mathbb{R}_+u\) is extreme when
\[
x,y\in K,\ x+y\in R_u\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in R_u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is closed under all nonnegative linear combinations. Its basic structure consists of its linear span and dimension, its lineality subspace, and its rays. Pointed cones have no nonzero reversible direction; full-dimensional cones span the ambient space; proper cones are closed, convex, pointed, and solid. A ray is extreme when a vector on it cannot be decomposed into two cone vectors lying outside that ray.
assumptions_latex: For the proper-cone designation, \(K\) is closed and has nonempty interior in addition to being convex and pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed closure under nonnegative combinations defines a convex cone, with span, dimension, lineality, pointedness, full-dimensionality, properness, and extreme rays defined as displayed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone iff \(K+K\subseteq K\) and \(\lambda K\subseteq K\) for every \(\lambda\geq0\).
\(R_u\) is extreme iff it is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).
special_cases_latex: Every linear subspace is a convex cone whose lineality equals the entire cone.
The nonnegative orthant is a proper cone in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty convex cone contains \(0\).
The closure of a convex cone is again a convex cone.
boundary_notes: A cone need not be convex or closed unless these properties are imposed.
A full-dimensional cone need not be pointed, and a pointed cone need not be full-dimensional.

notation.meaning: Ray generated by the nonzero vector u.
Dimension of the linear span of K.

children.title: Conic Generator Systems
children.top_down_role: Generation of cones from rays and arbitrary sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic hulls and generator systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be arbitrary. A finite sum over the empty index set is not used; the zero vector is obtained by taking all coefficients equal to zero in a nonempty finite combination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation is algebraic and uses finite nonnegative combinations. Closure is not inserted into the conic-hull operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conic hull generated by \(S\) is
\[
\operatorname{cone}S:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i:
 r\in\mathbb{N},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.
\]
A subset \(G\subseteq K\) is a generator system for a convex cone \(K\) when
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}G.
\]
For a finite list \(G=\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}\), this means
\[
K=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j a_j:\mu_j\geq0\right\}.
\]
The system is irredundant when \(a_j\notin\operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{a_j\})\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull of a set consists of all finite nonnegative linear combinations of its elements. A generator system for a cone is a subset whose conic hull equals the cone. A finite generator system gives a matrix-style representation by nonnegative coefficients, and it is irredundant when no listed generator can be generated by the remaining ones.
assumptions_latex: For a generator system, \(K\) is a convex cone and \(G\subseteq K\).
For irredundancy, \(G\) is a finite listed family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}S\) is the set of finite nonnegative combinations of points of \(S\), and \(G\) generates \(K\) exactly when \(K=\operatorname{cone}G\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_r]\), then \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}=\{A\mu:\mu\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\}\).
\(\operatorname{cone}S\) is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(S=\{u\}\) with \(u\neq0\), \(\operatorname{cone}S=\mathbb{R}_+u\) is a ray.
A linear subspace with basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_k\) is generated conically by \(\{\pm b_1,ldots,\pm b_k\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Scaling a generator by a positive scalar does not change its generated ray.
If \(G_1\subseteq G_2\), then \(\operatorname{cone}G_1\subseteq\operatorname{cone}G_2\).
boundary_notes: For infinite \(S\), the algebraic conic hull need not be closed.
Irredundancy of vectors is not the same as uniqueness of nonnegative coefficients.

notation.meaning: Matrix form of a finite conic combination.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Hull Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algebraic conic hull can be nonclosed; the displayed set generates the open positive quadrant together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{(1,t):t>0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), one has \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}\), which is not closed; for example, \((1,1/k)\to(1,0)\notin\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This distinguishes the algebraic conic hull from the closed conic hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Hull Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic hull is monotone and idempotent, converts unions into sums, and commutes with linear maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and a linear map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \(\operatorname{cone}(S\cup T)=\operatorname{cone}(S)+\operatorname{cone}(T)\) and \(A(\operatorname{cone}S)=\operatorname{cone}(A(S))\). Moreover, \(S\subseteq T\) implies \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{cone}(T)\), and \(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{cone}S)=\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are algebraic identities; no topological closure is taken.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Carathéodory Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of a conic hull has a conic representation using at most the dimension of the span many linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}S)\). Every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}(S)\) can be written as \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i s_i\), where \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(r\le d\), and the selected nonzero \(s_i\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i s_i\) for some \(r\le d\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and linearly independent nonzero \(s_i\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The sharp bound uses the dimension of the span of S, not necessarily the ambient dimension.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of S.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull of a subset S of Euclidean space consists of all finite nonnegative linear combinations of elements of S, including the empty combination, which equals zero. Thus the conic hull of the empty set is {0}, and the conic hull of S is the smallest convex cone containing S.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its conic hull is
\[
\operatorname{cone}(S):=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.
\]
The sum for \(m=0\) is interpreted as \(0\), so \(\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq 0\right\}\), where the sum for \(m=0\) equals \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real-vector-space definition, with the convention that the conic hull always contains the origin.

notation.meaning: Conic hull of the set S.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Section 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Rescaling Invariance of Generator Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent positive rescaling of generators, and insertion or deletion of zero generators, leaves the generated cone unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), choose \(\alpha_s>0\) for every \(s\in S\setminus\{0\}\), and set \(T=\{\alpha_s s:s\in S\setminus\{0\}\}\). Then \(\operatorname{cone}(T)=\operatorname{cone}(S)\). Consequently, if \(S\) generates \(K\), then so does \(T\), and adjoining or deleting zero generators has no effect.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generators may be rescaled independently; zero vectors may be inserted or removed without changing the generated cone.

notation.meaning: Positive scale assigned to generator s.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Generating Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset S of a convex cone K is a cone generating set when every element of K is a finite nonnegative linear combination of elements of S.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone. A subset \(S\subseteq K\) is a cone generating set for \(K\) precisely when
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(S).
\]
Thus every \(x\in K\) is a finite nonnegative linear combination of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition permits finite or infinite generating sets and does not require generators to be normalized.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Section 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Generator Systems Need Not Exist
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinitely generated nonclosed cone may have no inclusion-minimal generating system; the open positive quadrant together with the origin is an example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y>0\}\). Then \(K\) is generated, for example, by \(S=\{(1,t):t>0\}\), but it has no inclusion-minimal generating set. Indeed, for any generating set, the slopes of its nonzero elements must have infimum \(0\) and be unbounded above; deleting any one generator preserves those two properties and hence still generates \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no inclusion-minimal set \(S\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example concerns algebraic generation by arbitrary, possibly infinite sets; it does not contradict existence of irredundant systems for pointed finitely generated cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Generator Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-minimal finite generating systems for convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a finitely generated convex cone. A finite set \(G\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) is a minimal generator system for \(K\) if
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(G)\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{g\})\neq K\ \text{for every }g\in G.
\]
This is inclusion minimality: no generator can be deleted while retaining generation. It does not impose a normalization on generators, so positive rescaling of individual members preserves minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite generator system is minimal when it generates the cone but deleting any one generator destroys that property.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a finitely generated convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is minimal exactly when it generates \(K\) and no proper subset obtained by one deletion generates \(K\).

children.title: Proper Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Closed, pointed, and solid cone regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Failures of Proper-Cone Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray lacks solidity, a halfspace lacks pointedness, and the open positive quadrant with the origin lacks closedness, showing that the proper-cone hypotheses are independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), \(K_1=\mathbb R_+\times\{0\}\) is closed, convex, and pointed but not solid; \(K_2=\{(x,y):y\ge0\}\) is closed, convex, and solid but not pointed; and \(K_3=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}\) is convex, pointed, and solid but not closed. Hence none of solidity, pointedness, or closedness follows from the other two conditions.
assumptions_latex: The proper-cone convention requires convexity, closedness, pointedness, and nonempty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closedness, pointedness, and solidity are nonredundant requirements in the proper-cone definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These examples show why pointedness, solidity, and closedness cannot be dropped from the adopted definition.

notation.meaning: Cones witnessing distinct failures of properness.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper cone in finite-dimensional Euclidean space is a closed convex cone that contains no nontrivial line and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is proper if it is convex and closed, is pointed in the sense that
\[
K\cap(-K)=\{0\},
\]
and is solid in the sense that
\[
\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is proper exactly when it is convex and closed, \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the common finite-dimensional convention that a proper cone is closed, convex, pointed, and solid; some sources use different terminology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finitely generated and polyhedral cone classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(r,s\) denote positive integers, and let all generator and normal vectors lie in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence of finite generation and polyhedrality is finite-dimensional. The class includes cones with lineality and cones of dimension smaller than the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the finitely generated cone class and the polyhedral cone class by
\[
\mathcal{FG}_n:=\left\{\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}:r<\infty\right\},
\]
\[
\mathcal{PC}_n:=\left\{\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:b_j^Tx\leq0, j=1,\ldots,s\}:s<\infty\right\}.
\]
The finite-dimensional Minkowski–Weyl correspondence identifies these classes:
\[
\mathcal{FG}_n=\mathcal{PC}_n.
\]
A cone in either class is therefore called finitely generated or polyhedral. If it admits linearly independent generators \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) with \(k=\dim K\), it is simplicial in its span.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely generated cone is the conic hull of finitely many vectors. A polyhedral cone is the intersection of finitely many homogeneous closed halfspaces. In finite-dimensional spaces these are exactly the same class. A cone is simplicial in its span when it can be generated by as many linearly independent vectors as its dimension.
assumptions_latex: The generator list and homogeneous inequality list are finite.
For the simplicial designation, the chosen generators are linearly independent and their number equals \(\dim K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is finitely generated if and only if it is polyhedral, i.e. \(\mathcal{FG}_n=\mathcal{PC}_n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\in\mathcal{FG}_n\iff K=A\mathbb{R}_+^r\) for some finite matrix \(A\).
\(K\in\mathcal{PC}_n\iff K=\{x:Bx\leq0\}\) for some finite matrix \(B\).
special_cases_latex: Every ray and every finitely generated linear subspace belongs to \(\mathcal{FG}_n\).
The nonnegative orthant is both simplicial and polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finitely generated cone in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed.
Every polyhedral cone possesses a finite generator system.
boundary_notes: The equality of the two classes is a finite-dimensional result.
A finite generator list need not be irredundant or unique.

notation.meaning: Class of finitely generated cones in R^n.
Class of polyhedral cones in R^n.

source_refs.locator: §2.3.1, definitions of polyhedral and finitely generated cones, and Proposition 2.3.2, “Minkowski-Weyl Theorem”

knowledge_statements.title: Duals of Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a finitely generated cone is cut out by one inequality per displayed generator and is itself finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), then \(K^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,v_i\rangle\ge0, i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Hence \(K^*\) is polyhedral and therefore finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The positive-dual convention \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\) is used.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces Inherit Finite Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a finitely generated cone is generated by precisely those displayed generators that lie in the face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) and \(F\) is a face of \(K\), then \(F=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:v_i\in F\}\). In particular, every face of a finitely generated cone is finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formula applies to every face, including the zero face and the whole cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of the Finite-Generation Class under Conic Operations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear images, finite sums, finite intersections, and finite products of finitely generated cones are again finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite-dimensional finitely generated cones are closed under linear images, finite Minkowski sums, finite intersections, and finite Cartesian products. Thus, if \(K_1,\ldots,K_p\) are finitely generated and \(A\) is linear, then \(A(K_1)\), \(K_1+\cdots+K_p\), \(K_1\cap\cdots\cap K_p\), and \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_p\) are finitely generated cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K_1,\ldots,K_p\) are finitely generated cones in finite-dimensional spaces.
\(A\) is a linear map with finite-dimensional codomain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All spaces and indexed families are finite-dimensional and finite, respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski–Weyl Theorem for Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional convex cone is finitely generated exactly when it is the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) for some finite family, and \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\) for some finite matrix \(A\). Thus finitely generated cones are exactly polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is finitely generated if and only if \(K\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the homogeneous finite-dimensional Minkowski–Weyl equivalence.

notation.meaning: Matrix whose rows define homogeneous linear inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex cones generated by finitely many vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone. The cone \(K\) is finitely generated if there exist \(m\in\mathbb{N}_0\) and vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\in E\) such that
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\})=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\geq0\right\}.
\]
In finite-dimensional real vector spaces, finitely generated cones are exactly polyhedral cones, meaning intersections of finitely many closed homogeneous halfspaces. In particular, every finitely generated cone is convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional real vector space, a cone is finitely generated when finitely many vectors generate it by nonnegative combinations; these cones are exactly the polyhedral cones.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is finitely generated exactly when \(K=\operatorname{cone}(\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\})\) for some finite family; equivalently, \(K\) is polyhedral.

source_refs.locator: §19. Polyhedral Convex Sets and Functions p. 170

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Dual of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside its span, the dual of a simplicial cone is generated by the dual basis and is again simplicial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}K\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) be simplicial. If \(w_1,\ldots,w_d\in L\) is the dual basis, \(\langle w_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\), then \(K_L^*:=\{y\in L:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}=\operatorname{cone}\{w_1,\ldots,w_d\}\). Thus the relative dual is simplicial.
assumptions_latex: \(w_1,\ldots,w_d\) is dual to the simplicial generator basis.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a non-full-dimensional cone, the ambient dual additionally contains \((\operatorname{span}K)^\perp\); simpliciality here concerns the dual inside the span.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Face Lattice of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a simplicial cone is generated by a subset of its rays, so its face lattice is Boolean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) be simplicial. Its faces are exactly \(F_I=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:i\in I\}\), where \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Moreover, \(\dim F_I=|I|\), and inclusion, intersection, and generated join correspond respectively to subset inclusion, intersection, and union of index sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empty subset corresponds to the zero face and the full subset to K.

notation.meaning: Face generated by the rays indexed by I.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Representation and Unique Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A d-dimensional simplicial cone is linearly isomorphic to the nonnegative orthant and every point has unique nonnegative coordinates in its ray generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) with \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) linearly independent, then \(T:\mathbb R^d\to\operatorname{span}K\), \(T(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i v_i\), is an isomorphism satisfying \(T(\mathbb R_+^d)=K\). Consequently every \(x\in K\) has a unique representation \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i v_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mathbb R_+^d)=K\), and every \(x\in K\) has unique nonnegative coordinates in \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The isomorphism is between the cone's span and \(\mathbb R^d\), so it covers cones not full-dimensional in the ambient space.

notation.meaning: Coordinate isomorphism from the orthant to K.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cones generated by linearly independent rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone, and set \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\). The cone \(K\) is simplicial if there exist linearly independent nonzero vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\in E\) such that
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}).
\]
Equivalently, \(K\), considered within \(\operatorname{span}K\), is linearly isomorphic to the nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\). The coefficients in the representation of each element of \(K\) relative to \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) are unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial cone of dimension d is generated by d linearly independent rays, is linearly equivalent within its span to the nonnegative orthant, and has unique coefficients relative to those generators.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial exactly when it has \(d\) linearly independent generators.

notation.meaning: dimension of the linear span of K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine independence and the difference-vector criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point configurations in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let m\ge 0 and b_0,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb{R}^n. The points are affinely independent precisely when \dim\operatorname{aff}\{b_0,\ldots,b_m\}=m. Since \operatorname{aff}\{b_0,\ldots,b_m\}=b_0+\operatorname{span}\{b_1-b_0,\ldots,b_m-b_0\}, this is equivalent to linear independence of b_1-b_0,\ldots,b_m-b_0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A collection of m+1 points is affinely independent when its affine hull has dimension m. Equivalently, after fixing any one point as the base point, the differences from that point to the other m points are linearly independent.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependent Displayed Generators Do Not Imply Nonsimpliciality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone can have a dependent finite presentation while remaining simplicial; redundant generators must first be removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2\}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2\}=\mathbb R_+^2\). The displayed three-generator family is linearly dependent and redundant, but \(K\) is simplicial.
assumptions_latex: \(e_1,e_2\) are the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2\}\) is simplicial despite its dependent displayed generating family.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsimpliciality concerns the existence of an independent generating system, not whether a particular presentation is dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Extreme-Ray Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed nonsimplicial finitely generated cone has more extreme rays than its dimension and some nonzero point has two different decompositions using extreme-ray generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be pointed and finitely generated, let \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\), and choose nonzero representatives \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) of its distinct extreme rays. If \(K\) is nonsimplicial, then \(r>d\), and there exist distinct \(\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R_+^r\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i v_i=\sum_{i=1}^r\mu_i v_i\ne0\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is pointed, finitely generated, and nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The claim concerns representatives of all distinct extreme rays of a pointed nonsimplicial cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsimplicial Finite Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-ray criterion for pointed finitely generated cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a pointed finitely generated cone, and set \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\). Then \(K\) has finitely many extreme rays and
\[
K\text{ is simplicial}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\text{ has exactly }d\text{ extreme rays}.
\]
Consequently, \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if it has more than \(d\) extreme rays. In that case, any family consisting of exactly one nonzero representative from each extreme ray is linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed finitely generated d-dimensional cone is nonsimplicial exactly when it has more than d extreme rays; one representative from each extreme ray then forms a linearly dependent family.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a pointed finitely generated cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if the number of its extreme rays exceeds \(d\).

notation.meaning: dimension of the linear span of K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, exposed faces, and extreme rays of a cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone containing \(0\). Let \(K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces and extreme rays are defined for arbitrary convex cones. The generation consequence is stated only for nontrivial closed pointed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex subset \(F\subseteq K\) is a face of \(K\) when
\[
x,y\in K,\ 0<\lambda<1,\ \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in F.
\]
It is exposed when there exists \(y\in K^\circ\) such that
\[
F=K\cap y^\perp=\{x\in K:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.
\]
For \(u\in K\setminus\{0\}\), the ray \(\mathbb{R}_+u\) is an extreme ray exactly when it is a one-dimensional face; equivalently,
\[
x_1,x_2\in K,\ x_1+x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+u
\Rightarrow x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a convex cone is a convex subset that contains both endpoints whenever it contains an interior point of a segment in the cone. An exposed face is obtained by intersecting the cone with a supporting hyperplane through the origin. Extreme rays are precisely the one-dimensional faces and are characterized by indecomposability: a vector on the ray cannot be written as a sum of cone vectors outside the ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Faces, exposed faces, and extreme rays are characterized by the displayed segment, supporting-hyperplane, and decomposition conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathbb{R}_+u\) is extreme iff it is a half-line face emanating from the origin.
For a cone, a nonempty exposed face has the form \(K\cap y^\perp\) for a polar vector \(y\).
special_cases_latex: The faces \(\{0\}\) and \(K\) are called improper faces when they satisfy the face condition.
If \(K\) is closed, pointed, and nonzero, vectors chosen from all extreme rays generate \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed ray is an extreme ray.
A face of a face of \(K\) is a face of \(K\).
boundary_notes: Not every face of a general closed convex cone is exposed.
A cone with nonzero lineality has no extreme rays in directions affected by that lineality; facial analysis is commonly reduced modulo the lineality space.

notation.meaning: Optional notation indicating that F is a face of K.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence Boundary for Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero closed finite-dimensional convex cone has an extreme ray exactly when it is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\ne\{0\}\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space. Then \[K\text{ has an extreme ray}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\text{ is pointed}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\ne\{0\}\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) possesses an extreme ray if and only if \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional existence criterion for nonzero closed convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional faces of a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone and let \(r\in K\setminus\{0\}\). The ray \(R=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) if, whenever \(x,y\in K\) and \(x+y\in R\), one has \(x,y\in R\). Equivalently, \(R\) is a one-dimensional face of \(K\). The definition depends only on the ray, since replacing \(r\) by any positive multiple leaves \(R\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray is extreme when a sum of two cone elements can lie on it only if both summands lie on that same ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is extreme exactly when \(x+y\in R\) with \(x,y\in K\) implies \(x,y\in R\).

notation.meaning: ray generated by the nonzero vector r

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Is Contained in Every Nonempty Conic Face
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face is a cone containing the original cone's lineality space; the origin is a face exactly for pointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(K\). Then \(F\) is a convex cone and \[\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\subseteq F.\] Consequently, \(\{0\}\) is a face of \(K\) if and only if \(K\) is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a convex cone, \(\operatorname{lin}K\subseteq F\), and \(\{0\}\unlhd K\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural constraint on the facial hierarchy of a convex cone.

notation.meaning: F is a face of K.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection and Transitivity of Conic Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of a cone are closed under intersections, and a face of a face is a face of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every intersection of nonempty faces of a convex cone \(K\) is a face of \(K\). Moreover, if \(G\) is a face of \(F\) and \(F\) is a face of \(K\), then \(G\) is a face of \(K\).
assumptions_latex: Faces use the ordinary segment criterion, equivalently the additive conic criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_i\unlhd K\Rightarrow\bigcap_iF_i\unlhd K\), and \(G\unlhd F\unlhd K\Rightarrow G\unlhd K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary closure properties of the facial hierarchy of a convex cone.

notation.meaning: F is a face of K.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces specialized to convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone. A convex cone \(F\subseteq K\) is a face of \(K\) if
\[
x,y\in K,
\quad x+y\in F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in F.
\]
Equivalently, viewed as a convex subset, \(F\) has the segment-face property: if a point of the relative interior of a segment \([x,y]\subseteq K\) lies in \(F\), then both endpoints lie in \(F\). The sets \(\{0\}\) and \(K\) are faces whenever \(K\) is pointed for the former.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic face absorbs both cone summands whenever their sum belongs to it; this agrees with the usual segment definition of a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a face of \(K\) exactly when \(x+y\in F\) and \(x,y\in K\) imply \(x,y\in F\).

notation.meaning: closed line segment joining x and y

knowledge_statements.title: Ray-Face Incidence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme rays of a face F are exactly the extreme rays of the ambient cone K that lie in F.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a face of a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(R\subseteq F\) be a nonzero ray. Then
\[
R\text{ is an extreme ray of }F
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R\text{ is an extreme ray of }K.
\]
Consequently, the extreme rays incident with \(F\) are exactly the extreme rays of \(K\) that are contained in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is an extreme ray of \(F\) if and only if \(R\) is an extreme ray of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This incidence statement applies only to rays contained in the specified face.

notation.meaning: Nonzero ray contained in the face.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar and dual cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, with the standard inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). The polar convention uses nonpositive pairings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity is defined for an arbitrary nonempty set. Its value is always a closed convex cone, independently of whether the original set is closed, convex, or conic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar cone and positive dual cone of \(C\) are
\[
C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall x\in C)\;\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\},
\qquad C^*:=-C^\circ
 =\{y:(\forall x\in C)\;\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\}.
\]
Polarity is order reversing:
\[
C\subseteq D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ.
\]
It ignores closure, convexification, and conic generation:
\[
C^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}C)^\circ=(\operatorname{conv}C)^\circ=(\operatorname{cone}C)^\circ.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone contains the vectors pairing nonpositively with every point of the original set. The positive dual cone is its negative and uses nonnegative pairings. Polarity reverses inclusions and depends only on the closed convex cone generated by the original set. The polar is always a closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean inner product fixes the polarity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\), \(C^*=-C^\circ\), and polarity is antitone and invariant under closure, convex hull, and conic hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{cone}S\), then \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,s\rangle\leq0\ \forall s\in S\}\).
For a subspace \(L\), \(L^\circ=L^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: \((\mathbb{R}_+^n)^\circ=\mathbb{R}_-^n\) and \((\mathbb{R}_+^n)^*=\mathbb{R}_+^n\).
\(\{0\}^\circ=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \((\mathbb{R}^n)^\circ=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(C^\circ\) is a closed convex cone.
For cones \(K_1,K_2\), \((K_1+K_2)^\circ=K_1^\circ\cap K_2^\circ\).
boundary_notes: Some sources use the symbol \(C^*\) for the nonpositive polar; the sign convention must therefore be checked.
The polar cannot distinguish a set from its closed convex conic hull.

notation.meaning: Positive dual cone, equal to the negative polar.

source_refs.locator: §2.2, definition of the polar cone and Proposition 2.2.1(a)

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Calculus for Conic Sums and Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity converts conic sums into intersections and intersections into closures of sums of polar cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\) be closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional inner-product space. Then \[(K+L)^\circ=K^\circ\cap L^\circ,\qquad (K\cap L)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(K^\circ+L^\circ).\] The closure in the second identity may be omitted when \(K^\circ+L^\circ\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(K,L\) are closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic rules for negative polar cones, including the necessary closure boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Depends Only on the Closed Convex Conic Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking a polar retains only the closed convex cone generated by the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every subset \(C\) of a real Hilbert space, \[C^\circ=(\operatorname{cone}C)^\circ=(\overline{\operatorname{cone}C})^\circ,\] where \(\operatorname{cone}C\) denotes the convex conic hull. Thus a generating set and the closed convex cone it generates impose exactly the same polar inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The polar uses the nonpositive-pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical invariance and generator representation of a polar cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Cone Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone of C consists of all vectors having nonpositive inner product with every element of C. It is a closed convex cone, and polarity reverses set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\). The polar cone of \(C\) is
\[
C^{\circ}:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in C\}
=\bigcap_{x\in C}\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\}.
\]
It is always a closed convex cone, and \(C\subseteq D\) implies \(D^{\circ}\subseteq C^{\circ}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ}=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }x\in C\}\), and \(C^{\circ}\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the polar-cone convention with nonpositive inner products; the dual cone under the nonnegative convention is \(-C^{\circ}\).

notation.meaning: Polar cone of C under the nonpositive-pairing convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar completion of a set or cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and use the nonpositive polar \(C^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The general formula applies to an arbitrary nonempty set. Its specializations distinguish arbitrary cones, convex cones, and closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bipolar completion operator is
\[
\mathcal{B}(C):=C^{\circ\circ}=(C^\circ)^\circ.
\]
The cone bipolar theorem gives
\[
C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C).
\]
Equivalently, if \(K\) is already a cone,
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}K).
\]
Consequently, for a convex cone \(K\),
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K,
\]
and for a closed convex cone, \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar is obtained by applying the polar operation twice. For any nonempty set it equals the closed convex cone generated by that set. If the original object is a cone, the bipolar is its closed convex hull; if it is already convex, the bipolar merely closes it; and if it is closed and convex, polarity twice recovers it exactly.
assumptions_latex: The same inner product and nonpositive-polar convention are used in both polar operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C)\), with the stated cone, convex-cone, and closed-convex-cone specializations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}\) is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(C\).
\(x\in C^{\circ\circ}\iff\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\) satisfying \(\langle y,c\rangle\leq0\) for all \(c\in C\).
special_cases_latex: For a subspace \(L\), \(L^{\circ\circ}=L\).
For a ray \(K=\mathbb{R}_+u\), \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The bipolar operator is extensive, monotone, and idempotent.
Two nonempty sets have the same polar exactly when their closed convex conic hulls coincide.
boundary_notes: Exact recovery of the original set fails unless it is a closed convex cone.
The formula concerns conic polarity and differs from polar-set constructions normalized by an inequality such as \(\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\).
