knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Cone Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space, taking the polar cone twice recovers the original cone exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(K\subseteq H\) be a closed convex cone. Define
\[
K^{\circ}:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.
\]
Then the bipolar recovers the cone exactly:
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=K.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq H\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone bipolar theorem in a real Hilbert space, specialized to exact recovery of a closed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact recovery as a bipolar fixed point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty cone, and define \(K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record isolates the exact-recovery regime from the more general bipolar closure formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed convex-cone recovery class is the fixed-point family
\[
\operatorname{Fix}(\circ\circ):=\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:K\neq\varnothing,\ K^{\circ\circ}=K\}.
\]
It is exactly the family of nonempty closed convex cones:
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=K
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\text{ is a closed convex cone}.
\]
Equivalently, every closed convex cone admits the exact halfspace representation
\[
K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall y\in K^\circ)\;\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is recovered exactly from all of its polar inequalities precisely when it is closed and convex. Thus the fixed points of the double-polar operation are exactly the nonempty closed convex cones. In that regime, membership in the cone is equivalent to satisfying every homogeneous linear inequality indexed by its polar cone.
assumptions_latex: Polarity is taken with respect to the Euclidean inner product and the nonpositive convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\) if and only if \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in K\iff\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K^\circ\).
Closed convex cones are exactly the fixed points of the closure operator \(C\mapsto C^{\circ\circ}\).
special_cases_latex: Every closed linear subspace satisfies \(L^{\circ\circ}=L\).
Every polyhedral cone is recovered exactly because it is closed and convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed convex cone is completely determined by its polar cone.
If two closed convex cones have identical polars, then the cones are equal.
boundary_notes: Closedness and convexity are both essential for exact recovery.
The result recovers the cone as a set; it does not select a finite inequality representation.

notation.meaning: Fixed-point family of the bipolar operator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Constrained Fenchel Duality, Attainment, and Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional duality for minimizing a closed proper convex function over a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be closed proper convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and define
\[
K^*=\{x^*:\langle x^*,x\rangle\ge 0\ \forall x\in K\}.
\]
Then
\[
\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\inf_{x^*\in K^*}f^*(x^*)
\]
provided either (a) \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}K\ne\varnothing\), or (b) \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\cap\operatorname{ri}K^*\ne\varnothing\). Under (a), the infimum of \(f^*\) over \(K^*\) is attained; under (b), the infimum of \(f\) over \(K\) is attained. If \(K\) is polyhedral, \(\operatorname{ri}K\) and \(\operatorname{ri}K^*\) may respectively be replaced by \(K\) and \(K^*\). Moreover, for any \(x,x^*\),
\[
f(x)=\inf_K f=-\inf_{K^*}f^*=-f^*(x^*)
\]
if and only if
\[
x^*\in\partial f(x),\quad x\in K,\quad x^*\in K^*,\quad\langle x,x^*\rangle=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a closed proper convex function over a nonempty closed convex cone is dual to minimizing its conjugate over the positive dual cone, with a sign reversal. Either a primal or dual relative-interior intersection gives equality and the corresponding opposite-side attainment; polyhedral cones permit ordinary cone membership in those qualifications. A primal–dual pair is optimal with equal values exactly when it satisfies subgradient membership, cone feasibility, dual-cone feasibility, and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is closed proper convex on }\mathbb{R}^n
K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a nonempty closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\inf_{x^*\in K^*}f^*(x^*),\quad\text{with the stated attainment, polyhedral, and complementarity conclusions}

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Inequalities Cannot Detect Missing Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a convex cone does not change its dual, so dual inequalities cannot detect points omitted only from the cone's boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Then \[K^*=(\operatorname{cl}K)^*.\] Hence, if \(x\in\operatorname{cl}K\setminus K\), then \(\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in K^*\); no positive-dual inequality strictly separates \(x\) from \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=(\operatorname{cl}K)^*\), and missing boundary points admit no strictly negative positive-dual separator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information lost when bipolarity replaces a nonclosed convex cone by its closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Cone Closure Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar of a finite-dimensional convex cone is its closure. Hence a nonclosed cone is strictly smaller than its bipolar, while a closed convex cone equals its bipolar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every convex cone \(K\) in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, its bipolar equals its closure:
\[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K.\]
Thus a nonclosed convex cone is recovered from its bipolar only after closure.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone, not necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K.\] Consequently, \(K^{**}=K\) holds if and only if \(K\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone bipolar theorem using the positive-dual convention; the closure is essential when the cone is not closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar closure of a nonclosed convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex cone that is not assumed closed, and use the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the convex but potentially nonclosed specialization of the bipolar theorem. Nonconvex cones require convexification as well as closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bipolar closure completion of \(K\) is
\[
\widehat K:=K^{\circ\circ}.
\]
For every nonempty convex cone,
\[
\widehat K=K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K.
\]
Hence, in the genuinely nonclosed regime,
\[
K\subsetneq K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K.
\]
Polarity is insensitive to the missing boundary:
\[
K^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}K)^\circ,
\]
so polar data recover the closure rather than the original nonclosed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex cone that is not assumed closed, taking the polar twice produces exactly its topological closure. If the cone is genuinely nonclosed, the original cone is strictly contained in its bipolar. The cone and its closure have the same polar, so no reconstruction based only on polar inequalities can distinguish which boundary points were originally omitted.
assumptions_latex: For the strict inclusion, \(K\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K\), and if \(K\) is nonclosed then \(K\subsetneq K^{\circ\circ}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{cl}K\iff\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K^\circ\).
\(K^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}K)^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is already closed, the completion is exact: \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
For an arbitrary nonconvex cone \(Q\), \(Q^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}Q)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: All cones lying between \(K\) and \(\operatorname{cl}K\) and having the same closure possess the same polar.
The bipolar completion is idempotent: \(\widehat K^{\circ\circ}=\widehat K\).
boundary_notes: Double polarity cannot recover deliberately deleted boundary points.
For a nonconvex cone, closure alone is insufficient; convexification also occurs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-dual cones under a fixed inner product
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality depends on the selected inner product. The definition uses the positive dual cone, not the nonpositive polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The positive dual cone and nonpositive polar are
\[
K^*:=\{y\in E:(\forall x\in K)\;\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\},
\qquad K^\circ=-K^*.
\]
The self-dual regime is
\[
\mathfrak{SD}(E):=\{K\subseteq E:K\text{ is a nonempty convex cone and }K=K^*\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
K\in\mathfrak{SD}(E)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^\circ=-K.
\]
Because every dual cone is closed and convex, a self-dual cone is automatically a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive dual cone consists of vectors pairing nonnegatively with every cone vector. A cone is self-dual when it equals this positive dual under the chosen inner product. Equivalently, its nonpositive polar is its negative. Self-duality automatically supplies closedness and convexity, but it is not invariant under arbitrary changes of inner product.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone.
The same fixed inner product defines both the dual and self-duality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in K\iff\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\).
Using nonpositive polarity, self-duality is the relation \(K=-K^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is self-dual under the standard Euclidean inner product.
The cone of positive semidefinite symmetric matrices is self-dual under the Frobenius inner product.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every self-dual cone is closed and convex.
In a nonzero finite-dimensional ambient space, a self-dual cone is pointed and full-dimensional.
boundary_notes: Changing the inner product can change the dual cone and hence self-duality.
With the nonpositive-polar convention, writing \(K=K^\circ\) is not the standard self-duality relation.

notation.meaning: Family of self-dual cones in E.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Cones Are Proper
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonzero finite-dimensional inner-product space, every self-dual cone is closed, pointed, and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\ne\{0\}\) be finite-dimensional and let \(K\subseteq E\) satisfy \(K=K^*\). Then \(K\) is closed, pointed, and full-dimensional: \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{span}K=E,\qquad \operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing.\] Thus \(K\) is a proper cone.
assumptions_latex: \(E\ne\{0\}\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone satisfying \(K=K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural consequences of equality with the dual cone.

notation.meaning: Positive dual cone under the specified inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Cone Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is self-dual for a specified inner product when it equals the cone of all vectors having nonnegative inner product with every vector in the cone. Such a cone is necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(K\) is self-dual with respect to \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) when
\[K=K^*,\qquad K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\]
This equality implies that \(K\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality is defined relative to the displayed inner product and the positive-dual convention.

notation.meaning: Dual cone induced by the specified inner product.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, §6.3, “Polar and Dual Cones,” p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Cones Are Necessarily Non-Self-Dual
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed cone cannot equal its closed dual, although closedness alone does not imply self-duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every cone \(K\) in a finite-dimensional inner-product space, \(K^*\) is closed. Therefore \[K\text{ nonclosed}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad K\ne K^*.\] The converse fails: a closed cone may still be non-self-dual.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
Duality uses the fixed nonnegative-pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonclosedness implies \(K\ne K^*\), but the converse is false.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness obstruction to self-duality under a fixed inner product.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the fixed inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Self-Dual Cone Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is non-self-dual for a specified inner product when it differs from its dual cone. For example, the nonnegative horizontal ray in the plane has the right half-plane as its Euclidean dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(K\) is non-self-dual with respect to \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) when
\[K\ne K^*,\qquad K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\]
For example, under the Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb R^2\), the ray \(K=\{(t,0):t\ge0\}\) has dual \(K^*=\{(u,v):u\ge0\}\), so \(K\ne K^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record defines failure of self-duality for a fixed inner product; the same cone may behave differently under another inner product.

notation.meaning: Dual cone induced by the specified inner product.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, §6.3, “Polar and Dual Cones,” p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Change as a Euclidean Coordinate Transformation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring the metric converts a change of inner product into an invertible coordinate transformation; metric self-duality becomes Euclidean self-duality of the transformed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=T^{\mathsf T}T\), where \(G\) is symmetric positive definite and \(T\) is invertible. Then \(T:(\mathbb R^n,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_G)\to(\mathbb R^n,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is an isometry and \[(TK)^*=T^{-\mathsf T}K^*.\] Consequently, \[K=K^{*_{G}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad TK=(TK)^*.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isometric coordinate form of pairing-dependent cone duality.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the G-inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality Dependence on Inner Products
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an inner product is represented by a symmetric positive-definite matrix G, then the corresponding dual cone is the inverse image of the Euclidean dual under G. Thus self-duality can change when the inner product changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K^*\) denote the Euclidean dual cone and let \(K^{*_{G}}\) denote the dual under \(\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^{\mathsf T}Gy\). Then
\[K^{*_{G}}=\{y:y^{\mathsf T}Gx\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}=G^{-1}K^*.\]
Consequently,
\[K=K^{*_{G}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad GK=K^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb R^n\) carries the Euclidean inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}y\).
\(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^{*_{G}}=G^{-1}K^*.\] In particular, \(K\) is self-dual under \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_G\) if and only if \(GK=K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinate representation of how changing the inner product changes the dual cone.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the Euclidean inner product.
Dual cone under the inner product induced by the positive-definite matrix.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, §6.3, “Polar and Dual Cones,” p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-based sufficient criteria for closed images and sums
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are finite-dimensional sufficient criteria. They control escaping sequences through recession directions lying in a map kernel or canceling across a Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the linear-image asymptotic closedness condition by
\[
\mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{im}}(A,C):
\quad \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C.
\]
Whenever this condition holds,
\[
AC:=\{Ax:x\in C\}\text{ is closed}.
\]
For nonempty closed convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_r\), define the sum condition
\[
\mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{sum}}(C_1,\ldots,C_r):
\quad d_i\in\operatorname{rec}C_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^r d_i=0
\Rightarrow d_i\in\operatorname{lin}C_i\ \forall i.
\]
Whenever it holds,
\[
C_1+\cdots+C_r\text{ is closed}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set satisfies the linear-image asymptotic closedness condition when every recession direction annihilated by the linear map is reversible lineality. This condition guarantees that the image is closed. For a Minkowski sum, the corresponding condition requires every collection of recession directions that cancels to zero to consist entirely of lineality directions; this guarantees that the sum is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and every \(C_i\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
For the sum criterion, each \(d_i\) belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C\Rightarrow AC\) is closed, and the displayed zero-sum recession condition implies that \(C_1+\cdots+C_r\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A stronger image condition is \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\).
For two sets, the sum condition is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}C_1\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C_2)\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C_1\cap(-\operatorname{lin}C_2)\).
special_cases_latex: The linear image of every polyhedral set is closed.
If one summand is compact, its recession cone is \(\{0\}\), eliminating cancellation through that summand.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed convex set with no nonzero kernel recession direction has a closed linear image.
The criterion applies to projections by taking \(A\) to be a coordinate projection.
boundary_notes: The image condition is sufficient and is not asserted to be necessary in full generality.
Without recession regularity, a linear image or Minkowski sum of closed convex sets can fail to be closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common recession cone is preserved by a finite convex hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family closedness and exact recession-cone preservation under shared asymptotic geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets satisfying \(0^+C_i=K\) for every \(i\). Then \[C=\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_m)\] is closed and \(0^+C=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the union of finitely many nonempty closed convex sets having the same recession cone is closed and has that same recession cone.
assumptions_latex: C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and recession cone of a recession-compatible finite convex hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here the lineality space of \(C_i\) is \(0^+C_i\cap(-0^+C_i)\). At a zero coefficient, \(\lambda_iC_i\) is interpreted as \(0^+C_i\), not as \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Assume that whenever \(z_i\in0^+C_i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m z_i=0\), each \(z_i\) belongs to the lineality space of \(C_i\). If \(C=\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_m)\), then \[\operatorname{cl}C=\bigcup_{\substack{\lambda_i\geq0^+\\\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1}}\left(\lambda_1C_1+\cdots+\lambda_mC_m\right),\] where \(\lambda_iC_i=0^+C_i\) when \(\lambda_i=0\). Moreover, \[0^+(\operatorname{cl}C)=0^+C_1+\cdots+0^+C_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppose that any recession directions which cancel across a finite family of nonempty closed convex sets are individually lineality directions of their respective sets. The closure of the convex hull of the union is then the union of the indicated weighted Minkowski sums, with a zero weight interpreted as the corresponding recession cone. The recession cone of the closure is the sum of the individual recession cones.
assumptions_latex: C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
z_i\in0^+C_i\ \forall i\text{ and }\sum_{i=1}^m z_i=0\ \Longrightarrow\ z_i\in 0^+C_i\cap(-0^+C_i)\ \forall i

children.title: Nested Closed-Set Intersection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intersection behavior controlled by boundedness and recession structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Selection Criterion for Nested Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested sequence of nonempty closed sets has nonempty intersection exactly when one can select a bounded point from every level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_k)_{k\geq1}\) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space. Then
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k\neq\varnothing
\]
if and only if there exists a bounded sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq1}\) satisfying \(x_k\in C_k\) for every \(k\).
assumptions_latex: The ambient normed space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_kC_k\neq\varnothing\) if and only if there is a bounded sequence with \(x_k\in C_k\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential certificate for nonemptiness of a decreasing closed-set intersection in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: one selected point from each nested set

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Closed Sets May Escape to Infinity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex sets can escape to infinity and have empty intersection when no member is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C_k=[k,+\infty)\subset\mathbb R\), every \(C_k\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(C_{k+1}\subset C_k\). Nevertheless,
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k=\varnothing.
\]
Each member is unbounded and satisfies \(\operatorname{rec}(C_k)=[0,+\infty)\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nested-intersection nonemptiness when no member is bounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Cantor Singleton Intersection Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested nonempty closed sets with one bounded member and diameters tending to zero have a singleton intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_k)_{k\ge1}\) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space. If some \(C_m\) is bounded and
\[
\operatorname{diam}(C_k)\longrightarrow0,
\]
then there exists a unique point \(x_*\) such that
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k=\{x_*\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \((C_k)_{k\ge1}\) is decreasing and every \(C_k\) is nonempty and closed.
The ambient normed space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singleton refinement for nested closed sets whose diameters vanish.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Recession Criterion for Nested Convex Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If nested nonempty closed convex sets have empty intersection, they share a nonzero recession direction; hence trivial common recession guarantees intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_k)_{k\geq1}\) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space. Then
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k=\varnothing
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{rec}(C_k)\text{ contains a nonzero vector}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{rec}(C_k)=\{0\}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k\neq\varnothing.
\]
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_k\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The ambient normed space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Empty intersection implies a common nonzero recession direction; therefore \(\bigcap_k\operatorname{rec}(C_k)=\{0\}\) implies \(\bigcap_k C_k\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-geometric condition preventing a decreasing sequence of closed convex sets from escaping to infinity.

notation.meaning: recession cone of the kth closed convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Closed-Set Intersection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nested-intersection criterion using common recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1\supseteq C_2\supseteq\cdots\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\). If
\[
\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{rec}(C_n)=\{0\},
\]
then \(\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}C_n\ne\varnothing\). In particular, this conclusion holds if some \(C_n\) is bounded; in that case the intersection is compact. Equivalently, if the nested intersection is empty, the sets possess a common nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested nonempty closed convex sets intersect when they have no common nonzero recession direction; a bounded member guarantees this and makes the intersection compact.
assumptions_latex: \(C_n\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nested closed-convex intersection regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_k\}_{k\geq 0}\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(C_{k+1}\subseteq C_k\). Write \(R_k=\operatorname{rec}(C_k)\), \(L_k=R_k\cap(-R_k)\), \(R=\bigcap_{k\geq0}R_k\), and \(L=\bigcap_{k\geq0}L_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nested sequences are classified by compactness, common recession geometry, and retractiveness. These are sufficient-regime definitions, not an assertion that every nonempty intersection satisfies one of them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence is in the compact regime if some \(C_j\) is bounded. It is in the lineality-balanced regime if \(R=L\). An asymptotic sequence is a sequence \(x_k\in C_k\setminus\{0\}\) for which \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) and \(x_k/\|x_k\|\to d/\|d\|\) for some \(d\in R\setminus\{0\}\). Such a sequence is retractive if \(x_k-d\in C_k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\); the nested family is retractive when every asymptotic sequence is retractive. These conditions define the principal nested closed-set intersection regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex sets is in the compact regime when one member is bounded, and in the lineality-balanced regime when its common recession cone equals its common lineality space. An unbounded selection is asymptotic when its normalized vectors converge to a nonzero common recession direction. It is retractive when subtraction of that direction eventually leaves every selected vector in its corresponding set; the family is retractive if this holds for every asymptotic selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{compact regime: }\exists j\ C_j\text{ bounded};\qquad \text{balanced regime: }R=L;\qquad \text{retractive regime: }\forall\{x_k\}\text{ asymptotic},\ \exists k_0\ \forall k\geq k_0,\ x_k-d\in C_k.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), boundedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{0\}\).
The equality \(R=L\) says that every common recession direction is reversible in every \(C_k\).
special_cases_latex: If some \(C_j\) is compact, then every later \(C_k\) lies in the compact set \(C_j\).
A constant sequence \(C_k=C\) is retractive exactly when the closed convex set \(C\) is retractive in the corresponding single-set sense.
immediate_consequences_latex: A retractive nested sequence has nonempty intersection.
If \(R=L\), then the intersection is nonempty and has the form \(L+K\) for some nonempty compact convex set \(K\).
boundary_notes: Nestedness and closedness are essential to the stated regime terminology.
Retractiveness is sufficient for nonemptiness but is not necessary.
The definition is finite-dimensional; compactness and subsequence arguments require modification in general topological vector spaces.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set.
Lineality space of the kth set.
Common recession cone and common lineality space.

children.title: Closedness Under Linear Maps
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic criteria for preservation of closedness under linear transformation.

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial Recession Kernel Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The seed's recession-kernel test is sufficient but not necessary: the zero map sends the whole line to a closed singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness of \(A(C)\) does not imply \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\). For \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and the zero map \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\), \(A(C)=\{0\}\) is closed, while \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of the seed criterion, not an example of a nonclosed image.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Relaxed Recession Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image is closed when the recession directions annihilated by the map form only reversible lineality; requiring that intersection to be zero is a stronger special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, with \(E,F\) finite-dimensional. If \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace, then \(A(C)\) is closed. The seed condition \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) is the zero-subspace special case.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A broader finite-dimensional sufficient condition than the seed's trivial-intersection criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial Recession Kernel as Properness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absence of a nonzero kernel recession direction is equivalent to properness of the restricted map and therefore guarantees a closed image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear. Then \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) if and only if \(C\cap A^{-1}(K)\) is compact for every compact \(K\subseteq F\). Equivalently, \(A|_C:C\to F\) is proper; consequently \(A(C)\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\iff \forall K\subseteq F\text{ compact},\ C\cap A^{-1}(K)\text{ is compact};\quad A(C)\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent compact-preimage formulation of the seed's stronger sufficient condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Under Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient recession-kernel criterion for closed linear images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. If
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)\cap\ker A=\{0\},
\]
then the image \(A(C):=\{Ax:x\in C\}\) is a closed convex subset of \(\mathbb R^m\). The condition rules out unbounded sequences in \(C\) that escape along directions annihilated by \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a closed convex set is closed when the set has no nonzero recession direction lying in the map's kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-regular closedness under a linear map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Put \(R_C=\operatorname{rec}(C)\), \(L_C=R_C\cap(-R_C)\), and \(N(A)=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition isolates a standard finite-dimensional sufficient regime for preservation of closedness. It does not claim that the recession condition is necessary whenever the image happens to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((C,A)\) is recession-regular for closed images if \(R_C\cap N(A)\subseteq L_C\). It is strongly recession-regular if \(R_C\cap N(A)=\{0\}\). The set \(C\) is closed-image stable under \(A\) when \(A(C)\) is closed, equivalently when every convergent sequence \(Ax_j\to y\) with \(x_j\in C\) has a point \(x\in C\) satisfying \(Ax=y\). Recession regularity is the asymptotic criterion defining the canonical guaranteed-closedness regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set and a linear map form a recession-regular pair when every recession direction annihilated by the map is a lineality direction of the set. Strong regularity requires the only annihilated recession direction to be zero. Closed-image stability means that the linear image is closed, or equivalently that every limit of image points has a preimage in the set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(A(C)\text{ is closed}\iff \forall (x_j)\subset C,\ Ax_j\to y\Rightarrow \exists x\in C:\ Ax=y.\)
The condition \(R_C\cap\ker A\subseteq L_C\) means that no irreversible escape direction of \(C\) is collapsed to zero by \(A\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(R_C=\{0\}\), so \(A(C)\) is compact and closed.
If \(A\) is injective, then \(\ker A=\{0\}\), so strong recession regularity holds.
The image of a polyhedral convex set under any linear map is polyhedral and hence closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under recession regularity, \(\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(R_C)\).
The stronger condition \(R_C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) is an immediately checkable sufficient criterion.
boundary_notes: A continuous linear image of an arbitrary closed set need not be closed.
For nonclosed or nonconvex domains, the recession criterion in this form does not apply.
Failure of recession regularity signals possible degeneracy but does not by itself force nonclosedness.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the domain set.
Lineality space of the domain set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Domain Closed-Image Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary sufficient regime included as a useful exact specialization of the asymptotic criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is compact in a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(A\) is linear, then \(A(C)\) is compact and hence closed. In particular, every nonempty compact convex set satisfies \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a compact set is compact and closed; compact convex sets have no nonzero recession direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-Kernel Condition Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp logical boundary of the seed criterion; this is not a nonclosed-image pathology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness of \(A(C)\) does not imply \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\). For example, with \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and the zero map \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\), one has \(A(C)=\{0\}\), which is closed, but \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession-kernel test is sufficient but not necessary: the zero map sends the whole line to a closed singleton despite annihilating every recession direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Kernel Condition Is Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-Kernel Criterion as Properness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthens and equivalently formulates the immutable seed's sufficient closed-image condition in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear. Then \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) if and only if \(C\cap A^{-1}(K)\) is compact for every compact \(K\subseteq F\). Equivalently, the restriction \(A|_C:C\to F\) is proper. Under these conditions, \(A(C)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absence of a nonzero recession direction in the kernel is equivalent to properness of the map restricted to the closed convex set, and therefore guarantees a closed image.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\iff \forall K\subseteq F\text{ compact},\ C\cap A^{-1}(K)\text{ is compact};\quad A(C)\text{ is closed}.

notation.meaning: Restriction of the linear map to the set C

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Kernel Criterion as Properness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness of a Linear Image Under a Recession-Lineality Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional closedness and recession-cone criterion for a linear image of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty and convex, and let A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be linear. Suppose every nonzero z\in 0^+(\operatorname{cl}C) satisfying Az=0 belongs to \operatorname{lin}(\operatorname{cl}C). Then \operatorname{cl}(AC)=A(\operatorname{cl}C) and 0^+\!\left(A(\operatorname{cl}C)\right)=A\left(0^+(\operatorname{cl}C)\right). In particular, if C is closed and 0^+C\cap\ker A=\{0\}, then AC is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty convex set, closure commutes with a linear image and the recession cone of the image is the image of the original recession cone when every nonzero recession direction annihilated by the map is a lineality direction. If the set is closed and its recession cone meets the kernel only at zero, its image is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(AC)=A(\operatorname{cl}C),\qquad 0^+\!\left(A(\operatorname{cl}C)\right)=A\left(0^+(\operatorname{cl}C)\right);\qquad C\text{ closed and }0^+C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\implies AC\text{ closed}.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Witnesses of Nonclosed Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing image limit can only be approached through unbounded preimages, whose normalized escape directions yield nonzero recession directions annihilated by the map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. If \(x_k\in C\), \(Ax_k\to z\), and \(z\notin A(C)\), then \((x_k)\) is unbounded. For any \(c\in C\), every convergent subsequence of \((x_k-c)/\|x_k-c\|\) has a unit limit \(d\in C^\infty\cap\ker A\). Conversely, nonclosedness of \(A(C)\) supplies such a sequence for some \(z\in\overline{A(C)}\setminus A(C)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Missing image limits have unbounded preimage witnesses with unit cluster directions in \(C^\infty\cap\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary escape behavior of preimages approaching a missing image point.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Linear-Image Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite-cone projection exhibiting loss of closedness under a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb S_+^2\), the closed convex cone of real positive-semidefinite matrices \(X=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\), and define the linear map \(A(X)=(a,b)\). Then
\[
A(C)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},
\]
which is not closed: \((1/n,1)\in A(C)\) for every positive integer \(n\), while \((1/n,1)\to(0,1)\notin A(C)\). Hence a linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the two-by-two positive-semidefinite cone onto its first diagonal and off-diagonal entries produces a convex but nonclosed image.

notation.meaning: cone of real two-by-two positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial-extremal representation hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A segment is written \([x,y]=\{(1-t)x+ty:0\leq t\leq1\}\), and its relative interior is obtained by requiring \(0<t<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hierarchy combines the standard finite-dimensional notions of faces, exposed faces, extreme points and directions, and their internal representation roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex subset \(F\subseteq C\) is a face if \((1-t)x+ty\in F\), with \(x,y\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(x,y\in F\). It is exposed if \(F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\) for some nonzero \(a\), whenever the maximum is attained. A singleton face is an extreme point; a half-line face determines an extreme direction. Thus exposed points and directions lie within the corresponding extreme classes, and the extremal classes form the minimal generators used in finite-dimensional representation theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is a convex subset that contains both endpoints of every segment of the ambient convex set whose relative interior meets it. An exposed face is the maximizer set of a nonzero linear functional. Singleton faces are extreme points, while half-line faces define extreme directions. Exposed points and directions are therefore special extreme structures, and extreme structures provide the canonical internal generators of closed convex sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in C\) is extreme iff \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), \(y,z\in C\), and \(0<t<1\) imply \(y=z=x\).
A proper exposed face has the form \(C\cap H\), where \(H\) is a nontrivial supporting hyperplane of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed and bounded, then \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{Ext}(C))\).
If \(C\) is closed and contains no lines, it is generated by its extreme points and extreme directions.
For a pointed closed convex cone, the directional extremal objects are its extreme rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed point is extreme, but an extreme point need not be exposed.
Every face inherits its own facial-extremal hierarchy, and its extreme points and directions remain extreme in \(C\).
boundary_notes: The empty set and \(C\) are included as improper faces.
An exposing functional may define an empty maximizer set when its supremum is not attained.
Lineality can eliminate extreme points and extreme directions from an unbounded convex set.

notation.meaning: Set of extreme points of the convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces and facial depth
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set, and let \(\mathcal F(C)\) denote all faces of \(C\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats the facial hierarchy as the inclusion-ordered boundary structure of a finite-dimensional convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\) is a convex subset \(F\subseteq C\) such that \((1-t)x+ty\in F\), where \(x,y\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(x,y\in F\). A proper face satisfies \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(F\neq C\). A facial chain is a strictly increasing sequence \(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r\) in \(\mathcal F(C)\). Its length and the dimensions of its members measure facial depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is a convex subset that cannot contain an interior point of a segment from the ambient set without also containing both endpoints. The empty face and the entire convex set are improper faces; every other nonempty face is proper. Faces ordered by inclusion form the facial hierarchy, and a facial chain records successively larger boundary strata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\iff F\subseteq C,\ F\text{ convex},\ \forall x,y\in C\ \forall t\in(0,1),\ (1-t)x+ty\in F\Rightarrow x,y\in F.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex subset \(F\subseteq C\) is a face iff every closed segment in \(C\) whose relative interior meets \(F\) has both endpoints in \(F\).
For every proper face \(F\), one has \(F\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}(C)\) and \(\dim F<\dim C\).
special_cases_latex: A zero-dimensional nonempty face is an extreme point.
A codimension-one proper face is commonly called a facet.
A half-line face determines an extreme direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(G\) is a face of \(F\) and \(F\) is a face of \(C\), then \(G\) is a face of \(C\).
Every strictly decreasing chain of faces is finite in finite dimensions.
boundary_notes: Faces need not be exposed by a single supporting functional.
For a nonclosed convex set, a face need not be closed in the ambient space, though it is relatively closed in the stated sense \(F=C\cap\operatorname{cl}F\).
The codimension-one term facet is relative to the affine dimension of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Family of all faces of the convex set.
Relative boundary of the convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial classes and the minimal face of a set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set and \(S\subseteq C\). Let \(\mathcal F(C)\) be its family of faces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition organizes standard facial classes by dimension and defines the smallest facial container of a point or subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimal face of \(C\) containing \(S\) is \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\bigcap\{F\in\mathcal F(C):S\subseteq F\}\). For a point \(x\in C\), write \(F_C(x)=\operatorname{face}_C(\{x\})\). The facial classes comprise the improper faces \(\varnothing,C\), proper faces, extreme-point faces \(\{x\}\), half-line faces defining extreme directions, and facets satisfying \(\dim F=\dim C-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest face containing a subset is the intersection of all faces that contain it. For one point this is its minimal face. Faces are classified as improper, proper, singleton extreme-point faces, half-line faces giving extreme directions, or facets of relative codimension one. These classes locate a point or constraint set at its smallest facial level.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_C(x)\) is the unique face \(F\) whose relative interior contains \(x\).
A point \(x\) is extreme iff \(F_C(x)=\{x\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(C)\), then \(F_C(x)=C\).
If \(x\) lies in the relative interior of a facet \(F\), then \(F_C(x)=F\).
For \(S=\varnothing\), the intersection definition gives the least face \(\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(S\subseteq T\subseteq C\), then \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_C(T)\).
A face \(F\) contains \(S\) iff it contains \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\).
boundary_notes: A facet need not be exposed for an arbitrary convex set, although facets of polyhedral convex sets are exposed.
Half-line faces concern unbounded convex sets; extreme rays are the conic specialization.
The affine dimension of \(C\), not the dimension of the containing Euclidean space, determines facets.

notation.meaning: Smallest face of the ambient convex set containing the subset.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Faces Lie on the Relative Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face meeting the relative interior must be the whole set; therefore every proper face lies in the relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(C\). Then \[F\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F=C.\] Consequently, every proper face satisfies \[F\subseteq C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the intrinsic boundary placement of proper faces for finite-dimensional convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty proper faces of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space. A set \(F\) is a proper face of \(C\) if \(F\) is nonempty, convex, \(F\subsetneq C\), and whenever \(x,y\in C\), \(0<t<1\), and
\[
tx+(1-t)y\in F,
\]
then \(x,y\in F\). Thus a proper face excludes the improper face \(C\) itself and, under this convention, excludes the empty face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper face is a nonempty strict convex subset containing both endpoints whenever it contains a nontrivial convex combination of points of the ambient set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proper exactly when \(F\) is convex, \(\varnothing\ne F\subsetneq C\), and the facial endpoint condition holds.

notation.meaning: F is a strict subset of C

knowledge_statements.title: Improper Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the empty face included, the improper faces of a nonempty convex set are the empty set and the whole set itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the convention that the empty set is a face, the two improper faces of a nonempty convex set \(C\) are
\[\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
The empty face is admitted by convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{The improper faces of }C\text{ are exactly }\varnothing\text{ and }C.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Some authors omit the empty face; this record explicitly includes it.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The characterization is correct under the stated empty-face convention, and definition fits the leaf, but the convention-dependent terminology lacks a citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face containing a subset is the intersection of all faces containing that subset. It is the unique smallest such face under inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The minimal face of \(C\) containing \(S\) is
\[\operatorname{face}_C(S):=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a face of }C\text{ and }S\subseteq F\}.\]
It is itself a face, contains \(S\), and is contained in every face of \(C\) that contains \(S\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
The empty set is admitted as a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{face}_C(S):=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a face of }C\text{ and }S\subseteq F\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality is with respect to set inclusion among faces containing the prescribed subset.

notation.meaning: The unique smallest face of the ambient convex set containing the specified subset.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The intersection formula defines the unique minimal face containing S and has the stated universal property. The content kind fits, but no authoritative source is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Generated-Face Invariance and Joins
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking a convex hull before generating a minimal face changes nothing, and the face jointly generated by two subsets is also generated by their individual minimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\) and subsets \(S,T\subseteq C\), \[\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\operatorname{face}_C(\operatorname{conv}S)\] and \[\operatorname{face}_C(S\cup T)=\operatorname{face}_C\bigl(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\cup\operatorname{face}_C(T)\bigr).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are containment laws of the minimal-face operator, not a redefinition of minimal faces.

notation.meaning: Smallest face of C containing S.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Containment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal containment property of the face generated by a subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex, let \(S\subseteq C\), and let \(F\) be a face of \(C\). Then
\[S\subseteq F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq F.\]
Consequently, if \(S\subseteq T\subseteq C\), then \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_C(T)\); thus minimal-face generation is monotone with respect to set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face contains a subset exactly when it contains that subset's minimal face; minimal-face generation is monotone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex, \(S\subseteq C\), and \(F\) is a face of \(C\).

notation.meaning: minimal face of C containing S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Hull Invariance of Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an algebraic containment property of the minimal-face operator, not a redefinition of minimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and \(S\subseteq C\). Since every face of \(C\) is convex, a face contains \(S\) if and only if it contains \(\operatorname{conv}S\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\operatorname{face}_C(\operatorname{conv}S).\] More generally, for \(S,T\subseteq C\), \[\operatorname{face}_C(S\cup T)=\operatorname{face}_C\bigl(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\cup\operatorname{face}_C(T)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generating a minimal face is unchanged by first taking the convex hull. The minimal face generated jointly by two subsets is also the minimal face generated by their individual minimal faces.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.

notation.meaning: The smallest face of C containing S.

children.title: Face Inclusion Structure
children.top_down_role: Ordering and incidence relationships among faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Growth Along Face Chains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper inclusion of nonempty faces strictly increases affine dimension, so a chain has at most one face of each possible dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\subsetneq G\) are nonempty faces of a finite-dimensional convex set \(C\), then \[\operatorname{aff}F\subsetneq\operatorname{aff}G\quad\text{and hence}\quad \dim F<\dim G.\] Consequently, every strictly increasing chain of nonempty faces contains at most \(\dim C+1\) faces.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(F\) and \(G\) are nonempty faces of \(C\) with \(F\subsetneq G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension means affine dimension. Strict inclusion and nonemptiness are essential; no dimension convention for the empty face is used.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of a Face
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of a face G is a face of G exactly when it is a face of the ambient convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a face of a convex set \(C\). For every \(F\subseteq G\), \[F\text{ is a face of }G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\text{ is a face of }C.\] Thus the faces below \(G\) in the inclusion order are exactly the faces of \(G\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(G\) is a face of \(C\), and \(F\subseteq G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is a face of }G\Longleftrightarrow F\text{ is a face of }C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This includes the empty face when that convention is adopted and identifies the lower interval below \(G\) with the face family of \(G\).

knowledge_statements.title: Face Inclusion Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-lattice structure when the empty face is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F(C)\) denote all faces of a convex set \(C\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(C\), ordered by inclusion. Then \(\mathcal F(C)\) is a complete lattice. For any family \((F_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq\mathcal F(C)\),
\[\bigwedge_{i\in I}F_i=\bigcap_{i\in I}F_i,\qquad \bigvee_{i\in I}F_i=\operatorname{face}_C\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}F_i\right).\]
The empty meet is \(C\), the empty join is \(\varnothing\), and the bottom and top elements are respectively \(\varnothing\) and \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces ordered by inclusion form a complete lattice: meets are intersections and joins are minimal faces containing unions.
assumptions_latex: The empty set is admitted as a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal F(C),\subseteq)\) is a complete lattice with meet \(\bigcap\) and join \(\operatorname{face}_C(\bigcup\cdot)\).

notation.meaning: family of all faces of C
meet and join under face inclusion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete lattice of faces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and order \(\mathcal F(C)\) by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition captures incidence and containment among faces through their finite-dimensional complete-lattice structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any family \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal F(C)\), its meet is \(\bigwedge\mathcal A=\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal A}F\). Its join is the least face containing their union, \(\bigvee\mathcal A=\operatorname{face}_C(\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal A}F)\). With least element \(\varnothing\) and greatest element \(C\), these operations make \((\mathcal F(C),\subseteq)\) the face-inclusion lattice. Incidence means simply \(F\subseteq G\) for two faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces are ordered by inclusion. The greatest lower bound of any family is its intersection, while the least upper bound is the smallest face containing its union. The empty face and the whole set are respectively the least and greatest elements. This complete lattice is the canonical face-incidence structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigwedge\mathcal A=\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal A}F,\qquad \bigvee\mathcal A=\bigcap\{G\in\mathcal F(C):\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal A}F\subseteq G\}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\subseteq G\) is equivalent to saying that \(F\) is a face of the intermediate convex set \(G\).
For two faces, \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\) and \(F\vee G=\operatorname{face}_C(F\cup G)\).
special_cases_latex: The meet of the empty family is \(C\), and the join of the empty family is \(\varnothing\).
If \(F\subseteq G\), then \(F\wedge G=F\) and \(F\vee G=G\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Arbitrary intersections of faces are faces.
If \(H\) is a face of \(F\) and \(F\) is a face of \(C\), then \(H\in\mathcal F(C)\).
Every inclusion chain has well-defined infimum and supremum in \(\mathcal F(C)\).
boundary_notes: The face lattice need not be distributive.
The join is generally larger than the set-theoretic union, which need not be convex.
Strict face inclusion forces a dimension increase between nonempty faces in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: Meet and join in the inclusion-ordered face lattice.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Stratification by Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interiors of the nonempty faces of a finite-dimensional convex set form a disjoint partition. Each point lies in the relative interior of its unique minimal containing face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\ne\varnothing}(C)\) be the family of nonempty faces of \(C\). For \(x\in C\), define the minimal face \[F_C(x):=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a face of }C\text{ and }x\in F\}.\] Then \(F_C(x)\) is a face, \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_C(x)\), and it is the unique face whose relative interior contains \(x\). Consequently, \[C=\bigsqcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_{\ne\varnothing}(C)}\operatorname{ri}F.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigsqcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_{\ne\varnothing}(C)}\operatorname{ri}F\), and each \(x\in C\) belongs to the relative interior of its unique minimal face \(F_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional formulation; the disjoint union ranges over all nonempty faces, including the whole set.

notation.meaning: The family of nonempty faces of C.
The minimal face of C containing x.
Relative interior in the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-interior facial stratification
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set. For each nonempty face \(F\), take its relative interior \(\operatorname{ri}(F)\) in \(\operatorname{aff}(F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strata are relative interiors of all nonempty faces; no smooth-manifold or Whitney regularity is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial relative-interior stratification of \(C\) is \(\mathscr S(C)=\{\operatorname{ri}(F):F\in\mathcal F(C),\ F\neq\varnothing\}\). It is a partition: \(C=\bigsqcup_{F\neq\varnothing}\operatorname{ri}(F)\). Equivalently, every \(x\in C\) belongs to the relative interior of a unique face, namely its minimal face \(F_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The facial strata of a convex set are the relative interiors of its nonempty faces. These sets are pairwise disjoint and cover the convex set. Thus every point lies in exactly one stratum, which is the relative interior of its minimal face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Define \(x\sim y\) when \(x=y\) or some segment in \(C\) contains both \(x\) and \(y\) in its relative interior; the equivalence classes are precisely the sets \(\operatorname{ri}(F)\).
The strata are the maximal relatively open convex subsets of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: The top stratum is \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\).
Each extreme point forms a zero-dimensional stratum \(\{x\}\).
For a polytope, the strata are the relative interiors of all vertices, edges, higher-dimensional proper faces, and the polytope itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two faces with intersecting relative interiors are equal.
For every \(x\in C\), the closure of its stratum relative to \(C\) is the minimal face \(F_C(x)\) when that face is closed.
A relatively open convex subset of \(C\) lies in a single facial stratum.
boundary_notes: Different faces may intersect along lower-dimensional faces, but their relative interiors do not intersect.
This partition is finite only when \(C\) has finitely many faces.
Relative interior is taken in each face's own affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partition by relative interiors of faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial relative-interior stratification and the characterization of its strata as maximal relatively open convex subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C be a nonempty convex set and let \mathcal U=\{\operatorname{ri}F:F\text{ is a nonempty face of }C\}. Then the members of \mathcal U are pairwise disjoint and their union is C. Every relatively open convex subset D\subseteq C is contained in a member of \mathcal U, and the members of \mathcal U are precisely the maximal relatively open convex subsets of C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interiors of the nonempty faces of a nonempty convex set form a partition of the set. Every relatively open convex subset lies in one such stratum, and these strata are exactly the maximal relatively open convex subsets.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a nonempty convex set.}
\mathcal U=\{\operatorname{ri}F:F\text{ is a nonempty face of }C\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=\bigsqcup_{U\in\mathcal U}U,\qquad \forall D\subseteq C\;\bigl(D\text{ is convex and relatively open}\Rightarrow\exists U\in\mathcal U\;D\subseteq U\bigr),\qquad \mathcal U\text{ is the family of maximal relatively open convex subsets of }C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary facial construction calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(\mathcal F(C)\) be its faces, and let \(h_a(x)=\langle a,x\rangle\) be a linear functional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The calculus consists of source-supported operations that construct faces from intersections, nested faces, intermediate convex sets, and supporting functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The elementary facial construction operations are: \(\bigcap_iF_i\in\mathcal F(C)\) for any family \(F_i\in\mathcal F(C)\); transitivity, whereby \(G\in\mathcal F(F)\) and \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\) imply \(G\in\mathcal F(C)\); restriction, whereby \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\) and \(F\subseteq D\subseteq C\) with \(D\) convex imply \(F\in\mathcal F(D)\); and exposure, whereby a nonempty maximizer set \(F_a=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\) is an exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces may be constructed by arbitrary intersections, by taking faces of existing faces, by restricting an existing face to an intermediate convex set, and by maximizing a linear functional. These operations form the elementary facial construction calculus and preserve the endpoint property that defines a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_i\unlhd C\Rightarrow\bigcap_iF_i\unlhd C;\quad G\unlhd F\unlhd C\Rightarrow G\unlhd C;\quad F\unlhd C,\ F\subseteq D\subseteq C\Rightarrow F\unlhd D;\quad F_a\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow F_a\unlhd C.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The smallest face containing \(S\subseteq C\) is produced by intersection: \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\bigcap\{F\unlhd C:S\subseteq F\}\).
A proper exposed face is the intersection of \(C\) with a nontrivial supporting hyperplane.
special_cases_latex: If \(F\) is exposed in \(C\) and \(F\subseteq D\subseteq C\), then \(F\) is exposed in \(D\).
An extreme point of a face is an extreme point of the ambient convex set.
For finitely many faces, their intersection may be empty, which is still a face.
immediate_consequences_latex: The face family is closed under arbitrary meets.
Facial chains can be built recursively without losing facial status in the original set.
Linear optimization supplies a direct construction of exposed faces.
boundary_notes: An exposed face of a face need not be exposed in the original set.
Set unions and Minkowski sums do not generally preserve faces without additional hypotheses.
The symbol \(\unlhd\) is local shorthand for the face relation, not an order on arbitrary subsets.

notation.meaning: The set is a face of the ambient convex set.
Maximizer set of the functional indexed by the vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces Under Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty intersection of faces is a face of the corresponding nonempty intersection of their ambient convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an index set. For each \(i\in I\), let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(F_i\) be a face of \(C_i\). If \[C:=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\qquad\text{and}\qquad F:=\bigcap_{i\in I}F_i\neq\varnothing,\] then \(F\) is a face of \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an index set, \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex, and \(F_i\) is a face of \(C_i\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This includes the common special case in which all faces belong to the same convex set.

notation.meaning: The intersection of the selected faces.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The intersection property is mathematically correct and its property container fits the facial-calculus leaf, but no source or standard-field rationale is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Reflection and Invariants Under Affine Embeddings
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine embedding induces an order isomorphism of face lattices. It preserves and reflects exposed faces and preserves every face's relative dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine with \(A|_C\) injective. For every \(G\subseteq A(C)\), \[G\text{ is a face of }A(C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (A|_C)^{-1}(G)\text{ is a face of }C.\] Together with forward image preservation, \(F\mapsto A(F)\) is an inclusion-preserving bijection between the face lattices of \(C\) and \(A(C)\). It preserves and reflects exposed faces, and for every face \(F\) of \(C\), \[\dim A(F)=\dim F.\]
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is affine and injective on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto A(F)\) is a face-lattice isomorphism from \(C\) to \(A(C)\), preserving exposedness and dimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This supplements forward face preservation with reflection, exposed-face correspondence, and dimension preservation.

notation.meaning: Inverse image of G under the bijection from C onto A(C).

knowledge_statements.title: Faces Under Affine Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions ensuring that affine images preserve faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\) be convex, let \(T:X\to Y\) be affine, and let \(F\) be a face of \(C\). If \(F\) is saturated relative to \(C\) under \(T\), meaning
\[F=C\cap T^{-1}(T(F)),\]
then \(T(F)\) is a face of \(T(C)\). In particular, this condition holds for every face \(F\) when \(T|_C\) is injective. Without saturation, an affine image of a face need not be a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine image of a face remains a face when that face contains every point of the convex set sharing an image with one of its points; injectivity on the convex set guarantees this condition.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is convex, \(T:X\to Y\) is affine, and \(F\) is a face of \(C\).

notation.meaning: affine map from X to Y

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed Faces Under Affine Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This supplements the deferred face-preservation statement with preservation and reflection of exposedness and relative dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine with \(A|_C\) injective. Then a subset \(F\subseteq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\) if and only if \(A(F)\) is an exposed face of \(A(C)\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}A(C)\). For every face \(F\) of \(C\), \[\dim A(F)=\dim F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine embedding preserves and reflects exposed faces, and it preserves the relative dimension of every face.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is affine and injective on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exposed in \(C\iff A(F)\) is exposed in \(A(C)\), and \(\dim A(F)=\dim F\) for every face \(F\) of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Restriction of the affine map A to C.
Affine image of the face F.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Faces Under Affine Embeddings
Exposed Faces Pull Back to Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preimage inside C of an exposed face of its affine image is exposed by the adjoint-pulled functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(A(x)=Lx+b\) be affine, and let
\[
G=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in A(C)}\langle u,y\rangle
\]
be a nonempty exposed face of \(A(C)\). Then
\[
C\cap A^{-1}(G)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle L^*u,x\rangle,
\]
so the relative preimage is an exposed face of \(C\). It equals \(C\) if and only if \(x\mapsto\langle L^*u,x\rangle\) is constant on \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the nonempty face of \(A(C)\) exposed by \(u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-preimage preservation of exposed facial structure relative to the original convex set.

notation.meaning: adjoint of the linear part of A
exposed face of the affine image

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Correspondence for Affine Preimages
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of an affine image correspond exactly to faces of the original set that contain every feasible point in each affine fiber they meet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine. Call a face \(F\unlhd C\) \(A\)-saturated when
\[
F=C\cap A^{-1}(A(F)).
\]
Then
\[
G\longmapsto C\cap A^{-1}(G)
\]
is an inclusion-preserving bijection from the nonempty faces of \(A(C)\) onto the nonempty \(A\)-saturated faces of \(C\). Its inverse is \(F\mapsto A(F)\). Consequently, for every nonempty face \(G\unlhd A(C)\),
\[
A\bigl(C\cap A^{-1}(G)\bigr)=G.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maps \(G\mapsto C\cap A^{-1}(G)\) and \(F\mapsto A(F)\) are inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between nonempty faces of \(A(C)\) and nonempty \(A\)-saturated faces of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-preserving correspondence between image faces and affine-fiber-saturated faces of the original convex set.

notation.meaning: F is a face of C

knowledge_statements.title: Faces Under Affine Preimages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine preimages preserve faciality both for full preimage convex sets and after restriction to a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces and let \(T:X\to Y\) be affine. If \(D\subseteq Y\) is convex and \(G\) is a face of \(D\), then \(T^{-1}(G)\) is a face of \(T^{-1}(D)\), allowing the empty face. Likewise, if \(C\subseteq X\) is convex and \(H\) is a face of \(T(C)\), then
\[C\cap T^{-1}(H)\]
is a face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine preimage of a face is a face of the corresponding preimage convex set, and restricting the map to a convex domain gives the analogous facial preimage property.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces and \(T:X\to Y\) is affine.
\(D\subseteq Y\) is convex and \(G\) is a face of \(D\).
For the restricted-domain formulation, \(C\subseteq X\) is convex and \(H\) is a face of \(T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}(G)\text{ is a face of }T^{-1}(D)\), and \(C\cap T^{-1}(H)\text{ is a face of }C.\)

notation.meaning: affine map from X to Y
convex subset of the domain in the restricted formulation

knowledge_statements.title: Merger of Distinct Faces Under Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of a square onto one coordinate sends two distinct vertex faces to the same endpoint face, merging their facial identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=[-1,1]^2,\qquad T(x,y)=x.\] The distinct singleton faces \(F_+=\{(1,1)\}\) and \(F_-=\{(1,-1)\}\) satisfy \[T(F_+)=T(F_-)=\{1\}.\] Thus a noninjective affine map can merge distinct faces, even though their common image remains a face of \(T(C)=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distinct faces \(F_+\) and \(F_-\) have the same image \(\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This example isolates merger of facial distinctions, complementing the seed's example in which a facial image ceases to be a face.

notation.meaning: The upper-right and lower-right vertex faces of the square.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face \(F=\{(0,1)\}\) satisfies \(A(F)=\{0\}\), but \(\{0\}\) is not a face of \(A(C)=[-1,1]\).

notation.meaning: The top vertex, which is a face of C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional example isolates the loss of facial structure caused by a noninjective affine projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \[C:=\operatorname{conv}\{(-1,0),(0,1),(1,0)\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2,\qquad A(x,y):=x.\] The singleton \(F:=\{(0,1)\}\) is an exposed face of \(C\), while \[A(C)=[-1,1]\qquad\text{and}\qquad A(F)=\{0\}.\] Since \(0=\tfrac12(-1)+\tfrac12(1)\) but neither endpoint belongs to \(\{0\}\), the set \(A(F)\) is not a face of \(A(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a triangle onto its horizontal axis sends its top-vertex face to the interior point zero of an interval. Thus a noninjective affine map need not preserve faces.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial Collapse Under Noninjective Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit projection example is correct, and counterexample is the exact mathematical role for this failure leaf. Nevertheless, no evidence accompanies the record.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Saturation Criterion for Preservation of a Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This valid criterion is deferred because its canonical home is the positive forward-image calculus sibling, not this failure-boundary leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine, and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(C\). Define \(\operatorname{sat}_T(F):=C\cap T^{-1}(T(F))\). Then \[T(F)\text{ is a face of }T(C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{sat}_T(F)\text{ is a face of }C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face has a facial image exactly when the union within C of all affine fibers meeting that face is itself a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(F)\) is a face of \(T(C)\) if and only if \(C\cap T^{-1}(T(F))\) is a face of \(C\).

notation.meaning: The portion of C in all affine fibers whose images meet F.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Saturation Criterion for Preservation of a Face

The proposed saturation equivalence is mathematically sound but deferred as canonically belonging to Faces Under Affine Images; positive image and inverse-image calculus are excluded.
