knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed faces, points, and directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Its support function is \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\), possibly taking the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposure is defined by attainment of a finite supporting value of a nonzero linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\neq0\) with \(\sigma_C(a)<+\infty\) and attained, the exposed face selected by \(a\) is \(F_C(a)=\{x\in C:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\). An exposed point is a point \(x\) for which \(F_C(a)=\{x\}\) for some \(a\neq0\). An exposed direction is the direction of an exposed half-line face; for a cone, such a half-line face is an exposed ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero linear functional exposes the set of points where it attains its finite maximum over a convex set. That maximizer set is an exposed face. If it consists of one point, that point is exposed; if it is a half-line face, its direction is exposed. For cones, exposed half-lines are exposed rays.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper nonempty subset \(F\) is an exposed face iff \(F=C\cap H\) for a nontrivial supporting hyperplane \(H\) of \(C\).
A point \(x\) is exposed iff some supporting hyperplane through \(x\) contains no other point of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: For a compact convex set, \(F_C(a)\) is nonempty for every \(a\neq0\).
For a polytope, every nonempty face is exposed.
For a closed pointed cone, exposed rays are exposed directional faces.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is a face.
Every exposed point is an extreme point, and every exposed direction is an extreme direction.
Positive rescaling of the exposing vector does not change the exposed face: \(F_C(\lambda a)=F_C(a)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
boundary_notes: A supremum that is infinite or unattained does not define a nonempty exposed face.
Different functionals may expose the same face.
Not every face or extreme point is exposed.

notation.meaning: Support function of the convex set.
Face exposed by the linear functional with normal vector a.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed-Object Reconstruction of a Line-Free Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional reconstruction using the standard point-direction hull convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex and contain no affine line. Let \(E\) be the set of exposed points of \(C\), and let \(D\) be the set of its exposed recession directions. Then \[C=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\operatorname{conv}(E)+\operatorname{cone}(D)\bigr).\] Equivalently, in the source's point-direction convention, if \(S\) consists of all exposed points and exposed directions of \(C\), then \(C=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-free closed convex set is the closure of the point-direction hull generated by its exposed points and exposed recession directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Internal representations, faces, and exposed or extreme objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and immediate inclusion relations for general convex sets, with the corresponding ray notions for convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set C, an internal representation has the form C=\operatorname{conv}S or C=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S), with generators that may include points and directions, whereas an external representation expresses C as an intersection of half-spaces. A convex subset F\subseteq C is a face when every segment [y,z]\subseteq C satisfying \operatorname{ri}[y,z]\cap F\ne\varnothing has y,z\in F; both \varnothing and C are faces. The zero-dimensional faces are the extreme points, equivalently x\in C is extreme iff x=(1-\lambda)y+\lambda z, y,z\in C, 0<\lambda<1, implies y=z=x. An extreme direction is the direction of a half-line face; for a convex cone, extreme rays correspond one-to-one with extreme directions. If a linear functional h attains \alpha=\max_{x\in C}h(x), then F_h=\{x\in C:h(x)=\alpha\} is an exposed face. Apart from the conventional cases C and possibly \varnothing, exposed faces are precisely C\cap H for nontrivial supporting hyperplanes H. Singleton exposed faces are exposed points, directions of exposed half-line faces are exposed directions, and exposed half-line faces of a cone are exposed rays. Every exposed point, exposed direction, and exposed ray is respectively an extreme point, extreme direction, and extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An internal representation generates a convex set by convex combinations, possibly followed by closure and possibly using directions; an external representation intersects half-spaces. A face is a convex subset that contains both endpoints of every segment in the set whose relative interior meets the subset. The empty set and the whole set are faces. Extreme points are the zero-dimensional faces and are exactly the points admitting no nontrivial two-point convex representation. Directions of half-line faces are extreme directions, and extreme rays of a convex cone correspond to its extreme directions. A maximizing set of an attained linear functional is an exposed face; nontrivial exposed faces are intersections with supporting hyperplanes. Exposed points, directions, and rays are respectively extreme points, directions, and rays.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a convex cone for the cone-specific ray statements.}
h\text{ is linear and attains its maximum over }C\text{ when }F_h\text{ is formed.}

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Intersection Closure of Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite intersection of exposed faces is exposed by the sum of their exposing directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \[F_i=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u_i,x\rangle\] be nonempty contact sets with \(\sigma_C(u_i)<+\infty\). If \(F:=\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i\neq\varnothing\), then \[F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^m u_i,x\right\rangle.\] Thus every nonempty proper finite intersection of exposed faces is exposed.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is a nonempty contact set with finite support value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle\sum_i u_i,x\rangle\); a proper such intersection is exposed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The intersection must be nonempty; a proper intersection is exposed by the sum of the exposing directions.

notation.meaning: Contact set exposed by direction u_i.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper exposed face is the set of all maximizers of a nonconstant linear functional over the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the support function by \[\sigma_C(u):=\sup_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle.\] A nonempty proper subset \(F\subsetneq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\), the supremum is attained, and \[F=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an exposed face exactly when \(F=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) for some \(u\neq0\) with \(\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\) attained on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record defines proper exposed faces using maximization; reversing the normal gives the equivalent minimization convention.

notation.meaning: The support function of C at u.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support, exposure, and extremality hierarchy for points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(x\in C\). For \(a\neq0\), write \(F_C(a)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle\) when the maximum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hierarchy distinguishes boundary points touched by a supporting hyperplane from points uniquely selected by one and from segment-indecomposable points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The point \(x\) is a support point if \(x\in F_C(a)\) for some \(a\neq0\); it is an exposed point if \(F_C(a)=\{x\}\) for some \(a\neq0\); and it is an extreme point if \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), with \(y,z\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(y=z=x\). Hence \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C)\subseteq C\), while support points need not be extreme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support point lies on a supporting hyperplane. An exposed point is the unique point of the set on some supporting hyperplane. An extreme point cannot be expressed as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points of the set. Every exposed point is extreme and supported, whereas a supported point may lie in a positive-dimensional face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ exposed}\Rightarrow x\text{ extreme and supported};\qquad x\text{ supported}\iff\exists a\neq0:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)<+\infty.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\) is exposed iff a nontrivial supporting hyperplane intersects \(C\) exactly in \(\{x\}\).
\(x\) is extreme iff \(\{x\}\) is a face of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: Every relative-boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set admits a supporting hyperplane, although it need not be exposed.
Every vertex of a polytope is exposed.
A point in \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\) is not a support point unless \(C\) lies in a proper affine hyperplane and the functional is constant on \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An exposing functional supplies a strict linear preference for \(x\) over every other point of \(C\).
A support point belongs to the exposed face determined by its supporting functional.
The set of exposed points may be strictly smaller than the set of extreme points.
boundary_notes: Support is understood relative to a nonzero functional and a finite attained support value.
A supporting hyperplane may contain an entire edge or higher-dimensional face.
For nonclosed sets, boundary support and attainment require separate verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Points Are Exactly Included Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support points of a convex set are exactly its included ambient-boundary points; consequently every point of a lower-dimensional convex set is an ambient support point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Then \[\{x\in C:x\text{ is a support point of }C\}=C\cap\operatorname{bd}C.\] In particular, if \(\operatorname{aff}C\neq\mathbb{R}^n\), then every point of \(C\) is a support point in the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary means ambient Euclidean boundary. Under the seed's convention, a supporting hyperplane may contain an entire lower-dimensional convex set.

notation.meaning: Set of support points of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support point is a point at which some nonzero linear functional attains its finite maximum over the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\sigma_C(u):=\sup_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle\). A point \(x\in C\) is a support point of \(C\) if there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)<+\infty.\] Equivalently, a supporting hyperplane of \(C\) passes through \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is a support point exactly when \(\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\) for some \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses finite-dimensional Euclidean duality and the maximization convention.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1, Support Points, p. 133

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed point is the unique maximizer of some nonzero linear functional over the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in C\) is an exposed point of \(C\) if there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) for which \[\{x\}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle.\] Thus the exposing functional has \(x\) as its unique maximizer on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is exposed exactly when \(\{x\}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle\) for some \(u\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exposed point is precisely a singleton exposed face.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.4, Exposed Faces, p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed points of a conjugate epigraph characterized by gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes all exposed points of the epigraph of the conjugate of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper and convex. The exposed points of \operatorname{epi}f^*\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1} are exactly the points \bigl(x^*,f^*(x^*)\bigr) such that, for some x\in\mathbb R^n, f is differentiable at x and \nabla f(x)=x^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point on the graph of the conjugate is an exposed point of its epigraph exactly when its dual coordinate is the gradient of the original proper convex function at some differentiability point.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Exp}(\operatorname{epi}f^*)=\left\{\bigl(x^*,f^*(x^*)\bigr)\mid \exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ f\text{ is differentiable at }x,\ \nabla f(x)=x^*\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Straszewicz Density Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density of exposed points within the extreme points of a finite-dimensional closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the exposed points of \(C\) are dense in the extreme points of \(C\). Equivalently, for every \(x\in\operatorname{ext}(C)\), there exists a sequence \((x_k)\subseteq\operatorname{exp}(C)\) such that \(x_k\to x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every finite-dimensional closed convex set, each extreme point is a limit of exposed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Need Not Imply Exposure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The midpoint of a square's upper edge is supported but not exposed because every supporting contact set through it contains the entire edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[-1,1]^2\) and \(x=(0,1)\). Then \(x\) is a support point, but every supporting functional maximized at \(x\) is constant on the upper edge \([-1,1]\times\{1\}\). Thus no supporting functional uniquely maximizes at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is a support point of \(C\), but \(x\notin\operatorname{exp}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This example isolates nonsingleton contact as the obstruction to exposure.

notation.meaning: Set of exposed points of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-to-Exposure Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support point becomes an exposed point precisely when at least one of its supporting hyperplanes touches the convex set only at that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the support function by \[\sigma_C(u):=\sup_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle.\] For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) with attained finite support value, define the contact set \[E_C(u):=\{y\in C:\langle u,y\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}.\] A support point \(x\) is exposed if and only if there exists such a supporting normal \(u\) satisfying \[E_C(u)=\{x\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is exposed if and only if some supporting normal \(u\neq0\) has contact set \(E_C(u)=\{x\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The transition is governed by uniqueness of the maximizer, not merely existence of a supporting hyperplane.

notation.meaning: The contact set of the supporting functional with normal u.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexposed faces and extreme points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\), and let \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposure failure is defined relative to selection by one supporting functional; it does not mean that the face lacks supporting hyperplanes altogether.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face \(F\) is nonexposed if there is no \(a\neq0\) such that \(F=\{x\in C:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\). An extreme point \(x\) is nonexposed if \(\{x\}\) is a face but no nonzero linear functional has \(x\) as its unique maximizer on \(C\). The exposure-failure boundary is the class \(\mathcal F(C)\setminus\mathcal F_{\mathrm{exp}}(C)\), particularly \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\) at the point level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is nonexposed when no single nonzero linear functional selects exactly that face as its maximizer set. An extreme point is nonexposed when it is a singleton face but is never the unique maximizer of a linear functional. These objects form the boundary between facial extremality and functional exposure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ nonexposed}\iff F\in\mathcal F(C)\ \text{and}\ \forall a\neq0,\ F\neq\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle;\quad x\text{ nonexposed extreme}\iff x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ExpPt}(C).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: An extreme point \(x\) is nonexposed iff every supporting hyperplane through \(x\) contains another point of \(C\).
A face is exposed exactly when it is the intersection of \(C\) with a single nontrivial supporting hyperplane; failure of every such representation is nonexposure.
special_cases_latex: Every face of a polyhedral convex set is exposed, so its exposure-failure class is empty.
A positive-dimensional exposed face may contain extreme points of \(C\) that are not exposed in \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonexposed extreme point remains extreme despite the failure of unique linear selection.
For a closed convex set in finite dimensions, nonexposed extreme points can be approximated by exposed points.
Exposure of a face does not imply that all faces contained in it are exposed in the ambient set.
boundary_notes: The whole set and empty face require conventions and are excluded from the usual proper-face exposure comparison.
Nonuniqueness of an exposing functional is not exposure failure; only nonexistence matters.
Nonexposure is ambient-set dependent: a point may be exposed in a face but not in the whole set.

notation.meaning: Family of exposed faces of the convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexposed face is a proper face that is not the complete contact set of any supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty proper face \(F\subsetneq C\) is nonexposed if there is no \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that the finite support value is attained and \[F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is nonexposed exactly when no nonzero linear functional has \(F\) as its complete maximizer set over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only nonempty proper faces are classified here, avoiding convention-dependent treatment of the whole set and empty face.

notation.meaning: The contact set exposed by the normal u.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.4, Exposed Faces, p. 113

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexposed extreme point cannot lie inside a nontrivial segment of the convex set, yet no linear functional uniquely maximizes there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in C\) is a nonexposed extreme point if \(\{x\}\) is a face of \(C\), equivalently \[x=(1-t)y+t z,\quad y,z\in C,\quad 0<t<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=z=x,\] but there exists no \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \[\{x\}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is a nonexposed extreme point exactly when \(\{x\}\) is a face of \(C\) but \(\{x\}\neq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle\) for every \(u\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates extremality, which is facial, from exposure, which requires a uniquely maximizing linear functional.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.3, Extreme Points, p. 110; III.2.4, Exposed Faces, p. 113

knowledge_statements.title: Exposure Failure Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face fails to be exposed exactly when every supporting hyperplane that contains it also touches the convex set along a strictly larger face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), define \[E_C(u):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle,\qquad N_C(F):=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}:F\subseteq E_C(u)\}.\] The face \(F\) is exposed if and only if some \(u\in N_C(F)\) satisfies \(E_C(u)=F\). Hence exposure fails exactly when \[E_C(u)\supsetneq F\qquad\text{for every }u\in N_C(F).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is nonexposed if and only if every supporting contact set containing \(F\) strictly contains \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness ensures every linear functional attains its support value; the statement identifies enlargement of every supporting contact set as the exact failure mechanism.

notation.meaning: The exposed contact set determined by u.
The set of normals whose contact sets contain F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme points, directions, and rays
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. When \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a convex cone, write \(\mathbb R_+d=\{\lambda d:\lambda\geq0\}\) for \(d\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point extremality concerns indecomposable locations, while ray extremality concerns indecomposable conic directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in C\) is extreme if \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), with \(y,z\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(y=z=x\). A half-line face of \(C\) determines an extreme direction. For a convex cone \(K\), the ray \(\mathbb R_+d\) is extreme if it is a face of \(K\); equivalently, \(u,v\in K\) and \(u+v\in\mathbb R_+d\) imply \(u,v\in\mathbb R_+d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point cannot be split as a nontrivial convex combination of distinct points. An extreme direction is the direction of a half-line face. In a convex cone, an extreme ray is a one-dimensional face; equivalently, any two cone vectors whose sum lies on that ray must themselves lie on the ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\iff \{x\}\unlhd C;\qquad \mathbb R_+d\text{ extreme in }K\iff \mathbb R_+d\unlhd K\iff [u,v\in K,\ u+v\in\mathbb R_+d\Rightarrow u,v\in\mathbb R_+d].\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\) is extreme iff it lies in no open segment joining two distinct points of \(C\).
A nonzero \(d\in K\) generates an extreme ray iff every decomposition \(d=u+v\) with \(u,v\in K\) has \(u\) and \(v\) nonnegative scalar multiples of \(d\).
special_cases_latex: The origin is the only possible extreme point of a nontrivial convex cone.
For a pointed polyhedral cone, its one-dimensional faces are exactly its extreme rays.
A closed bounded convex set has extreme points but no extreme directions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Extreme points are precisely the zero-dimensional nonempty faces.
Extreme rays are invariant under positive rescaling of their generators.
Extreme directions of a closed convex set are also extreme directions of its recession cone, though the converse may fail.
boundary_notes: A cone containing a line has no extreme rays along that line in the pointed sense.
A recession direction need not determine a half-line face and hence need not be extreme.
Ray extremality concerns the ray, not a particular normalized generator.

notation.meaning: Closed ray generated by a nonzero vector.

children.title: Extreme Points
children.top_down_role: Pointwise extremal elements of convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Tests for an Extreme Point
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is extreme exactly when it passes the midpoint test, its singleton is a face, deleting it leaves a convex set, or each positive finite convex representation of it is trivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space and let \(x\in C\). The following are equivalent: \[x\in\operatorname{ext}C;\] \[x=\frac{y+z}{2},\quad y,z\in C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=z=x;\] \[\{x\}\text{ is a face of }C;\] and \[C\setminus\{x\}\text{ is convex}.\] They are also equivalent to finite-combination rigidity: if \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\), where \(x_i\in C\), \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\), then \(x_i=x\) for every \(i\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{ext}C\iff\{x\}\text{ is a face of }C\iff C\setminus\{x\}\text{ is convex}, with equivalent midpoint and finite-combination tests.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These algebraic equivalences require neither topology nor finite dimensionality. The empty set is convex in the deletion formulation.

notation.meaning: set of extreme points of C

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point of a convex set is extreme when it cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points of that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\). A point \(x\in C\) is an extreme point of \(C\) when, for all \(y,z\in C\) and \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[
x=(1-t)y+tz\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=z=x.
\]
The set of all extreme points is denoted by \(\operatorname{ext}C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ext}C\) if and only if every equality \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), with \(y,z\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(y=z=x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the algebraic definition of an extreme point; no topology or closedness is required.

notation.meaning: Set of extreme points of C.

source_witnesses.locator: III, §2.3, “Extreme Points,” p. 110

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-Point Representation of Closed Bounded Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional reconstruction of a closed bounded convex set from its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed, bounded, and convex. Then \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Elements Must Occur Among the Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary membership of extremal elements in a point-direction generating set, including the nonaccumulation condition for directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C=\operatorname{conv}S\), where \(S\) consists of point elements \(S_p\) and direction elements \(S_d\). Then \(\operatorname{ext}C\subseteq S_p\). If every half-line \(L\subseteq C\) has \(L\cap S_p\) bounded, then every extreme direction of \(C\) belongs to \(S_d\). The half-line condition holds, in particular, when \(S_p\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of a convex set generated by specified points and directions must be one of the specified points. Every extreme direction must likewise be one of the specified directions provided no half-line in the set contains an unbounded collection of specified points; boundedness of all specified points is sufficient for this condition.
assumptions_latex: S=S_p\cup S_d\text{ consists of points }S_p\text{ and directions }S_d

children.title: Extreme Rays
children.top_down_role: Indecomposable directional elements of cones and recession structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Obstructs Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone containing a nonzero line has no extreme rays; hence a cone with an extreme ray must be pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If a convex cone \(K\) has nontrivial lineality,
\[
\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\ne\{0\},
\]
then \(K\) has no extreme rays. Consequently, existence of an extreme ray implies that \(K\) is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness is necessary, but without additional hypotheses it is not asserted to be sufficient for existence of extreme rays.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays as One-Dimensional Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero ray of a convex cone is extreme exactly when it is a one-dimensional face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a convex cone and let \(R=\mathbb{R}_+r\subset K\) with \(r\ne0\). Then
\[
R\text{ is an extreme ray of }K
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R\text{ is a one-dimensional face of }K.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is extreme if and only if it is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The zero face is excluded. No topology, closedness, or finite-dimensional assumption is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero ray in a convex cone is extreme when any two cone elements whose sum lies on that ray must themselves lie on the ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a real vector space \(X\), let \(r\in K\setminus\{0\}\), and set \(R=\mathbb{R}_{+}r=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\). The ray \(R\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) if
\[
u,v\in K\ \text{ and }\ u+v\in R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u,v\in R.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ray \(R=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\) is extreme exactly when \(u,v\in K\) and \(u+v\in R\) imply \(u,v\in R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is invariant under replacing the generator by a positive scalar multiple.

notation.meaning: The ray generated by the nonzero vector r.

children.title: Extremality Under Intersections
children.top_down_role: Creation and preservation of extreme points by constraint intersections.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremality Under Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point of any one constraint set remains extreme after imposing further convex constraints, provided it remains feasible. The intersection may also acquire extreme points absent from every individual constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be convex subsets of a real vector space, and suppose \(C=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). If there is an index \(j\in I\) such that \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{ext}C_j\), then
\[
x\in\operatorname{ext}C.
\]
The converse need not hold: for example, two closed half-planes in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\) may have no extreme points individually while their intersection is a pointed wedge with an extreme vertex.
assumptions_latex: \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of convex subsets of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a sufficient preservation rule. Intersections can also create new extreme points even when the point is not extreme in any individual set.

notation.meaning: The feasible intersection of the family.

source_witnesses.locator: III, §2.3, “Extreme Points,” p. 110

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inherited and created extreme points under intersection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex with nonempty intersection \(E=C\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates extreme points inherited from either operand from new extreme points produced by simultaneous constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extreme point \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(E)\) is inherited from \(C\) if \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\), inherited from \(D\) if \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(D)\), and intersection-created if \(x\notin\operatorname{Ext}(C)\cup\operatorname{Ext}(D)\). Extremality is preserved upon restriction: \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\cap D\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C\cap D)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}(D)\cap C\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C\cap D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point of an intersection is inherited when it was already extreme in one of the intersected sets. It is intersection-created when it is extreme only after both constraint systems are imposed. Any extreme point of one set that remains feasible for the other remains extreme in the intersection.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C\cap D)\) iff \((1-t)y+tz=x\), with \(y,z\in C\cap D\) and \(0<t<1\), forces \(y=z=x\).
If \(F\) is a face of \(C\) and \(F\subseteq D\subseteq C\), then \(F\) remains a face of \(D\); singleton faces give the preservation inclusion.
special_cases_latex: If \(D\) is a supporting hyperplane section of \(C\), then \(C\cap D\) is an exposed face and its extreme points are extreme in \(C\).
Intersecting a strictly convex body with affine constraints can create endpoints that were not extreme points of the uncut affine space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Restriction cannot destroy an extreme point that remains feasible.
The reverse inclusion generally fails because active constraints can create new extreme points.
If \(C\cap D\) is a face of \(C\), every extreme point of the intersection is extreme in \(C\).
boundary_notes: An extreme point of \(C\) outside \(D\) is irrelevant to the intersection.
Created extremality depends on both operands and is not intrinsic to either set alone.
The definition concerns binary intersections; finite families are handled by iteration.

notation.meaning: Intersection of the two convex sets.

children.title: Extremality Under Affine Maps
children.top_down_role: Preservation, collapse, and lifting of extremal structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Extreme-Point Lifting Without a Compact Fiber
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of a half-plane containing a line gives an extreme endpoint in the image, but its fiber has no extreme point, so extreme-point lifting fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2,\qquad T(s,t)=s.\] Then \(T(C)=[0,\infty)\), so \(0\in\operatorname{ext}T(C)\). Its fiber is \(C\cap T^{-1}(\{0\})=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\), which is a face of \(C\) but has no extreme point. Indeed, \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\). Consequently, the extreme image point \(0\) has no extreme preimage.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example isolates the extremal-existence requirement for the fiber in the lifting portion of the accepted theorem.

notation.meaning: The closed convex half-plane used in the counterexample.

knowledge_statements.title: Assumption-Free Fiber and Injective-Map Rules
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fibers above extreme image points are faces without compactness, and affine maps injective on the convex set preserve and reflect extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine. If \(y\in\operatorname{ext}T(C)\), then \[C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})\] is a face of \(C\). Moreover, if \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then for every \(x\in C\), \[x\in\operatorname{ext}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(x)\in\operatorname{ext}T(C),\] and hence \(T(\operatorname{ext}C)=\operatorname{ext}T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme image fibers are faces; if \(T|_C\) is injective, then \(x\) is extreme in \(C\) exactly when \(T(x)\) is extreme in \(T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness is unnecessary for faciality of an extreme image fiber or for preservation and reflection under an affine map injective on the set.

notation.meaning: The restriction of T to C.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremality Under Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of the affine image of a compact convex set lifts to an extreme point of the original set. An affine map that is injective on the set preserves and reflects all extreme points; a noninjective map may collapse extremal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\) be affine, with \(T(x)=Ax+b\). If \(y\in\operatorname{ext}T(C)\), then
\[
F=C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})
\]
is a nonempty compact face of \(C\). Consequently, there exists \(x\in\operatorname{ext}C\) with \(T(x)=y\). If, in addition, \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then
\[
T(\operatorname{ext}C)=\operatorname{ext}T(C).
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fiber \(F=C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})\) is a nonempty compact face of \(C\), and some \(x\in\operatorname{ext}C\) satisfies \(T(x)=y\). If \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then \(T(\operatorname{ext}C)=\operatorname{ext}T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The compact finite-dimensional lifting form is stated. Without injectivity, an extreme point of the domain may map to a nonextreme point or collapse with other points.

notation.meaning: Fiber over the image point y.

source_witnesses.locator: III, §2.3, “Extreme Points,” p. 110

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-image extremality and facial fibers
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine, \(T(x)=Ax+b\). For \(y\in T(C)\), define the fiber \(C_y=C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The fiber criterion exactly distinguishes preservation and collapse under arbitrary affine maps; injective maps form the preservation-only regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(y\in T(C)\) is extreme in \(T(C)\) exactly when its fiber \(C_y\) is a face of \(C\). An extreme point \(x\in C\) is preserved when \(T(x)\in\operatorname{Ext}(T(C))\), collapsed when another point of \(C\) has the same image, and lifted over an extreme image point when \(x\in C_y\). If \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then \(x\mapsto T(x)\) bijects \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}(T(C))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An image point is extreme precisely when all of its preimages in the convex set form a face. This facial-fiber condition captures both lifting and collapse. Under an injective affine map, no fiber contains more than one point, so extreme points are preserved in both directions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\) is extreme iff whenever \((1-t)x_1+tx_2\in C_y\), with \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), one has \(x_1,x_2\in C_y\).
For injective \(T|_C\), \(x\) is extreme in \(C\) iff \(T(x)\) is extreme in \(T(C)\).
special_cases_latex: An affine isomorphism preserves the entire face lattice by \(F\mapsto T(F)\).
A projection may send several extreme points to one image point or send an extreme point into a nonextreme image point.
If \(C_y\) is a singleton face, the extreme image point has a unique extreme lift.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every preimage fiber of an extreme image point contains only facially compatible decompositions.
Noninjective affine maps may collapse extremal distinctions.
The preimage of an extreme image point is never an arbitrary convex slice; it is a face.
boundary_notes: The image of an extreme point need not be extreme when the map is noninjective.
An extreme image point may have a positive-dimensional facial fiber.
Affine maps preserve convex combinations but need not preserve closedness of unbounded closed convex sets.

notation.meaning: Fiber of the affine map over an image point, restricted to the convex set.
Restriction of the affine map to the convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-exposure correspondence package
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex set. Write \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\) and \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\) for its extreme and exposed points, and use analogous notation for directions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The correspondence is finite-dimensional and combines inclusion, density, and representation. Closure is required in the density statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extreme-exposure correspondence consists of: \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C)\); \(\operatorname{ExpDir}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{ExtDir}(C)\); and the density identity \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C))\). Thus every extreme point is a limit of exposed points. When \(C\) contains no lines, its exposed points and exposed directions generate it after convexification and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exposed points and directions are always extreme. Conversely, for a closed finite-dimensional convex set, exposed points are dense among extreme points: every extreme point can be approximated by exposed points. For a closed convex set without lines, exposed points and exposed directions recover the entire set after taking the convex hull and closure.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(z\in\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\) with \(\|z-x\|<\varepsilon\).
The closure of the exposed-point set and the closure of the extreme-point set coincide.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, no directional generators are needed and \(C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C))\).
If every extreme point is exposed, then \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)=\operatorname{Ext}(C)\).
For a pointed closed convex cone, exposed rays generate the cone after conic hull and closure.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed convex set with an extreme point has exposed points arbitrarily near that point.
Nonexposed extreme points do not obstruct approximation by uniquely supported points.
Exposure-based representations may require closure even when extreme-point representations do not.
boundary_notes: Density does not assert that every extreme point is exposed.
The finite-dimensional result differs from general infinite-dimensional Krein–Milman-type statements.
For sets containing lines, point-and-direction representations require first separating the lineality space.

notation.meaning: Exposed directions of the convex set.
Closure of the convex hull, with directions interpreted as recession generators.

children.title: Isolation Theorem Family
children.top_down_role: Isolation of compact convex geometry through supporting functionals.

knowledge_statements.title: Isolation Theorem Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every neighborhood of an extreme point of a compact finite-dimensional convex set contains an entire face exposed by some supporting linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{ext}C\), and let \(U\) be any neighborhood of \(x\). Then there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}\) such that the nonempty exposed face
\[
F_a=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle
\]
satisfies \(F_a\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This records the finite-dimensional compact isolation lemma: an extreme point can be isolated to an arbitrary neighborhood by a supporting functional, although that functional need not expose the point alone.

notation.meaning: The face of C exposed by the functional with normal a.

source_witnesses.locator: III, §2.3, “Extreme Points,” p. 110

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolation by an Affine Hyperplane
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space, let \(A\subseteq V\), and write an affine hyperplane as \(H=\{x\in V:f(x)=\alpha\}\), where \(f:V\to\mathbb R\) is a nonzero linear functional and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic isolation is defined without topology. The accompanying existence regimes distinguish algebraically open convex sets in general vector spaces from arbitrary nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hyperplane \(H\) isolates \(A\) if either \(f(x)\leq\alpha\) for every \(x\in A\), or \(f(x)\geq\alpha\) for every \(x\in A\). It strictly isolates \(A\) if the corresponding inequality is strict for every \(x\in A\). For \(u\notin A\), an isolation certificate through \(u\) is a pair \((f,\alpha)\) with \(f\neq0\), \(f(u)=\alpha\), and one of these uniform inequalities on \(A\). The isolation-theorem family asserts existence of a strict certificate when \(A\) is algebraically open and convex, and existence of a non-strict certificate when \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine hyperplane isolates a set when the entire set lies in one of its closed halfspaces, and strictly isolates it when the set lies in one open halfspace. A certificate through an exterior point is a nonzero linear functional whose level hyperplane contains that point and whose values on the set all lie strictly or non-strictly on one side. Strict existence holds for algebraically open convex sets in a real vector space; ordinary isolation exists for every nonempty convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ isolates }A\iff [\sup_{x\in A}f(x)\leq\alpha]\lor[\inf_{x\in A}f(x)\geq\alpha]\), with strict isolation obtained by replacing \(\leq,\geq\) by \(<,>\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: After replacing \(f\) by \(-f\) if necessary, isolation through \(u\) can be normalized as \(f(u)=\alpha\) and \(f(x)\leq\alpha\) for all \(x\in A\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and convex and \(u\notin A\), some affine hyperplane through \(u\) isolates \(A\).
If \(A\) is algebraically open and convex, the isolating inequality may be chosen strict.
immediate_consequences_latex: An isolating hyperplane meeting a closed convex set determines an exposed face.
The definition supplies a functional certificate that the set does not cross the hyperplane.
boundary_notes: Strict isolation is stronger than ordinary isolation and is not guaranteed for an arbitrary convex set containing boundary points on the hyperplane.
In infinite-dimensional algebraic settings, convexity alone does not guarantee an isolation certificate through every exterior point.

notation.meaning: Affine hyperplane represented by a nonzero functional level set.
Functional and level defining the hyperplane.

children.title: Straszewski Theorem Family
children.top_down_role: Approximation of extreme structures by exposed structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Straszewski Theorem Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty compact convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, every exposed point is extreme and every extreme point is a limit of exposed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. A point \(x\in C\) is exposed if there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
\{x\}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{exp}C\subseteq\operatorname{ext}C\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{exp}C}.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Straszewski Exposed-Point Approximation Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact convex set. Write \(\operatorname{ext}K\) for its extreme points and \(\operatorname{exp}K\) for the points uniquely maximizing some nonzero linear functional on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compact convex geometry. The definition packages the two standard forms of Straszewski’s theorem: density of exposed points among extreme points and exposed-point generation of the whole set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in K\) is exposed if there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(\langle c,x\rangle>\langle c,y\rangle\) for every \(y\in K\setminus\{x\}\). The set \(K\) has the Straszewski property when \(\operatorname{ext}K\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{exp}K}\). For compact convex \(K\), the associated generation form is \(K=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{exp}K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed point is the unique maximizer of a nonzero linear functional over the set. The Straszewski approximation property says that every extreme point of a finite-dimensional compact convex set can be approximated by exposed points. Equivalently at the level of set generation, the compact convex set is the closure of the convex hull of its exposed points.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{exp}K\) if and only if there is a supporting hyperplane whose intersection with \(K\) is exactly \(\{x\}\).
The density form means that for every \(x\in\operatorname{ext}K\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(z\in\operatorname{exp}K\) with \(\|z-x\|<\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: Every exposed point is extreme, so \(\operatorname{exp}K\subseteq\operatorname{ext}K\).
The set \(\operatorname{exp}K\) need not itself be closed, even when \(K\) is compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: Continuous affine optimization over \(K\) can be studied through exposed and extreme boundary structure.
Combining density with finite-dimensional extreme-point generation recovers \(K\) from exposed points after closure.
boundary_notes: An extreme point need not itself be exposed.
The closure in the convex-hull formulation cannot generally be removed.
This record does not assert the corresponding statement in arbitrary infinite-dimensional locally convex spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Krein–Milman Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact convex set. A point \(e\in K\) is extreme when it cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean formulation, also called Minkowski’s theorem in the cited source. Unlike the general locally convex Krein–Milman theorem, no closure is needed around the convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{ext}K=\{e\in K:(e=(1-t)x+ty,\ x,y\in K,\ 0<t<1)\Rightarrow x=y=e\}\). The finite-dimensional Krein–Milman property is the identity \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\). Thus the compact convex set is generated exactly by its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of a compact convex subset of Euclidean space are those points that do not lie in any open segment contained in the set. The finite-dimensional Krein–Milman property states that the whole set equals the convex hull of these points. In finite dimensions the convex hull is already the required set, so the closure appearing in the infinite-dimensional version is unnecessary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x\in K\), there are \(m\geq1\), points \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\in\operatorname{ext}K\), and coefficients \(\lambda_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) such that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i e_i\).
The midpoint definition of extremality is equivalent, for convex \(K\), to the formulation using every \(t\in(0,1)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a singleton, its unique point is extreme and the identity is immediate.
For a polytope, \(\operatorname{ext}K\) is its vertex set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty compact convex set in \(\mathbb R^d\) has an extreme point.
A linear functional attaining a maximum on \(K\) attains a maximum at some extreme point.
boundary_notes: Compactness is essential for this exact family statement.
The infinite-dimensional theorem generally uses the closed convex hull and an appropriate locally convex topology.

notation.meaning: Set of all finite convex combinations of points of \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-Point Existence Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(\operatorname{ext}K\) denote the set of points not lying in a nondegenerate open segment contained in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty compact convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The record isolates the existence component from the stronger generation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extreme-point existence property for \(K\) is \(\operatorname{ext}K\neq\varnothing\), where \(e\in\operatorname{ext}K\) precisely when, for all \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), the equality \(e=(1-t)x+ty\) forces \(x=y=e\). Every nonempty compact convex \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) has this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact convex set has the extreme-point existence property when it contains at least one point that cannot be placed strictly between two different points of the set. Every nonempty compact convex subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space has such a point. This is only an existence assertion; it does not by itself say that all points of the set are generated by extreme points.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(e\in K\) such that \(e=(x+y)/2\) with \(x,y\in K\) implies \(x=y=e\).
special_cases_latex: Every singleton has its sole point as an extreme point.
More generally, a nonempty closed convex set in \(\mathbb R^d\) containing no straight line has an extreme point.
immediate_consequences_latex: The extreme-point generating set in the finite-dimensional Krein–Milman identity is nonempty.
Every compact convex face has an extreme point, since the face is again compact and convex.
boundary_notes: Nonemptiness is necessary.
Compactness cannot simply be omitted: an open convex set of positive dimension has no extreme points.
For closed noncompact sets, absence of lines is a useful sufficient condition, but it is not part of this compact-set definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty compact convex set in finite-dimensional space is exactly the convex hull of its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, then

C=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generation by Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(\operatorname{conv}S\) denotes all finite convex combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional compact generation, not merely density or closed-convex-hull generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(K\) is extreme-point generated when \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\). Explicitly, this means that every \(x\in K\) belongs to some finite simplex whose vertices are extreme points of \(K\): there exist \(m\geq1\), \(e_i\in\operatorname{ext}K\), and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i e_i\). Every nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb R^d\) is extreme-point generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extreme-point generation means that each point of the compact convex set is a finite convex combination of extreme points of that same set. Equivalently, every point lies in a finite simplex whose vertices are extreme. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space every nonempty compact convex set has this exact generation property.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\).
Every point of \(K\) lies in the convex hull of a finite subset of \(\operatorname{ext}K\).
special_cases_latex: For a compact polytope, this is generation by its vertices.
For a line segment, the two endpoints generate every point of the segment.
immediate_consequences_latex: A convex subset containing every extreme point of \(K\) must equal \(K\) if it is closed under finite convex combinations.
The values of an affine map on \(K\) are generated by its values on \(\operatorname{ext}K\).
boundary_notes: The generating points must be extreme points of the same set \(K\).
For noncompact convex sets the equality may fail, even when the set is closed.
Infinite-dimensional variants generally require closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dimension Extreme-Point Representation and Sharpness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point is a convex combination of at most affine-dimension plus one affinely independent extreme points, and relative-interior points of a simplex show the bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and set \(r:=\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\). Every \(x\in C\) admits a representation \[x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i v_i,\qquad v_i\in\operatorname{ext}C,\quad \lambda_i>0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1,\quad k\le r+1,\] in which \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) are affinely independent. The bound is sharp: if \(C\) is an \(r\)-simplex, every point of \(\operatorname{ri}C\) requires all \(r+1\) vertices in any extreme-point representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in C\) is a convex combination of at most \(r+1\) affinely independent extreme points; relative-interior points of an \(r\)-simplex require \(r+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the intrinsic-dimension refinement of the accepted ambient-dimensional representation; the simplex clause establishes sharpness.

notation.meaning: Affinely independent extreme points in the representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Extreme-Point Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of a compact convex subset of n-dimensional space is a convex combination of at most n plus one extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. For every \(x\in C\), there exist an integer \(k\leq n+1\), extreme points \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\operatorname{ext}C\), and scalars \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\geq0\) such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i v_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(k\leq n+1\), points \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\operatorname{ext}C\), and coefficients \(\lambda_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1\), such that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i v_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This combines Minkowski extreme-point generation with the ambient-dimensional Carathéodory bound; the sharper bound uses one plus the affine dimension of the set.

notation.meaning: Extreme points used in the representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Extremal Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without compactness, extreme points may not exist, and even when they do exist they need not generate the set. An open interval has no extreme points, while the closed unbounded ray has only its endpoint as an extreme point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Compactness cannot simply be deleted from finite-dimensional extreme-point generation. The open convex set \(C_1=(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{ext}C_1=\varnothing.
\]
The closed unbounded convex set \(C_2=[0,\infty)\subset\mathbb{R}\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{ext}C_2=\{0\},
\qquad
\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C_2)=\{0\}\neq C_2.
\]
Likewise, any nonempty affine subspace of positive dimension has no extreme points.
assumptions_latex: The compactness hypothesis in finite-dimensional extreme-point generation is removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conclusions \(\operatorname{ext}C\neq\varnothing\) and \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C)\) may fail, even for simple convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The examples separately exhibit loss of extreme-point existence for an open set and loss of extreme-point generation for a closed unbounded set.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty convex set, not assumed compact, and let \(\operatorname{ext}C\) denote its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundary class marking where compact extreme-point generation can fail. It includes open, lineal, and many unbounded convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the noncompact extremal-failure class by \(\mathcal F_d=\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^d:C
eq\varnothing,\ C	ext{ convex and noncompact},\ C
eq\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C)\}\). A sufficient failure condition is \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\), since then \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C)=\varnothing
eq C\). Every nonempty open convex set of positive dimension and every affine subspace of positive dimension has no extreme points and therefore belongs to \(\mathcal F_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The noncompact extremal-failure class consists of nonempty, noncompact convex sets that are not generated by their extreme points. The most direct failure occurs when there are no extreme points at all. Positive-dimensional open convex sets and positive-dimensional affine subspaces have this defect. Noncompactness permits failure but does not force it: some closed unbounded convex sets still possess extreme points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\in\mathcal F_d\iff C\neq\varnothing,\ C\text{ convex and noncompact},\ C\neq\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C).\)

If \(C\) is an affine line or a higher-dimensional affine subspace, then \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\).
A nonempty closed convex set containing no straight line does have an extreme point, although generation may still require additional recession data.
immediate_consequences_latex: The compactness hypothesis in the finite-dimensional Krein–Milman equality cannot be deleted without replacement.
Extreme points alone are generally insufficient to represent unbounded convex geometry.

A set containing a line need not be classified solely from that fact without checking its complete extreme-point structure.
This record defines a boundary class; it does not claim a full characterization of all noncompact convex sets generated by extreme points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance and Projection Data of a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space metric geometry. The inner product is essential for the normal and firm-nonexpansiveness structures recorded here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal H\), define \(d_C(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\) and \(\Pi_C(x)=\{p\in C:\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\}\). The metric geometry of \(C\) is governed by the fact that \(\Pi_C(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\); its unique element is denoted \(P_Cx\). It satisfies \(P_Cx\in C\), \(\|x-P_Cx\|=d_C(x)\), and \(\langle y-P_Cx,x-P_Cx\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance to a nonempty closed convex set is the infimum of the distances to its points. The metric projection set consists of all points attaining that infimum. In a real Hilbert space, every nonempty closed convex set has exactly one nearest point to each ambient point, defining the projector. The displacement from the projected point to the original point forms a right or obtuse angle with every feasible direction in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_C(x)=\{P_Cx\}\quad\text{and}\quad p=P_Cx\iff p\in C\ \land\ \forall y\in C,\ \langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_Cx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\frac12\|x-y\|^2\).
\(x-P_Cx\in N_C(P_Cx)\), where \(N_C(p)=\{u:\langle u,y-p\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in C\), then \(P_Cx=x\) and \(d_C(x)=0\).
If \(C\) is a closed affine subspace, the variational inequality strengthens to orthogonality to its parallel subspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: The projector is everywhere defined and single-valued.
Projection connects metric approximation with the normal cone of convex analysis.
boundary_notes: A closed nonconvex set need not have a unique nearest point.
In a general Banach space, existence and uniqueness require additional geometric hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best Approximation, Proximinality, and Chebyshev Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, and let \(x\in\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General nearest-point terminology for subsets of Hilbert space, followed by the closed-convex regime guaranteeing existence and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(p\in C\) is a best approximation to \(x\) from \(C\) if \(\|x-p\|=d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\). The set \(C\) is proximinal if every \(x\in\mathcal H\) has at least one best approximation, and Chebyshev if every \(x\in\mathcal H\) has exactly one. When \(C\) is Chebyshev, \(P_Cx\) denotes that unique point. Every nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathcal H\) is Chebyshev.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A best approximation is a point of the set that realizes the smallest possible distance from a prescribed ambient point. A set is proximinal when at least one nearest point exists for every ambient point, and Chebyshev when that nearest point is always unique. For a nonempty closed convex set in a Hilbert space, both existence and uniqueness hold, so the nearest-point assignment is a well-defined projector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\Pi_C(x)\iff p\in C\ \land\ \|x-p\|=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|;\quad C\text{ Chebyshev}\iff\forall x,\ |\Pi_C(x)|=1.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Best approximations are minimizers of \(y\mapsto\frac12\|x-y\|^2\) over \(C\).
For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(p\) is the best approximation precisely when \(p\in C\) and \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
special_cases_latex: Every closed affine subspace is Chebyshev.
In finite-dimensional Hilbert space, every nonempty closed set is proximinal, although it need not be Chebyshev.
immediate_consequences_latex: For closed convex \(C\), the symbol \(P_Cx\) is defined for every \(x\in\mathcal H\).
Every proximinal set is necessarily nonempty and closed.
boundary_notes: Closedness alone does not ensure proximinality in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Convexity is used for uniqueness; nonconvex proximinal sets can admit several nearest points.

children.title: Existence of Nearest Points
children.top_down_role: Closed convex regimes admitting best approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Nonattainment in a Nonreflexive Space
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The kernel of a norm-nonattaining functional on l1 is a closed convex set that need not contain a nearest point to a given ambient point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(X=\ell^1\), define \(f(y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-1/n)y_n\), let \(C=\ker f\), and let \(x=2e_2\). Then \(C\) is a closed linear subspace and \[d_C(x)=1,\qquad P_C(x)=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is closed and convex, but }d_C(x)=1\text{ and }P_C(x)=\varnothing.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This shows that closedness and convexity alone do not ensure nearest-point existence in an arbitrary Banach space.

notation.meaning: Second standard unit vector of l1.
Set of nearest points in C to x.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximinal Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is proximinal when every ambient point has at least one nearest point in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty subset \(C\) of a normed space \(X\) is proximinal if, for every \(x\in X\), the metric projection set \[P_C(x):=\{p\in C:\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\}\] is nonempty, where \(d_C(x)=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This names the global nearest-point existence property without asserting uniqueness.

notation.meaning: Set of nearest points in C to x.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflexive Banach-Space Existence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty closed convex subset of a reflexive Banach space is proximinal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then for every \(x\in X\) there exists \(p\in C\) satisfying \[\|x-p\|=d_C(x):=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the weak-compactness extension of Hilbert-space existence and makes no uniqueness claim.

notation.meaning: Set of nearest points in C to x.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Closed-Set Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty closed subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space admits a nearest point to each ambient point, even if the set is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed. Then for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) there exists \(p\in C\) such that \[\|x-p\|=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: In finite dimensions convexity is unnecessary for existence; it becomes relevant to uniqueness and variational geometry.

notation.meaning: Set of nearest points in C to x.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence of Nearest Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in a real Hilbert space has at least one nearest point in each nonempty closed convex subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in H\). Then there exists \(p\in C\) such that
\[
\|x-p\|=d_C(x):=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(p\in C\) such that \(\|x-p\|=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the Hilbert-space projection existence theorem; finite-dimensional Euclidean space is a special case.

notation.meaning: A nearest point to x in C.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4, §4.3, “Projectors onto Convex Sets,” p. 74
III, §3.1, “The Projection Operator,” p. 116

children.title: Uniqueness of Nearest Points
children.top_down_role: Strict metric geometry supporting unique projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure in a Non-Strictly-Convex Norm
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the max norm, an entire closed convex segment consists of nearest points to a point above it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\mathbb R^2\) with \(\|z\|_\infty\). Let \(C=[-1,1]\times\{0\}\) and \(x=(0,1)\). Then every \((t,0)\in C\) satisfies \[\|x-(t,0)\|_\infty=1=d_C(x),\] so the nearest point is not unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This shows why strict convexity is the natural sufficient norm assumption for universal uniqueness over convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed nonconvex set {-1,1} has two nearest points to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), let \(C=\{-1,1\}\) and \(x=0\). Then \(d_C(0)=1\) and \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C}|c|=\{-1,1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and finite dimensionality do not ensure uniqueness when the approximating set is nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Convexity Uniqueness Principle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a strictly convex normed space, a convex set has at most one nearest point to any given point whenever a nearest point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a strictly convex normed space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in X\). If \(p,q\in C\) satisfy \(\|x-p\|=\|x-q\|=d_C(x)\), then \(p=q\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a strictly convex normed space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This isolates a sufficient norm-geometric condition for uniqueness; attainment is assumed separately.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of Nearest Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every point in a real Hilbert space, the nearest point in a nonempty closed convex set is unique, so metric projection onto that set is a well-defined function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in H\). There exists exactly one \(p\in C\) such that
\[
\|x-p\|=d_C(x).
\]
Thus the metric projection is the single-valued map \(P_C:H\to C\) defined by \(P_Cx=p\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is exactly one \(p\in C\) satisfying \(\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\); hence the metric projection \(P_Cx=p\) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness follows from the strict convexity induced by the Hilbert norm together with convexity of the feasible set.

notation.meaning: Unique metric projection of x onto C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Nearest-Point Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global uniqueness property for all ambient points. The guaranteed regime is nonempty closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) has the unique nearest-point property, or is Chebyshev, if for every \(x\in\mathcal H\) there exists a unique \(p\in C\) such that \(\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\). Equivalently, \(\Pi_C(x)=\{p\}\) for every \(x\). For nonempty closed convex \(C\), the unique point is characterized by \(p\in C\) and \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set has unique nearest points when every point of the ambient Hilbert space has exactly one distance-minimizing point in the set. Such a set is called Chebyshev, and its unique nearest-point map is the projector. Every nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space has this property; without convexity, two or more nearest points may occur.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\) is Chebyshev if and only if the set-valued map \(\Pi_C:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows C\) is everywhere singleton-valued.
For closed convex \(C\), uniqueness accompanies the variational inequality \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in C\), the unique nearest point is \(x\) itself.
Every nonempty closed affine subspace is Chebyshev.
immediate_consequences_latex: The projector \(P_C:\mathcal H\to C\) is a genuine function.
For closed convex \(C\), \(P_C\) is continuous and in fact firmly nonexpansive.
boundary_notes: Proximinality asserts existence but not uniqueness.
A nonempty closed nonconvex subset can fail uniqueness.
Whether every Chebyshev subset of an arbitrary infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is convex is not asserted here.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and finite dimensionality do not prevent multiple nearest points when convexity is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), let \(C=\{-1,1\}\) and \(x=0\). Then \(C\) is closed and \(d_C(0)=1\), while both \(-1\) and \(1\) attain this distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed nonconvex set can have two nearest points: both endpoints of {-1,1} are nearest to zero.
