knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strength and Ambient Classification of Separators
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and put \(L=\operatorname{aff}(A\cup B)\), with direction space \(V=L-L\). For \(a\neq0\), define \(u_A(a)=\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\) and \(\ell_B(a)=\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A definition of the theorem-family regimes, organized by inequality strength and by whether separation is taken in the full or effective affine ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separating-hyperplane regime is classified by the relation between \(u_A(a)\) and \(\ell_B(a)\):
\[\text{weak: }u_A(a)\leq\ell_B(a);\qquad\text{strict: }u_A(a)<\ell_B(a).\]
A weak separator is proper when it is not constant on \(A\cup B\), equivalently when its restriction to \(V\) is nonzero and
\[\inf_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\sup_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
It is an effective-ambient separator when only the component \(P_Va\) is retained and \(P_Va\neq0\). Thus the family distinguishes weak, proper, strict, closed-target, and relative-affine regimes by adding the corresponding topological and dimensional hypotheses to the same functional ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The separating-hyperplane family is organized by the strength of one functional inequality and by the ambient affine space. Weak separation permits contact at the separating level. Proper separation excludes a functional that is constant on both sets. Strict separation requires a positive functional gap. If the sets are lower-dimensional, the meaningful normal is the component in the direction space of their affine hull; a separator whose normal is purely orthogonal to that space is ambiently trivial.
assumptions_latex: When strict separation is asserted, both extremal functional bounds are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{strict separation}\Rightarrow\text{proper separation}\Rightarrow\text{weak separation},\] with effective-ambient nontriviality imposed by \(P_Va\neq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict separation is \(\sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)<0\).
Proper separation is weak separation together with nonconstancy of \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\) on \(A\cup B\).
Effective-ambient separation is ordinary separation after identifying \(L\) with \(\mathbb R^{\dim L}\).
special_cases_latex: For full-dimensional \(A\cup B\), every nonzero normal is effective-ambient.
For point-set separation with closed convex target, the closed-target regime supplies a strict separator.
immediate_consequences_latex: The same pair of convex sets may admit separators of several strengths.
Projection of a separating normal onto \(V\) removes the component that is constant along \(L\).
boundary_notes: The labels describe distinct hypotheses and conclusions; they are not interchangeable theorem statements.
Weak ambient separation can be vacuous for sets contained in a common proper affine subspace.

notation.meaning: Direction space parallel to the effective affine ambient set.
Orthogonal projection of the normal onto \(V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Functional Characterizations of Proper and Strong Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes proper and strong separation of arbitrary nonempty subsets of Euclidean space through extrema of a linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty. A hyperplane properly separates C_1 and C_2 if and only if there exists b\in\mathbb{R}^n such that \inf_{x\in C_1}\langle x,b\rangle\ge\sup_{x\in C_2}\langle x,b\rangle and \sup_{x\in C_1}\langle x,b\rangle>\inf_{x\in C_2}\langle x,b\rangle. A hyperplane strongly separates C_1 and C_2 if and only if there exists b\in\mathbb{R}^n such that \inf_{x\in C_1}\langle x,b\rangle>\sup_{x\in C_2}\langle x,b\rangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty sets are properly separated exactly when some linear functional weakly orders them while preventing both sets from lying in the separating hyperplane. They are strongly separated exactly when some linear functional has a strictly positive gap between its values on the two sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}\exists H\text{ properly separating }C_1,C_2&\iff\exists b:\ \inf_{C_1}\langle\cdot,b\rangle\ge\sup_{C_2}\langle\cdot,b\rangle\ \land\ \sup_{C_1}\langle\cdot,b\rangle>\inf_{C_2}\langle\cdot,b\rangle,\\\exists H\text{ strongly separating }C_1,C_2&\iff\exists b:\ \inf_{C_1}\langle\cdot,b\rangle>\sup_{C_2}\langle\cdot,b\rangle.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hyperplane Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ordinary, proper, strong, and strict separation for two nonempty subsets of Euclidean space; convexity and disjointness are not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, let H=\{x:\langle b,x\rangle=\alpha\} with b\ne0, and let B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}. Up to reversing b, H separates C_1 and C_2 if C_1\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle\ge\alpha\} and C_2\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle\le\alpha\}. The separation is proper if C_1 and C_2 are not both contained in H. It is strong if there exists \varepsilon>0 such that C_1+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle>\alpha\} and C_2+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle<\alpha\}. It is strict if C_1 and C_2 themselves are contained in the opposing open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane separates two nonempty sets when they lie in opposing closed half-spaces. Separation is proper when the sets are not both contained in the hyperplane, strong when uniform Euclidean neighborhoods of both sets lie in opposing open half-spaces, and strict when the sets themselves lie in opposing open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}H\text{ separates }C_1,C_2&\iff C_1\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle\ge\alpha\},\ C_2\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle\le\alpha\}\quad\text{(up to orientation)},\\H\text{ separates properly}&\iff H\text{ separates and }\neg(C_1\subseteq H\land C_2\subseteq H),\\H\text{ separates strongly}&\iff \exists\varepsilon>0:\ C_1+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle>\alpha\},\ C_2+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle<\alpha\},\\H\text{ separates strictly}&\iff C_1\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle>\alpha\},\ C_2\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle<\alpha\}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Characterization of Weak Separators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-separation normals form the polar of the difference set; a nonzero normal exists exactly when the closed conic hull of that difference does not fill the space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and define \(S^\circ:=\{a:\langle a,s\rangle\le0\text{ for every }s\in S\}\). The normals oriented from \(C\) toward \(D\) that satisfy the weak-separation inequalities are exactly \((C-D)^\circ\). Hence a nonzero such normal exists if and only if \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-D)\ne\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{a:\sup_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\le\inf_{d\in D}\langle a,d\rangle\}=(C-D)^\circ\), and this cone contains a nonzero vector iff \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-D)\ne\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural characterization for arbitrary nonempty convex pairs, including pairs that intersect.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Separation Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak separation places two disjoint convex sets in opposite closed halfspaces but permits both sets to approach or touch the separating hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\langle a,c\rangle\le\alpha\le\langle a,d\rangle\qquad\text{for all }c\in C\text{ and }d\in D.\] Equivalently, \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\le\inf_{d\in D}\langle a,d\rangle\). Equality may hold, so neither a positive margin nor strict placement of either set is part of the weak-separation conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) with \(\langle a,c\rangle\le\alpha\le\langle a,d\rangle\) for all \(c\in C\), \(d\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional weak separation, allowing contact with the separating hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-Set Form of Proper Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper separation is equivalent to the origin lying outside the relative interior of the convex difference set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{ri}(C-D)=\operatorname{ri}C-\operatorname{ri}D\). Consequently, \(C\) and \(D\) are properly separable if and only if \(0\notin\operatorname{ri}(C-D)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional formulation of the proper-separation criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Separation Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex sets are properly separable exactly when their relative interiors are disjoint; proper separation requires a strict distinction somewhere, not a uniform gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sets \(C\) and \(D\) have disjoint relative interiors if and only if there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\le\inf_{d\in D}\langle a,d\rangle\] and the functional is not constant with the same value on \(C\cup D\). Equivalently, separation holds and there are \(c_0\in C\), \(d_0\in D\) with \(\langle a,c_0\rangle<\langle a,d_0\rangle\). This is proper separation, not necessarily strong separation by a positive uniform margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) and \(D\) are properly separable if and only if \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap\operatorname{ri}D=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of proper separation by disjoint relative interiors.

notation.meaning: relative interior of the first convex set
relative interior of the second convex set
normal vector of a properly separating hyperplane

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Criterion for Proper Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a necessary and sufficient condition for proper separation of two nonempty convex sets, without closedness or full-dimensionality assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty convex sets. There exists a hyperplane properly separating C_1 and C_2 if and only if \operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets admit a proper separating hyperplane exactly when their relative interiors are disjoint.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Target Membership-Exclusion Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Its support function is \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separation used as an exact membership-exclusion test for a nonempty closed convex target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed-target separation certificate for exclusion of \(z\) from \(C\) is a vector \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying
\[\sigma_C(a)<\langle a,z\rangle.\]
The closed-target separation regime is the pair \((C,z)\) with \(C\) nonempty closed convex and \(z\notin C\). In this regime such a certificate exists. Equivalently,
\[z\in C\iff \langle a,z\rangle\leq\sigma_C(a)\quad\forall a\in\mathbb R^n,\]
whereas one strict violation certifies \(z\notin C\). Any \(\beta\) between \(\sigma_C(a)\) and \(\langle a,z\rangle\) defines a hyperplane that places \(C\) and \(z\) in opposite open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex target, an exterior point has a nonzero linear functional whose value at the point is strictly larger than its support value on the target. Such a functional is a membership-exclusion certificate. Consequently, a point belongs to the closed convex target exactly when it satisfies every support inequality of the target; a single strict violation proves nonmembership.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The certificate is strict separation of \(\{z\}\) and \(C\).
It is strict homogeneous separation of \(0\) from \(C-z\).
It is a violated half-space inequality in the outer representation of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: The projection direction \(a=z-P_Cz\) supplies a certificate.
For a closed convex cone \(K\), exclusion is certified by a polar vector \(a\in K^\circ\) with \(\langle a,z\rangle>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed convex sets are intersections of their supporting closed half-spaces.
Support inequalities form a complete, possibly infinite, certificate system for membership.
boundary_notes: Closedness is essential: a point in \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) cannot be strictly separated from \(C\).
The certificate need not correspond to a support value attained by an unbounded target unless an appropriate maximizing point exists.

notation.meaning: Support function of the closed convex target.

knowledge_statements.title: Exterior-Point Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point outside a nonempty closed convex subset of Euclidean space can be separated from it by a hyperplane with a positive point-to-set margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\notin C\). Then there exist \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
\langle u,c\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }c\in C.
\]
Thus a closed hyperplane strictly separates the exterior point from the target set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strong separation of one exterior point from a closed convex target.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Set Targets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set equals the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing it; every exterior point violates some valid affine inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), define \(H^-_{u,\beta}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,z\rangle\leq\beta\}\). For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\). Every nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies
\[
C=\bigcap_{\substack{u\neq0,\,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\\ C\subset H^-_{u,\beta}}}H^-_{u,\beta}
=\bigcap_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,z\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\},
\]
where an inequality with \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\) imposes no restriction. Equivalently, every point in \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C\) violates at least one valid affine inequality for \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is the intersection of all closed affine halfspaces containing it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer halfspace representation of finite-dimensional closed convex targets.

notation.meaning: Support value of the target in direction u
Closed halfspace with normal u and bound beta

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Distance Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets at positive Euclidean distance admit a unit-normal separating hyperplane whose directional gap is at least their distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets with \(\delta=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\). Then there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\|u\|=1\) such that
\[
\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle+\delta\leq\inf_{d\in D}\langle u,d\rangle.
\]
Consequently, any \(\alpha\) strictly between the two displayed bounds defines a hyperplane that strongly separates \(C\) and \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is \(u\) with \(\|u\|=1\) such that \(\inf_D\langle u,\cdot\rangle-\sup_C\langle u,\cdot\rangle\geq\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive set distance supplies a strong separating margin without requiring distance attainment.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance between the two sets

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Closure Boundary for Strict Point Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is strictly separable from a convex target exactly when it lies outside the target's closure; omitted boundary points are the precise obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\langle u,c\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }c\in C\] if and only if \(x\notin\overline C\). In particular, every \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\) is a nonmember for which strict separation fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict affine separation of \(x\) from \(C\) holds if and only if \(x\notin\overline C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp characterization of strict separation from a possibly nonclosed convex target.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Target Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper halfspace cannot be strictly separated from its excluded boundary origin, showing why closedness is essential for exterior-point strong separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t>0\}\) and \(x=(0,0)\). The set \(C\) is convex but not closed, \(x\notin C\), and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=0\). There are no \(u\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying
\[
\langle u,c\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }c\in C.
\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of strict exterior-point separation when target closedness is removed.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

children.title: Effective-Ambient Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Separation within effective affine ambient spaces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation Relative to the Effective Affine Ambient Space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets, \(L=\operatorname{aff}(A\cup B)\), and \(V=L-L\). Every affine functional on \(L\) has a normal represented by a vector in \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative separation for lower-dimensional convex sets; nontriviality is measured inside their joint affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An effective-ambient separator of \(A\) and \(B\) is an affine hyperplane of \(L\),
\[H_L(v,\beta):=\{x\in L:\langle v,x\rangle=\beta\},\qquad v\in V\setminus\{0\},\]
such that
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle v,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\inf_{y\in B}\langle v,y\rangle.\]
It is strict when both inequalities are strict. An ambient normal \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) induces this separator exactly through \(v=P_Va\). The separator is trivial relative to \(L\) when \(P_Va=0\), because then \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\) is constant on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective ambient space for two convex sets is their joint affine hull. Separation in this space uses a nonzero normal lying in its parallel direction space. An ambient normal matters only through its projection onto that direction space. If the projection vanishes, the functional is constant on the entire affine hull and any apparent separation is geometrically trivial. Strict and weak relative separation use the usual functional inequalities restricted to the effective ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[a\text{ defines a nontrivial separator relative to }L\iff P_Va\neq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Choose an affine isometry \(L\cong\mathbb R^{\dim L}\); effective-ambient separation becomes ordinary full-dimensional separation there.
Two ambient normals differing by an element of \(V^\perp\) induce the same ordering on \(L\), up to an additive constant.
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\mathbb R^n\), effective-ambient and ordinary separation coincide.
For support at \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}C\), taking \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\) excludes hyperplanes containing all of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative-boundary points can have nontrivial supporting hyperplanes even when ordinary interior is empty.
Orthogonal projection of an ambient separator onto \(V\) preserves all functional differences between points of \(L\).
boundary_notes: A hyperplane containing \(L\) is not a nontrivial effective-ambient separator.
Relative separation must use the affine hull of all participating sets, not necessarily the affine hull of either set alone.

notation.meaning: Joint affine hull and its parallel direction space.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Closedness Characterized by Exterior-Point Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subset of an affine space is relatively closed exactly when every excluded point in that space admits strict intrinsic separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=a+L\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty affine subspace and let \(C\subset A\) be nonempty and convex. Then \(C\) is closed in \(A\) if and only if, for every \(x\in A\setminus C\), there exists \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle\).
assumptions_latex: \(A=a+L\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is closed in }A\iff (\forall x\in A\setminus C)(\exists u\in L\setminus\{0\})\;\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic characterization inside a fixed finite-dimensional affine ambient space.

notation.meaning: Direction space of the affine ambient space

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Ambient Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relatively closed convex target and an exterior point in the same affine space admit strict separation by a functional nonconstant on that space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=a+L\) be an affine subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(C\subset A\) be nonempty, convex, and relatively closed in \(A\), and let \(x\in A\setminus C\). Then there exist \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
\langle u,c\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,x\rangle
\qquad\text{for every }c\in C.
\]
The normal lies in \(L\), so the induced affine functional is nonconstant on the effective ambient space.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset A\) is nonempty, convex, and closed in the relative topology of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) satisfies \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exterior-point separation performed inside the target's effective affine ambient space.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.title: Nondegenerate Separation in a Proper Affine Carrier
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional relatively closed convex target can be strictly separated from an exterior point by a normal parallel to its affine direction space; normals orthogonal to that space are exactly the degenerate ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=a+L\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(C\subset A\) be nonempty, convex, and relatively closed in \(A\), and let \(x\in A\setminus C\). Then there exists \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle.\] More generally, an ambient normal \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) can distinguish points of \(A\) only if \(P_Lw\neq0\); every \(w\in L^\perp\) is constant on \(A\) and cannot strictly separate \(x\) from \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset A\) is nonempty, convex, and relatively closed in \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a strict separator \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\), while normals in \(L^\perp\) cannot distinguish points within \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation of an exterior point from a relatively closed convex target inside a proper affine carrier, with the exact ambient-normal degeneracy boundary.

notation.meaning: Direction space of the affine carrier
Orthogonal projector onto the direction space
Orthogonal complement of the direction space

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between relative separators and ambient normals for targets in a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=x_0+V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be an affine subspace and let \(A,B\subseteq L\). If \(u\in V\) separates \(A\) and \(B\) within \(L\) at level \(\alpha\), then every \(u+w\), with \(w\in V^\perp\), gives the same ordering on \(L\) at level \(\alpha+\langle w,x_0\rangle\), since
\[
\langle u+w,x\rangle=\langle u,x\rangle+\langle w,x_0\rangle\qquad(x\in L).
\]
Conversely, an ambient normal \(a\) restricts nontrivially to \(L\) exactly when its projection onto \(V\) is nonzero; if that projection vanishes, the functional is constant on \(L\) and cannot properly distinguish \(A\) from \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For sets in an affine subspace, only the normal component parallel to that subspace affects separation; orthogonal components merely shift the hyperplane level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separation on \(L\) depends only on the projection of the ambient normal onto \(V\); a zero projection makes the functional constant on \(L\).

notation.meaning: chosen base point of the affine subspace

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Hull Reduction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation by a base point identifies an affine hull with its direction space while preserving convexity, relative closedness, distances, and separation inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=a+L\) and define \(T:A\to L\) by \(T(z)=z-a\). The map \(T\) is an affine isometry. Consequently, \(C\subset A\) is convex or relatively closed in \(A\) exactly when \(T(C)\) is convex or closed in \(L\), respectively, and
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(T(C),T(D)).
\]
Moreover, an inequality \(\langle u,z\rangle\leq\alpha\) on \(A\), with \(u\in L\), corresponds to \(\langle u,T(z)\rangle\leq\alpha-\langle u,a\rangle\) on \(L\).
assumptions_latex: \(A=a+L\) is a nonempty affine subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Translation by \(-a\) converts convexity, relative closure, distance, and affine separation in \(A\) into their ordinary counterparts in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation identifies an affine ambient space with its linear direction space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=a+L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(P_L\) be orthogonal projection onto \(L\), and let \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(z=a+\ell\in A\), \[\langle w,z\rangle=\langle w,a\rangle+\langle P_Lw,\ell\rangle.\] Thus the restriction is constant on \(A\) exactly when \(w\in L^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction of \(\langle w,\cdot\rangle\) to \(A\) is constant if and only if \(w\in L^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Gap Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets. For \(a\neq0\), define the oriented gap \(g(a;A,B)=\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict or strong separation, with explicit distinction between the positive-gap property and hypotheses ensuring its existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(A\) and \(B\) are strictly separated when there exists \(a\neq0\) with
\[g(a;A,B)>0.\]
A normalized strict-separation certificate is \(u=a/\|a\|\) with margin
\[\gamma(u;A,B):=\inf_{y\in B}\langle u,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle u,x\rangle>0.\]
The strict-separation family comprises configurations for which this certificate is ensured, notably: a point outside a nonempty closed convex set, and two disjoint nonempty closed convex sets when one is bounded. Any \(\beta\) in the open gap gives
\[\langle u,x\rangle<\beta<\langle u,y\rangle\quad\forall(x,y)\in A\times B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict separation is the existence of a nonzero linear functional with a positive gap between its supremum on one convex set and its infimum on the other. Normalizing the functional makes the gap a geometric margin. The standard existence regimes include an exterior point versus a closed convex set and two disjoint closed convex sets when one is bounded. Every level inside the positive gap defines a hyperplane leaving both sets in opposite open half-spaces.
assumptions_latex: The relevant support bounds are finite in a strict-separating direction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict separation is \(\sigma_A(u)+\sigma_B(-u)<0\).
It is strict separation of \(0\) from \(A-B\).
It is the existence of disjoint parallel closed supporting levels with positive spacing.
special_cases_latex: For \(B=\{z\}\), the margin is \(\langle u,z\rangle-\sigma_A(u)\).
If \(A\) is compact, \(B\) is closed, and \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), a strict certificate exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict separation implies positive Euclidean distance between the two sets.
The normalized margin is invariant under positive rescaling of the original normal.
boundary_notes: Closedness without boundedness does not ensure strict separation of two disjoint sets.
Weak or proper separation may remain possible when every normalized strict margin is nonpositive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Separation When One Closed Convex Set Is Bounded
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional strong-separation theorem retaining nonemptiness, closedness, convexity, disjointness, and the one-set-bounded hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1,Q_2\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets with \(Q_1\cap Q_2=\varnothing\). If at least one of \(Q_1,Q_2\) is bounded, then there exist \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\sup_{x_2\in Q_2}\langle g,x_2\rangle<\gamma<\inf_{x_1\in Q_1}\langle g,x_1\rangle.\] Equivalently, there is a nonzero \(g\) for which \[\sup_{x_2\in Q_2}\langle g,x_2\rangle<\inf_{x_1\in Q_1}\langle g,x_1\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty, disjoint, closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are strongly separable when at least one is bounded. A nonzero linear functional then has a strict gap between its supremum on the second set and its infimum on the first, and a separating level can be chosen inside that gap.
assumptions_latex: Q_1\text{ and }Q_2\text{ are closed and convex}
Q_1\text{ is bounded or }Q_2\text{ is bounded}

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Closed Strict-Separation Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint nonempty convex sets are strongly separated when one is compact and the other closed, because their Euclidean distance is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K,C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets such that \(K\) is compact, \(C\) is closed, and \(K\cap C=\varnothing\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(K,C)>0\), and there exist \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) with \(\alpha<\beta\) such that
\[
\langle u,k\rangle\leq\alpha<\beta\leq\langle u,c\rangle
\qquad\text{for all }k\in K\text{ and }c\in C.
\]
Thus compactness and closedness rule out asymptotic contact and produce a positive separating gap.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact, \(C\) is closed, and \(K\cap C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(u\neq0\) and \(\alpha<\beta\) with \(\langle u,k\rangle\leq\alpha<\beta\leq\langle u,c\rangle\) for all \(k\in K,c\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict separation of disjoint compact and closed convex sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Closed Positive-Margin Configuration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K,C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets with \(K\) compact, \(C\) closed, and \(K\cap C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict separation where compactness of one target and closedness of the other exclude asymptotic contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A compact-closed strict-separation regime is an ordered pair \((C,K)\) satisfying
\[C\neq\varnothing,\quad K\neq\varnothing,\quad C\text{ closed convex},\quad K\text{ compact convex},\quad C\cap K=\varnothing.\]
A certificate for this regime is a nonzero \(a\) such that
\[\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle<\min_{y\in K}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
Every compact-closed regime admits such a certificate. Its normalized gap is
\[\gamma=\frac{\min_{y\in K}\langle a,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle}{\|a\|}>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The compact-closed regime consists of two disjoint nonempty convex sets, one compact and the other closed. Compactness turns the relevant extremal functional value into a minimum and, together with closedness and disjointness, prevents asymptotic contact. The regime therefore admits a nonzero functional whose largest value on the closed set is strictly below its smallest value on the compact set. After normalization, the difference is a positive geometric margin.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(0\notin C-K\), and \(C-K\) is closed convex because \(K\) is compact.
There exist \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq\beta-\varepsilon\) on \(C\) and \(\langle u,y\rangle\geq\beta+\varepsilon\) on \(K\).
special_cases_latex: A singleton \(K=\{z\}\) yields strong point-set separation.
If both sets are compact, either set may be assigned the compact role.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Euclidean distance between \(C\) and \(K\) is positive and attained.
A separating level can be chosen anywhere inside the open functional gap.
boundary_notes: If compactness is removed, two disjoint closed convex sets can have zero distance and fail strict separation.
Convexity is required for the stated affine separation guarantee.

notation.meaning: Normalized positive separation gap for the certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Maximum-Margin Point-Set Normal
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized projection residual is the unique unit-bounded direction maximizing the point-set separation margin, whose value is the point-to-set distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\notin C\), and put \(p=P_Cx\), \(\delta=\|x-p\|\), and \(u_*=(x-p)/\delta\). Then \[\max_{\|v\|\le1}\left(\langle v,x\rangle-\sup_{c\in C}\langle v,c\rangle\right)=\delta,\] and \(u_*\) is the unique maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_*=(x-p)/\delta\) uniquely maximizes the directional point-set gap over \(\|v\|\le1\), and the maximum equals \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality and uniqueness of the normalized projection residual among unit-bounded directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Point-Set Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection residual from a closed convex set is a strict separating normal, with normalized margin equal to the point-to-set distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C\), and let \(p=P_Cx\). For \(u=x-p\neq0\),
\[
\langle u,c-p\rangle\leq0\qquad\text{for every }c\in C,
\]
and
\[
\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\leq\langle u,p\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle.
\]
The corresponding unnormalized gap is \(\|x-p\|^2\); for the unit normal \(u/\|u\|\), the gap is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=\|x-p\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(u=x-p\), \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\leq\langle u,p\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle\), with normalized margin \(\|x-p\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based positive-margin separation of an exterior point and a closed convex set.

notation.meaning: Metric projection of x onto C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Separation of an Exterior Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\notin C\). Write \(p=P_Cz\) for the Euclidean projection and \(d_C(z)=\|z-p\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional positive-margin separation of a point from a closed convex set, including its canonical projection normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A strong point-set separator is a triple \((u,\beta,\varepsilon)\) with \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[\langle u,x\rangle\leq\beta-\varepsilon\quad\forall x\in C,\qquad \langle u,z\rangle\geq\beta+\varepsilon.\]
Equivalently, \(u\) is a unit vector satisfying
\[\langle u,z\rangle-\sigma_C(u)>0.\]
For the closed convex target, the canonical choice
\[u=\frac{z-P_Cz}{\|z-P_Cz\|}\]
has directional gap \(d_C(z)>0\). A midpoint level yields a symmetric half-gap \(\varepsilon=d_C(z)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong point-set separation places a closed convex set and an exterior point in opposite open half-spaces with a positive margin. Equivalently, a unit functional has a strictly larger value at the point than its support value on the set. The normalized displacement from the projection of the point onto the set is a canonical separating normal, and its functional gap equals the point-to-set distance.
assumptions_latex: \(z\notin C\), so \(d_C(z)>0\) and the normalized projection displacement is defined.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(a\neq0\) with \(\langle a,z\rangle>\sigma_C(a)\).
The singleton \(\{z\}\) and \(C\) have a positive normalized separation margin.
The projection residual belongs to \(N_C(P_Cz)\) and points toward \(z\).
special_cases_latex: For an affine subspace, \(u\) is the normalized orthogonal residual.
For a closed convex cone, the projection residual gives a polar-cone exclusion certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: The separating inequality certifies both \(z\notin C\) and \(z\notin\operatorname{cl}C\).
The best unit-direction point-set margin equals \(d_C(z)\).
boundary_notes: If the target is not closed and \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), the distance and every strong margin are zero.
The symmetric parameter \(\varepsilon\) is half the full functional gap when the midpoint level is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Normalized Separation Margin
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty sets. For each unit vector \(u\), define its oriented directional gap by \(g_u(A,B)=\inf_{y\in B}\langle u,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle u,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean finite-dimensional metric interpretation of strong separation; extended-real values are allowed directionwise, while positive finite values are separation margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum normalized separation margin from \(A\) toward \(B\) is
\[\Gamma(A,B):=\sup_{\|u\|=1}\left(\inf_{y\in B}\langle u,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle u,x\rangle\right).\]
A direction \(u\) is a positive-margin separator when \(g_u(A,B)>0\). The corresponding parallel supporting levels are separated by Euclidean distance \(g_u(A,B)\), because \(u\) has unit norm. Thus
\[A,B\text{ are strongly separated}\iff\Gamma(A,B)>0.\]
Whenever a closest pair \((x_*,y_*)\in A\times B\) exists for closed convex \(A,B\), the unit displacement \(u=(y_*-x_*)/\|y_*-x_*\|\) realizes the margin and
\[\Gamma(A,B)=\operatorname{dist}(A,B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a unit direction, the separation margin is the smallest functional value on the second set minus the largest functional value on the first. Its supremum over unit directions is the maximum normalized margin. A positive value is exactly strong separation. Geometrically, the value is the distance between two parallel supporting levels orthogonal to the unit normal. When closed convex sets possess a closest pair, the normalized displacement between that pair is an optimal direction and the maximum margin equals their Euclidean distance.
assumptions_latex: Convexity is required for the stated closest-pair support interpretation.
The equality with distance assumes that a closest pair exists.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(g_u(A,B)=-\sigma_A(u)-\sigma_B(-u)\).
The symmetric half-margin about a midpoint separating level is \(g_u(A,B)/2\).
special_cases_latex: For \(B=\{z\}\) and closed convex \(A\), \(\Gamma(A,\{z\})=d_A(z)\).
For a compact set and a disjoint closed convex set, a closest pair exists and the margin is positive.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive margin implies positive set distance.
The margin is invariant under common translation and scales linearly under common positive dilation.
boundary_notes: Zero maximum margin does not imply intersection; disjoint sets may approach each other asymptotically.
Without closest-pair attainment, equality between the supremal directional margin and distance requires separate closure analysis.

notation.meaning: Oriented gap in the unit direction \(u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Criterion for Strong Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes strong separation of two nonempty convex sets by positive Euclidean distance and by exclusion of the origin from the closure of their difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty convex sets. There exists a hyperplane strongly separating C_1 and C_2 if and only if \inf\{\|x_1-x_2\|:x_1\in C_1,\ x_2\in C_2\}>0. Equivalently, strong separation holds if and only if 0\notin\operatorname{cl}(C_1-C_2).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets are strongly separable exactly when their Euclidean distance is positive, equivalently when the origin does not belong to the closure of their difference set.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure, Symmetry, and Scaling of Set Distance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set distance is symmetric, closure invariant, invariant under common translation, and homogeneous under common scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,C)=\operatorname{dist}(\overline C,\overline D).\] For every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) and scalar \(\lambda\), \[\operatorname{dist}(C+z,D+z)=\operatorname{dist}(C,D),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\lambda C,\lambda D)=|\lambda|\operatorname{dist}(C,D).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set distance is symmetric, closure invariant, translation invariant, and homogeneous under common scaling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental invariances of Euclidean distance between two nonempty sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Distance Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance between two sets is the distance from zero to their displacement set; zero distance means zero is a limit displacement, not necessarily an intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\inf_{c\in C,\,d\in D}\|c-d\|.
\]
With \(D-C=\{d-c:d\in D,\ c\in C\}\), one has
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(0,D-C)
=\operatorname{dist}(0,\overline{D-C}).
\]
Therefore \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=0\) exactly when \(0\in\overline{D-C}\). This condition need not mean that \(C\) and \(D\) intersect, even when both sets are closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set distance expressed through the displacement set and its closure.

notation.meaning: Set difference of D and C

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Some Results on the Euclidean Distance to a Closed Set p. 73

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 3.2 Some Results on the Euclidean Distance to a Closed Set p. 73

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Pair Representation of an Optimal Margin
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive nearest displacement, when it exists, supplies an optimal unit separator supported at the nearest points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) have a nearest pair \((c_*,d_*)\) with \(\delta=\|d_*-c_*\|>0\). Then \(u_*=(d_*-c_*)/\delta\) satisfies \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle u_*,c\rangle=\langle u_*,c_*\rangle,\qquad \inf_{d\in D}\langle u_*,d\rangle=\langle u_*,d_*\rangle,\] and the difference of these support levels is \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u_*=(d_*-c_*)/\delta\), the directional gap equals \(\delta\) and is attained at \(c_*\) and \(d_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal normalized separator induced by an attained positive set distance.

notation.meaning: unit direction of the nearest displacement

knowledge_statements.title: Existence of an Optimal Margin Normal
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized directional-gap problem has an optimal normal; at positive distance every optimizer is a unit vector realizing the distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and define \(g(u)=\inf_{d\in D}\langle u,d\rangle-\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\). The extended-real upper-semicontinuous function \(g\) attains its maximum on \(\{u:\|u\|\le1\}\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\), every maximizer has norm one and its gap equals \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{\|u\|\le1}g(u)\) is attained; if \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\), every maximizer \(u_*\) satisfies \(\|u_*\|=1\) and \(g(u_*)=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and normalization of the directional-gap maximization problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Separating-Margin Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty convex sets, Euclidean distance equals the largest directional gap over normals of norm at most one; positive distance is equivalent to positive-margin separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
g(u)=\inf_{d\in D}\langle u,d\rangle-
\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle.
\]
Then the maximal normalized separating gap satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\sup_{\|u\|\leq1}g(u).
\]
In particular, a positive-margin separator exists exactly when \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\). When the supremum is attained by a unit vector \(u\), its directional gap equals the Euclidean distance between the sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean set distance as the optimal normalized affine separation gap.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance between C and D

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Pair Normal-Cone Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair is nearest exactly when its connecting displacement is an outward normal to the two sets with opposite orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and \((c_*,d_*)\in C\times D\). Then \((c_*,d_*)\) attains \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\) if and only if \[\langle d_*-c_*,c-c_*\rangle\le0\quad(c\in C),\qquad \langle d_*-c_*,d-d_*\rangle\ge0\quad(d\in D).\] Equivalently, \(d_*-c_*\in N_C(c_*)\) and \(c_*-d_*\in N_D(d_*)\), where \(N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((c_*,d_*)\) is a nearest pair if and only if \(d_*-c_*\in N_C(c_*)\) and \(c_*-d_*\in N_D(d_*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality certificate for a candidate nearest pair of convex sets.

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to C at the candidate nearest point

knowledge_statements.title: Displacement-Set Criterion for Distance Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearest pair exists exactly when the displacement set has a minimum-norm element; closedness of that set guarantees attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\), the distance \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\) is attained if and only if \(D-C\) contains an element of minimum norm. In particular, if \(D-C\) is closed, then some \(c_*\in C\) and \(d_*\in D\) satisfy \(\|d_*-c_*\|=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\) is attained iff \(D-C\) has a minimum-norm element; closedness of \(D-C\) implies attainment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nearest-pair existence criterion and a closed-displacement sufficient condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Attainment Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance between a nonempty compact set and a nonempty closed set is attained; if they are disjoint, the attained distance is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K,C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, with \(K\) compact and \(C\) closed. Then there exist \(k_*\in K\) and \(c_*\in C\) such that
\[
\|k_*-c_*\|=\operatorname{dist}(K,C).
\]
If additionally \(K\cap C=\varnothing\), then this attained distance is positive. Closedness of both sets alone does not generally guarantee attainment when neither set is compact, because minimizing pairs may escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(k_*\in K\) and \(c_*\in C\) with \(\|k_*-c_*\|=\operatorname{dist}(K,C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional distance attainment when one set is compact and the other closed.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Some Results on the Euclidean Distance to a Closed Set p. 73

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 3.2 Some Results on the Euclidean Distance to a Closed Set p. 73

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Margin Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sets at zero distance cannot have a positive uniform gap between two parallel separating hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\|u\|=1\), let \(\gamma(u)=\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle-\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), then \(\gamma(u)\le 0\) for every such \(u\). Consequently, there do not exist \(u\), \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) satisfying \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\|u\|=1}\gamma(u)\le 0\), so no positive-margin affine separation exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional zero-distance obstruction to positive-margin separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Touching-Closure Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open upper halfspace and the complementary closed lower halfspace are disjoint and weakly separable, but their touching closures prevent positive-margin separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\) and \(B=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\le0\}\). Then \(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty, convex, and disjoint, but \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\). They are weakly separated by \(y=0\), yet no affine separator has a positive uniform margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), so no positive-margin affine separator exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-set failure of positive-margin separation caused by finite touching of the closures.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Separation Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential epigraph and the horizontal axis are disjoint closed convex sets at zero distance and admit no positive-margin affine separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge e^x\}\) and \(B=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). These are nonempty, closed, convex, and disjoint sets satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\). There are no \(u\in\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), but no positive-margin affine separation exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed, asymptotically contacting configuration showing failure without positive distance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Distance and Asymptotic-Contact Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets with \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). Define \(D=A-B\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=\inf\{\|a-b\|:a\in A,b\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure boundary for positive-margin separation of disjoint convex sets, including nonclosed and asymptotically contacting configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pair \((A,B)\) lies on the strict-separation failure boundary when
\[0\in\operatorname{cl}(A-B).\]
Equivalently,
\[\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0,\]
or there exist sequences \(a_k\in A\), \(b_k\in B\) with \(\|a_k-b_k\|\to0\). At such a pair every unit directional gap satisfies
\[\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle-\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\leq0,\]
so no positive-margin separator exists. The boundary includes nonclosed point-set configurations \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) and disjoint unbounded closed convex sets having asymptotic contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two disjoint convex sets are on the failure boundary for strict separation when zero belongs to the closure of their difference set. This is equivalent to zero set distance and to the existence of point sequences, one from each set, whose mutual distance tends to zero. Every normalized functional gap is then nonpositive, so no hyperplane can leave a positive margin. Typical boundary configurations arise from a missing limit point of a nonclosed set or from unbounded sets approaching one another only at infinity.
assumptions_latex: Closure and distance are taken in the Euclidean ambient space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There are \(a_k\in A\), \(b_k\in B\) such that \(a_k-b_k\to0\).
The maximum normalized separation margin is nonpositive.
For point-set separation, the boundary condition is \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is nonclosed and \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), \(C\) and \(\{z\}\) are disjoint but not strongly separable.
Two unbounded closed convex sets may be disjoint while their difference is not closed and contains sequences converging to zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak or proper separation must replace strict separation at this boundary.
Compactness of either closed set rules out this failure configuration for disjoint sets.
boundary_notes: Zero distance is the failure boundary for positive margin, not necessarily for weak separation.
If the sets intersect, zero belongs to \(A-B\) itself; the definition here isolates the disjoint boundary case.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support, Contact, and Exposed-Face Geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set. For \(a\neq0\) and finite \(\sigma_C(a)\), put \(H_a=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support geometry, including ambient support, relative nontrivial support, and exposed contact faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A supporting hyperplane of \(C\) in direction \(a\neq0\) is
\[H_a=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\]
provided the support value is finite and attained:
\[F_C(a):=\{x\in C:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\neq\varnothing.\]
The set \(F_C(a)=C\cap H_a\) is the exposed face associated with \(a\). The support is at \(x\in C\) when \(x\in F_C(a)\), equivalently
\[\langle a,y-x\rangle\leq0\quad\forall y\in C.\]
If \(V=\operatorname{aff}C-ar x\), the support is nontrivial relative to \(C\) when \(P_Va\neq0\); otherwise the hyperplane contains the whole affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting hyperplane is a level set of a nonzero linear functional at an attained finite support value. Its contact set with a convex set is an exposed face. A support is said to occur at a point when the point maximizes the functional over the set, equivalently when the normal belongs to the point's normal cone. For a lower-dimensional set, support is nontrivial only when the normal has a nonzero component parallel to the set's affine hull.
assumptions_latex: The direction \(a\neq0\), and \(\sigma_C(a)\) is finite and attained for a contacting support.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A hyperplane supports \(C\) at \(x\) when \(C\subseteq\{y:\langle a,y\rangle\leq\langle a,x\rangle\}\).
The contact set is \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle a,y\rangle\).
Relative nontriviality is \(a\notin V^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: A singleton exposed face is an exposed point.
For a convex cone, support at the origin uses a linear hyperplane and a polar normal.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is convex.
Every boundary point of a nonempty convex set has an ambient supporting hyperplane; every relative-boundary point has a nontrivial relative support.
boundary_notes: A finite support value need not be attained on a nonclosed or unbounded set.
Not every face is exposed, so supporting hyperplanes do not enumerate all faces in general.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Half-Spaces, Supporting Hyperplanes, and Nontriviality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of geometric support for convex subsets of Euclidean space, including the normal-direction correspondence and the trivial-support boundary for lower-dimensional sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex, let b\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}, and define H^-_{b, eta}=\{x:\langle x,bangle\leq eta\} and H_{b, eta}=\{x:\langle x,bangle= eta\}. The half-space H^-_{b, eta} supports C if and only if C\subseteq H^-_{b, eta} and C\cap H_{b, eta}
eq\varnothing; its boundary H_{b, eta} is then a supporting hyperplane. If a\in C\cap H_{b, eta}, the chosen supporting orientation satisfies b\in N_C(a). The supporting hyperplane is nontrivial if and only if C
subseteq H_{b, eta}. When \operatorname{aff}C
eq\mathbb{R}^n, supporting hyperplanes containing all of C are trivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting half-space contains the convex set and has boundary contact with it, and its boundary is a supporting hyperplane. With the containing side oriented by its outward normal, a contact normal belongs to the normal cone. A support is nontrivial exactly when its hyperplane does not contain the whole set; lower-dimensional sets also admit trivial supports containing the entire set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H^-_{b,\beta}\text{ supports }C\iff C\subseteq H^-_{b,\beta}\text{ and }C\cap H_{b,\beta}\neq\varnothing;\qquad H_{b,\beta}\text{ is nontrivial}\iff C\nsubseteq H_{b,\beta}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Hyperplane and Tangent Half-Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness-based tangency for supporting hyperplanes of closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex and let \(x\in C\). A hyperplane \(H\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(x\) if and only if \(H\) is the unique supporting hyperplane to \(C\) at \(x\). A half-space \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) if and only if \(Q\) is a supporting half-space of \(C\) and \(\partial Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at some point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent hyperplane at a point is the unique supporting hyperplane there. A tangent half-space is a supporting half-space whose boundary is tangent at some contact point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(H\text{ tangent to }C\text{ at }x\iff H\text{ is the unique supporting hyperplane to }C\text{ at }x\bigr)\;\land\;\bigl(Q\text{ tangent to }C\iff Q\text{ supports }C\text{ and }\exists y\in C:\partial Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }y\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex, and let \varnothing\neq D\subseteq C be convex. There exists a nontrivial supporting hyperplane H of C with D\subseteq H if and only if D\cap\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing, where nontrivial means C\nsubseteq H.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A subgradient supports the corresponding sublevel set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting geometry of a convex function's sublevel set at a point possessing a subgradient; a genuine supporting hyperplane requires a nonzero subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be convex, let x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f, and let g\in\partial f(x_0). For \mathcal{L}_f(f(x_0)):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\le f(x_0)\}, one has \langle g,x-x_0\rangle\le 0 for every x\in\mathcal{L}_f(f(x_0)). Consequently, if g\neq0, the hyperplane \{x:\langle g,x-x_0\rangle=0\} supports \mathcal{L}_f(f(x_0)) at x_0; when g=0, the inequality remains valid but the displayed set is not a hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every subgradient at a point gives a support inequality for the sublevel set through that point. A nonzero subgradient defines a genuine supporting hyperplane; the zero subgradient yields only the degenerate inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathcal{L}_f(f(x_0)),\ \langle g,x-x_0\rangle\le0;\qquad g\neq0\implies\{x:\langle g,x-x_0\rangle=0\}\text{ supports }\mathcal{L}_f(f(x_0))\text{ at }x_0

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Point Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set admits a supporting hyperplane through that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a nonzero vector \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[\langle u,x\rangle\le\langle u,\bar x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Therefore the affine hyperplane \(H=\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\langle u,\bar x\rangle\}\) contains \(\bar x\), while \(C\) lies in the closed halfspace \(\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\le\langle u,\bar x\rangle\}\). Thus \(H\) supports \(C\) at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(u\ne0\) such that \(\langle u,x\rangle\le\langle u,\bar x\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean supporting-hyperplane theorem at an ordinary boundary point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Hyperplane at a Boundary Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(x\in C\). The normal cone is \(N_C(x)=\{a:\langle a,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ambient boundary support; a separate relative formulation is needed to exclude trivial supports for lower-dimensional sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hyperplane supports \(C\) at \(x\) when there exists \(a\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[H=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle a,y\rangle=\langle a,x\rangle\}\]
and
\[\langle a,y\rangle\leq\langle a,x\rangle\qquad\forall y\in C.\]
Thus boundary-point support is equivalent to the existence of a nonzero normal at the point. For every \(x\in\operatorname{bd}C\), such a supporting hyperplane exists. Its contact set is
\[F=C\cap H=\{y\in C:\langle a,y\rangle=\langle a,x\rangle\},\]
an exposed face containing \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting hyperplane at a point of a convex set has a nonzero normal whose linear functional is maximized over the set at that point. Equivalently, the normal belongs to the point's normal cone. Every ordinary boundary point of a nonempty convex set possesses such a support. The points sharing equality with the supporting level form an exposed face containing the supported point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Support at \(x\) is \(a\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\).
It is attainment of the support function: \(\sigma_C(a)=\langle a,x\rangle\).
It is the half-space containment \(C\subseteq\{y:\langle a,y-x\rangle\leq0\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is full-dimensional, a point admitting a nonzero normal cannot lie in \(\operatorname{int}C\).
For lower-dimensional \(C\), every point has normals orthogonal to \(\operatorname{aff}C\); nontrivial relative support requires a normal component parallel to that affine hull.
immediate_consequences_latex: The contact set of a boundary support is an exposed face.
A uniquely exposed contact point is an exposed point of \(C\).
boundary_notes: An ambient supporting hyperplane may contain all of a lower-dimensional convex set and therefore be trivial relative to it.
Relative-interior points have no nontrivial support within \(\operatorname{aff}C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-point support for a closed convex set in the source's finite-dimensional setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q$ be a closed convex set and let $x_0\in\operatorname{bd}Q$. Then there exist $g\ne0$ and $\gamma$ such that $$\langle g,x\rangle\le\gamma\quad\text{for all }x\in Q,\qquad \langle g,x_0\rangle=\gamma.$$ Equivalently, the supporting hyperplane $\mathcal H(g,\gamma)=\{x:\langle g,x\rangle=\gamma\}$ contains $x_0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every boundary point of a closed convex set lies on a supporting hyperplane of that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists g\ne0,\ \exists\gamma:\ \langle g,x\rangle\le\gamma\ \forall x\in Q\ \text{ and }\ \langle g,x_0\rangle=\gamma.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Convex Subgradient Supports the Corresponding Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The supporting inequality holds for every subgradient, including the zero vector; the usual supporting-hyperplane interpretation requires a nonzero subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be convex, let $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and let $g\in\partial f(x_0)$. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex subgradient at a point satisfies the outward-normal inequality for the sublevel set through that point. A nonzero subgradient therefore defines a supporting hyperplane there; a zero subgradient still satisfies the inequality but does not define a genuine hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Boundary Characterization by Nontrivial Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point of a convex set lies on its relative boundary exactly when a nonconstant functional on the affine hull supports the set there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\), \(V=L-L\), and \(x\in C\). Then \[x\in\operatorname{rbd}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists u\in V\setminus\{0\}:\ \langle u,z-x\rangle\le0\quad\forall z\in C.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) exactly when no affine functional nonconstant on \(L\) supports \(C\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization inside the effective affine ambient space; affine-hull-orthogonal normals are excluded.

notation.meaning: Direction space parallel to the affine hull
Relative interior and relative boundary in the affine hull

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Boundary Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relative-boundary point has a supporting hyperplane that is nontrivial within the set's affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\) and \(V=L-L\). There exists a nonzero vector \(u\in V\) such that \[\langle u,x\rangle\le\langle u,\bar x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] The set \(H_L=\{x\in L:\langle u,x\rangle=\langle u,\bar x\rangle\}\) is a proper affine hyperplane of \(L\) through \(\bar x\), and \(C\) is contained in one of its closed halfspaces relative to \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonconstant affine functional on \(\operatorname{aff}C\) supports \(C\) at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support is taken inside the effective affine ambient space.

notation.meaning: Direction space of the affine hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nontrivial support at a relative-boundary point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set. Its effective affine ambient space is \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\), its relative interior is \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and its relative boundary is \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex geometry; support is required to be nonconstant on the set, thereby excluding hyperplanes that merely contain the entire affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in C\) has relative-boundary support if there exist \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \(\langle u,y\rangle\leq\alpha\) for every \(y\in C\), \(\langle u,x\rangle=\alpha\), and the functional \(y\mapsto\langle u,y\rangle\) is not constant on \(C\). Equivalently, \(H=\{y:\langle u,y\rangle=\alpha\}\) is a nontrivial supporting hyperplane of \(C\) through \(x\). For convex \(C\), the points admitting such support are precisely \(C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point of a convex set has relative-boundary support when a linear functional, nonconstant on the set, attains its maximum there at that point. Thus the associated hyperplane supports the set without containing all of it. Exactly the points of the set lying on its relative boundary have this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists u,\alpha:\ \langle u,y\rangle\leq\alpha\ \forall y\in C,\ \langle u,x\rangle=\alpha,\ \langle u,\cdot\rangle\text{ is nonconstant on }C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exposed maximizer set \(F_u=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle\) is nonempty, contains \(x\), and is a proper subset of \(C\).
Relative to \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\), the restriction of \(u\) has a nonzero component in the direction space \(L-L\), and \(C\subseteq\{y\in L:\langle u,y\rangle\leq\langle u,x\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is full-dimensional, then \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\partial C\), so this is ordinary boundary-point support.
If \(C\) is a singleton, its relative boundary is empty and no nontrivial supporting functional exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every relative-boundary point of a non-singleton convex set lies in at least one proper exposed face.
No point of \(\operatorname{ri}C\) can maximize a linear functional that is nonconstant on \(C\).
boundary_notes: The condition differs from allowing any ambient supporting hyperplane: when \(C\) is lower-dimensional, a hyperplane containing \(\operatorname{aff}C\) is trivial and does not certify relative-boundary membership.
Closure of \(C\) is used in the definition of relative boundary; the supported point itself is required to belong to \(C\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed faces selected by support functionals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(u\in\mathbb R^n\). Write \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\), allowing the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial geometry. The definition covers empty and improper exposed faces by convention while distinguishing the proper faces cut out by nontrivial supporting hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The face exposed by \(u\) is \(F_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) when \(\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\), and \(F_C(u)=\varnothing\) otherwise. A subset \(F\subseteq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if \(F=F_C(u)\) for some \(u\). It is proper and nonempty precisely when the level hyperplane \(H(u,\sigma_C(u))\) is a nontrivial supporting hyperplane and \(F=C\cap H(u,\sigma_C(u))\). An exposed point is an exposed face consisting of one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed face is the set on which a linear functional attains its supremum over a convex set. A nonempty proper exposed face is exactly the intersection of the set with a nontrivial supporting hyperplane. A singleton exposed face is an exposed point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty proper \(F\), exposedness is equivalent to the existence of \(u\) and \(\alpha\) with \(C\subseteq\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\}\) and \(F=C\cap\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\alpha\}\).
The set \(F_C(u)\) is the contact set between \(C\) and the supporting hyperplane normal to \(u\).
special_cases_latex: For \(u=0\) and nonempty \(C\), one has \(F_C(0)=C\).
If \(F_C(u)=\{x\}\), then \(x\) is exposed and therefore extreme.
For a convex cone, a one-dimensional exposed face is an exposed ray.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is a face: if a relative-interior point of a segment in \(C\) lies in \(F_C(u)\), both endpoints lie in \(F_C(u)\).
Different normals may expose the same face.
boundary_notes: Not every face is exposed; exposedness requires selection by one linear functional.
If the support value is infinite, the chosen direction does not determine a supporting hyperplane or a nonempty contact face.

notation.meaning: face of C exposed by u

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Face Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling preserves a support face, and a nonempty finite intersection of support faces is selected by the sum of their directions; a proper intersection is a proper exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. For \(\alpha>0\), \(F_C(\alpha u)=F_C(u)\). If \(\sigma_C(u)\) and \(\sigma_C(v)\) are finite and attained and \(F_C(u)\cap F_C(v)\ne\varnothing\), then \[\sigma_C(u+v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_C(v),\qquad F_C(u+v)=F_C(u)\cap F_C(v).\] Iteration gives the analogous rule for any finite family with nonempty common intersection. If that intersection is proper, the summed functional is nonconstant on \(\operatorname{aff}C\), so the intersection is a proper exposed face.
assumptions_latex: The relevant support values are finite and attained.
The support faces in the addition rule have nonempty common intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(\alpha u)=F_C(u)\) for \(\alpha>0\), and \(F_C(u+v)=F_C(u)\cap F_C(v)\) under the stated common-contact condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling and finite-intersection rules for attained support faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Face Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The points where a nonzero supporting functional attains its finite maximum form the face cut out by the corresponding supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\) is finite and attained, the contact set \[F_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=C\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\] is a nonempty convex face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(u)=C\cap\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) is a nonempty face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of the contact set cut out by a supporting hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed-Face Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty proper subset is an exposed face when it is exactly the contact set of one supporting hyperplane, equivalently the maximizer set of a nonzero linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty proper subset \(F\subsetneq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}.\] Equivalently, \(F\) is exactly the intersection of \(C\) with a supporting hyperplane. Every exposed face is a face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exposed exactly when it is the maximizer set of a nonzero linear functional on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and immediate face property for proper exposed faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Exposing Directions of a Face
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directions exposing exactly a fixed exposed face form the relative interior of that face's normal cone; boundary normal directions may select a larger face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F\) be a nonempty proper exposed face. For \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), define \(N_C(F)=N_C(x)\). Then \[\{u\in\mathbb R^n:F_C(u)=F\}=\operatorname{ri}N_C(F).\] Thus relative-interior directions of the face normal cone expose exactly \(F\), while directions on its relative boundary may expose a strictly larger face.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F\) is a nonempty proper exposed face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All directions selecting a fixed nonempty proper exposed face, including lower-dimensional affine geometry.

notation.meaning: Normal cone associated with the relative interior of the face
Support face selected by direction u

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Direction Exposure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector exposes a point exactly when it belongs to that point's normal cone, and the points sharing that normal direction form its exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\) and \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[u\in N_C(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in F_C(u).\] In particular, for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[F_C(u)=\{x\in C:u\in N_C(x)\}.\] When \(u\ne0\) and this set is nonempty, it is the face exposed by the supporting direction \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in N_C(x)\) if and only if \(x\in F_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal cones encode exactly which directions expose a point or face.
